News.title: Hitler’s closest friends expose chilling truth of how monster charmed them before unleashing evil
News.content:
Fixing her with his penetrating blue eyes, he dropped to his knees and lay his head in her lap. To Helene Hanfstaengl he was a charming, charismatic young man. She was unaware that she was gazing into the face of pure evil. Helene recalls: “Oh, he could lay it on, he really could. I was sitting on the sofa and he sank to his knees, put his head in my lap and said, ‘Oh, if I only had someone to look after me.’ And I said, ‘Why don’t you find a lovely wife and marry?’”

Adolf Hitler’s reply was: “I can never marry because my life is dedicated to my country.’” This startling revelation comes in a new Channel 4 series, Dictator: The Hitler Interviews, which is available to watch and stream at 9pm on Saturday 1 August. The three-part series features archive footage from Hitler’s loyal supporters - put together as a documentary film for the first time.

Secrets of iconic red despatch box that links Andy Burnham with Angelina Jolie READ MORE :

Their interviews give a valuable insight into Hitler the man, and how he manipulated people into supporting his murderous plans. New York-born Helene Hanfstaengi was the wife of Ernst “Putzi” Hanfstaengl, a Harvard-educated German-American businessman, who became an early confidante, financial backer, and the foreign press chief for the Fuhrer. He played the piano to soothe the dictator and helped shape the early Nazi public image.

View 6 Images New York-born Helene Hanfstaengi was the wife of Ernst “Putzi” Hanfstaengl

‌



Putzi said of their first encounter, soon after Hitler became Nazi Party leader in 1921: “When I heard this man for the first time in a very noisy meeting, I absolutely felt myself irresistibly drawn to him.” Praising his gift for oratory, he added: “He crushed any man with his voice.”

Putzi’s memoir, Hitler: The Missing Years, claims the dictator was in love with his New York-born wife. Helene said: “In a way he was. I mean, in as far as he was able to be in love with anyone. “He had big blue eyes and he used them. And then he would have a terrifically Austrian way of hand-kissing… and so on.”

His unshakeable self-belief was also mesmerising. Helene says: “He was absolutely convinced about himself. He couldn’t stand anybody who wanted to talk. He was the one who talked, the others listened.”

By 1923, Hitler was ambitious to make the Nazis a powerful force. Like many Germans, defeat in the First World War had radicalised him. Someone who knew him differently was Elisabeth Popp. She’d been eight in May 1913, when an impoverished Austrian named Adolf Hitler rented a room in her family’s Munich flat. Because he spent his nights quietly reading and struggled for money, her father allowed him to stay without raising the rent.

‌



View 6 Images Elisabeth Popp, who knew Hitler before the war (Image: Supplied)

And, after Hitler rose to power and her father died, he provided financial assistance to the Popp family through royalties from Mein Kampf. Elisabeth said: “Losing the war shook him up. It was terrible. So many Germans had been so brave. And that made him harder.” Of embittered Hitler’s hatred for the Jews, she added: “This wasn’t just a political thing, it was something personal… It began as personal and then he built it up into a theory.”

Winifred Wagner, daughter-in-law of the German composer Richard Wagner, was once one of Hitler’s closest confidantes. She joined the Nazi Party in 1923 - the year she met Hitler - and, breaking her silence about him in 1975, she remained loyal to the dictator until her death in 1980, despite undergoing a denazification programme.

Winifred said of Hitler: “After the war we old Nazis invented a code name for him since we couldn’t talk about him in public. We called him U-S-A - ‘Unser Seliger Adolf’ Our Blessed Adolf. At the tribunal hearing, they thought I was crazy. I said, ‘What’s this got to do with politics?’ The bond between us was a special and private one based on our reverence and love for Richard Wagner.”

‌



Of her first meeting with Hitler, she said: “I must confess, he left a deep impression on me straight away. His personality and his eyes were compelling, very blue, large and expressive. He often dropped by on his way between Munich and Berlin. He took every opportunity to see us. Mostly he came here alone, and often I fetched him myself. I sat at the wheel with him next to me, which he found strange at first.

View 6 Images Winifred Wagner, who did not denounce Hitler by the time she died in 1980

"And he’d always shout, ‘Look out, woman driver!’ But sometimes he complimented me on my driving skills. He was simply…how shall I put it…a fascinating and interesting person.”

But Helene’s story is the most chilling. In November 1923, Hitler, Putzi and the Nazis tried to overthrow the left-wing government - staging a violent insurrection in a Munich beer hall. The revolt was put down, but Hitler became a wanted man.

‌



Nursing a broken collarbone, he fled to Putzi and Helene’s home, where she stopped him from shooting himself. Putzi said: “Police surrounded the whole house. The game was up and out comes the revolver. He said, ‘oh, I’ll be damned if I go and surrender, I’ll make it end’.”

Helene interjected: “I just went up and took it away from him, without any trouble at all. I shouted at him, I said, ‘what do you think you’re doing? After all, your ideas of saving the country and you take your life and leave all your workers behind? They’re looking for you to carry on.’”

View 6 Images Adolf Hitler of Germany pictured being greeted by Mrs. Winifred Wagner upon his arrival in Bayreuth (Image: Bettmann Archive)

Had he killed himself, the lives of 6 million Jews, slaughtered in the Holocaust, would have been spared. She and Pitzi thought by saving Hitler - who spent just nine months in jail for the attempted coup - they were saving Germany, Pitzi said: “I tried to save the man who appeared to me as the one saviour.”

‌



The couple were not alone. In July 1932, 13 million Germans voted for Hitler, who had campaigned on a promise to dismantle democracy and install himself as dictator. Meanwhile, during his prison spell, Winifred Wagner made sure he was looked after.

She said: “For Christmas, I organised a collection for him. The local Nazis brought their Christmas gifts here, I packed them up and sent them to Landsberg prison.” Hitler asked for writing paper. She continued: “I sent him heaps of writing paper. Now I’m accused of having supplied the paper for Mein Kampf! In other words, I’m indirectly to blame for Mein Kampf.”

Rather than stand trial for crimes including the Holocaust, the murder of Romani people, those with disabilities, the murder of Soviet civilians and the starvation and execution of Soviet prisoners of war - more than 50% died in captivity - Hitler died by suicide in April 1945.

View 6 Images Baldur von Schirach, who led the Hitler Youth and spent 20 years behind bars for crimes against humanity (Image: ullstein bild via Getty Images)

‌



Many top Nazi officials were prosecuted at the Nuremberg Trials. Baldur von Schirach, who led the Hitler Youth and spent 20 years behind bars for crimes against humanity, still saw Hitler as a twisted genius.

Describing him, he said: “A man without measure, a man with great gifts, a man who in some ways could be considered a genius. But because he had no sense of measure, he could not succeed. I do not know how else I could make a sort of summary of this fabulous monster.”

As dictators like Putin in Russia and King Jong Un in North Korea again take hold around the world, people should be mindful of Putzi’s warning from history. While Hitler was, at first, democratically elected, he said: “He starts his revolution and on it went. Not only was Hitler on the wrong train, he said: “It went faster and faster and faster, so nobody could jump off.”

*Dictator: The Hitler Interviews is available to watch and stream on Channel 4 at 9pm on Saturday 1 August.

‌

News.title: France wildfires live: 42C heatwave threatens nuclear plant after shock arrests
News.content:
A scorching heatwave threatens to force the closure of the Golfech nuclear power plant in south-west France just days after operations at the site resumed following a 17-day shutdown

A scorching heatwave threatens to worsen wildfires and force the closure of a nuclear power plant in south-west France just days after it came back online.

The Golfech nuclear power plant was shut down for 17 days after temperatures in the River Garonne, from which the plant draws water to cool its reactors, approached the regulatory limit of 28C. But France's latest heatwave - which will see temperatures in the region soar to 42C today - could force state-owned electricity company EDF to shut the plant down again.

Meanwhile, astonishing arrests have been made as firefighters continue to battle wildfires that have ravaged 42,000 hectares of south-west France and spread into parts of the Bordeaux metropolitan area. More than 220,000 people in the Gironde region have been evacuated over the past week in what has been France's largest peacetime evacuation.

But while many have sought refuge in evacuation centres, a handful of people have instead found themselves in police custody. A man was arrested after allegedly "posing" as a psychologist offering paid counselling sessions to those affected by the fires, French police told Sky News.

Two men were arrested several days ago on suspicion of "stealing food and supplies" intended for those affected by the wildfires, the broadcaster reported. Officers have been standing outside evacuation centres and fire-ravaged areas to keep people safe and ensure restricted zones are protected.

Although the regional prefecture said the wildfires remain "stabilised", with "several flare-ups" brought under control overnight, officials warned weather conditions remain "unfavourable" today.

News.title: Child in pushchair 'assaulted by woman' outside Sainsbury's supermarket
News.content:
Child in pushchair 'assaulted by woman' outside Sainsbury's supermarket

A 35-year-old woman has been arrested on suspicion of assault after she is alleged to have hit a child outside a Sainsbury's store in Lincolnshire

View Image The alleged incident took place at a Sainsbury's in Holland Market, Spalding (Image: Google Maps)

A woman has been arrested after she is alleged to have hit a child outside a Sainsbury's store in Lincolnshire.

‌



Police are investigating the incident, which took place at the store in Holland Market, Spalding on Monday.

‌



As well as the claims that the child was assaulted in a pushchair outside the Sainsbury's store, police also believe the youngster was sworn and shouted at inside the supermarket.

‌



A 35-year-old woman has been arrested on suspicion of assault and bailed while the investigation continues.

An appeal has been made by Lincolnshire Police, with the force urging anyone who saw or has information about the incident - which took place at around 3.30pm - to get in touch.

The force said: "A 35-year-old woman has been arrested on suspicion of assault after we received reports that a child had been hit while outside of a store in Spalding on Monday 27 July.

‌



"We are investigating an offence of assault and are appealing for information following reports of a child in a pushchair being assaulted outside of the Sainsbury's store, Holland Market, Spalding. We also believe the child was subjected to swearing and shouting inside the store as well.

"We would like to hear from anyone who was inside or outside the Sainsbury's store around 3.30pm on Monday 27 July and saw or heard anything they believe may be related to these reports.

"Safeguarding actions in relation to the child has been taken immediately. The woman has been bailed while our investigation continues.

‌



"As has happened in this case the police have been called, and we started our investigation as soon as we could.

"We have seen information being posted on social media and while we understand the concern, we must ask that people stop speculating and publishing information. This is because it can hinder our investigation and may taint witness evidence.

"It is vitally important that the criminal justice process is allowed to progress and that evidence given in a criminal investigation is evidence that has been seen or heard by the witness and not inadvertently affected by information they have seen elsewhere.

Article continues below

"Anyone who saw or heard anything they believe is connected to this incident is asked to contact the Investigating Officer by email at sabooha.richeux@lincs.police.uk. Incident 529 of 27 July."

News.title: Brit woman found dead and stuffed in suitcase inside abandoned Athens building
News.content:
Brit woman found dead and stuffed in suitcase inside abandoned Athens building

The body of a 38-year-old Scottish woman has been found stuffed inside a suitcase and dumped at a derelict building in Athens, Greece - a police probe is underway

View 2 Images The woman's body was found at a derelict building in Athens (Image: Google Maps)

A Scottish woman has been found dead inside a suitcase dumped at an abandoned building in Greece.

‌



The 38-year-old's remains were discovered by a homeless man in the Kypseli neighbourhood of Athens at around 1pm on July 18.

‌



The man is understood to have seen a human limb from outside the suitcase after noticing a foul smell at 7 Evelpidon Street - a derelict building which had been unoccupied for two years.

‌



The woman, thought to have been born in Scotland, had been dead for approximately eight days.

No visible wounds of any clear signs of struggle were found on the body, according to police.

Officers attended the scene and were unable to identify the woman because she had no identification on her.

‌



View 2 Images The woman was found in the Kypseli neighbourhood of Athens at around 1pm on July 18 (stock) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

The woman is believed to be around 5ft 4in tall with reddish hair tied in a bun and was dressed in a T-shirt and black shorts with a French university insignia on them.

An autopsy is due to be carried out in the coming days, reports the Daily Record.

‌



Greek authorities have called in Interpol and US investigators to assist with the probe.

On Monday, Interpol notified the Hellenic Police that DNA testing revealed that the body belonged to a British woman.

She is said to have travelled to Greece on June 29 via Cyprus after coming from the US. Her identity has still not been revealed by police.

‌



Officers are now speaking with anyone who may have come into contact with the woman before her death, as well as trying to find out her final movements.

No suspect has been identified at this time.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We are aware of the death of Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece.

Article continues below

"Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland."

The Mirror has contacted the UK Foreign Office for comment.

News.title: Andy Burnham speech recap: Emotional PM's THREE pledges to fix social care prioritised over assisted dying
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is outlining how he will fix the creaking social care sector in a major speech this morning, and even invited Kemi Badenoch and Ed Davey into cross-party talks

Andy Burnham today promised to fix the crisis-hit social care sector - and said a new dementia tsar would be appointed.

The new Prime Minister outlined three key parts to his strategy:

Bringing forward the deadline for a review into social care Reviewing pay and career progression for care workers Working cross-party to try and find some kind of consensus

He warned the creaking system can no longer be used as a political football while the NHS and families looking after loved ones count the cost.

He invited Tory chief Kemi Badenoch and Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey to urgent talks to discuss the problem governments have kicked into the long-grass for decades.

Ahead of his speech, Mr Burnham said: “Politicians might have different views but I’m serious about fixing this issue and to do that, we have to find common ground and listen to others to find a way forward.”

Thank you for following our live blog. It has now ended.

News.title: Dad 'with temper' downed 11 cans before leaving baby son blind and brain damaged
News.content:
Dad 'with temper' downed 11 cans before leaving baby son blind and brain damaged

Christopher Yates, of Morris Road, Swalwell, Gateshead, only called for an ambulance 'several' hours after the attack and lied to doctors about what had happened

View Image Christopher Yates drank 11 cans of lager and snorted one line of cocaine before he lost his temper and permanently injured his baby (Image: Chronicle Live)

A father left his baby blind and with catastrophic brain injuries as he lost his temper after drinking 11 cans of lager.

‌



Christopher Yates put his seven-month-old baby's life in danger when he shook him with so much force he caused the infant to suffer injuries similar to a high speed crash. The cruel attack was carried out as Yates was under the influence of alcohol and cocaine only three weeks and four days after the dad had gained custody of his son.

‌



Yates managed to get custody after finding out the baby was his son despite having known issues with alcohol. On the day of the attack in October last year, the baby woke up at 2am and was crying continuously.

‌



His dad then put him at arm's length and shook him forcefully five times, shouting "shut the f*** up". Yates then put the baby in his crib and went to the bathroom for an hour, wrapping a towel around his head to block out the sound of his son crying.

Dexter fan who became serial killer gets whole life order as police probe more deaths READ MORE :

He explained his behaviour was the result of frustration and desperation, Chronicle Live reports. Yates, of Morris Road, Swalwell, Gateshead, only took his son to hospital hours after the attack, lying to medical staff about what had happened and delaying adequate treatment as a result.

Newcastle Crown Court heard the baby was born in March last year and was placed with foster carers before Yates gained custody. At the time, it was said he had "the best of intentions but underestimated how difficult he would find it".

‌



During the assessment and settling period, Yates' family were aware the man had issues with alcohol as he was drinking in excess. Two weeks before the attack, they formed the view Yates was struggling to take care of the baby as he appeared angry and occasionally intoxicated.

The family didn't appreciate the full extent of the situation but did advise Yates to seek help from social services. Yates said he had expected more support from social services than he got once he had full and sole care at the beginning of September.

On one occasion, a family member visiting Yates found the baby had not been dressed, the home was in disarray, there were dirty nappies lying around and empty alcohol cans indicated the father was drinking heavily. Yates was also heard shouting angrily at his baby, which he referred to as a "little s***".

‌



When challenged about his drinking habits, Yates said "I can do whatever I want". Yates had been struggling with alcohol and drugs since he was a teenager and was known for his "explosive temper" when he was drunk.

He told his family he didn't think he could cope with taking care of his son and he might have to give him back. However, he didn't seek help from social services or the baby's foster parents.

In a victim impact statement, the child's foster mum said he was with them from birth and "melted our hearts". He is now back with the foster family.

‌



The mum said: "If we had known what we know now, we would never have let him go. [Yates] was the one person who should have loved and cared for him."

The woman added: "He suffered the most horrendous life-changing injuries at the hands of Christopher Yates. We didn't know if he was going to survive but he is a little fighter.

"He has lost his sight now and he will be on medication for the rest of his life. Christopher Yates has robbed this little boy of the life he should have had. He needed someone to look after him.

‌



"He has broken his brain, he has broken his life, he has broken everyone's hearts. All he had to do was phone us and we would have been straight there.

"[The baby's] dad, who was supposed to love and care for his every need, has caused these horrific injuries to his innocent little baby, who couldn't fight back. He has changed his life forever, and ours.

"He is our family, we love him and he is back where he is safe. We hope, one day, his sight may return. We promise we will never give up on [him]."

‌



On the day before the attack, the court heard that Yates had dropped the baby off with family members at the Metrocentre, asking them to look after the infant for longer than planned. He was under the influence of alcohol and had also taken cocaine when he later met up with them.

He returned home with the baby and called the ambulance service to say his baby was fitting at 8.15am the following day. Once at the hospital, Yates initially gave medics one account of the events before changing it to say the baby fell out of a rocking chair.

Once arrested, he admitted to being responsible for inflicting the a baby's injuries, saying he had consumed 11 cans of Foster's lager and snorted one line of cocaine. The full extent of the baby's potentially life-threatening injuries was only understood when a CT scan was carried out later, as the infant was initially treated for fits due to Yates' false account.

‌



It was then established the baby had suffered a bleed on the brain, was having seizures and had widespread haemorrhaging to both eyes. He also had bruises on his chin, a faint purple mark on the bridge of his nose, prominent blood vessels in both eyes and abrasions on his abdominal wall.

For a time, doctors were unsure if he would survive. As a result of the injuries, the baby was left with serious difficulties and his life expectancy is likely to be shortened.

Sentencing Yates, Judge Julie Clemitson said: "Only three weeks and four days after receiving [the baby] into your sole care, you admit, in the early hours of the morning, you lost control of your temper. You were under the influence of alcohol and cocaine, you'd had 11 cans of Foster's and a line of cocaine.

‌



"The episode of shaking is described as exacting the sort of force expected in a high velocity road accident. Yet it was several hours later you took him to hospital."

Judge Clemitson added: "Simply put, the effect of this offending has been catastrophic." Yates, who has eight previous convictions, pleaded guilty to causing a child to suffer serious physical harm in October last year and was jailed for four years.

Judge Clemitson said: "No sentence can undo any of the harm and distress to [the baby] and those who care about him. Their lives, and indeed yours, are changed irrevocably and forever.

‌



"[He] will never live the life he should have lived. He is consigned to a life of narrow horizons and a life of being reliant on carers.

"This sentence is not intended as a measure of the devastation that is done to his and [his foster parents'] lives. No sentence could ever be such a measure."

Rachel Hedworth, defending, explained Yates had been subjected to violence as a child and has mental health issues. She said: "He is unable to put into words how utterly sickened he is by his own behaviour.

Article continues below

"He was simply not equipped with the life skills to cope with the responsibilities of looking after a tiny baby. When asked by me why he didn't raise it with professionals that he couldn't cope with looking after the baby, he said he was terrified the baby would be taken from him.

"He didn't anticipate he would lose control in the way he did on that particular day. He is sad and sorry."

News.title: Scientists reverse autism-like traits in hours with one drug dose
News.content:
Scientists reverse autism-like traits in hours with one drug dose

The effect was seen within hours.

View Image Scientists have used a drug to reverse 'autism-like brain changes' within hours and said the results 'suggest the adult brain may be more adaptable than we assumed'

Scientists have used a drug to reverse 'autism-like brain changes' within hours. UCLA Health (a leading American hospital affiliated with the University of California, Los Angeles) says its new study "suggests that some autism-related brain changes may still be treatable in adulthood". However, it's important to note that the research was conducted on mice and that the effects of the drug are temporary.

‌



The study exposed mice to to inflammation during pregnancy and found that their offspring developed lasting autism-like brain and behaviour changes, "suggesting that early inflammation can disrupt brain development in ways that persist into adulthood".

‌



But a single dose of the drug rapamycin "rapidly improved several of those changes, including brain overactivity, seizure risk, sensory sensitivity, repetitive behaviours and abnormal brain functional network organization".

‌



UCLA Health said: "The findings suggest that some autism-related brain changes may still be treatable in adulthood, pointing to possible therapeutic approaches that target the underlying pathway rather than only symptoms. The effects of rapamycin are temporary, and repeated dosing loses efficacy, making rapamycin, itself, an unlikely candidate as a broadly-used treatment."

Scientists have previously said that even mild inflammation during mid-pregnancy has been shown to "result in offspring autism-like symptoms, abnormal brain growth, seizures and heightened sensitivity to everyday sensory input that persists into adulthood".

In the study published in the journal Nature Communications, UCLA researchers found that a single dose of the drug rapamycin given to the mice significantly improved brain signalling and behaviour symptoms in the offspring within about two hours, which they said was "a time too short to correct underlying physical brain changes created by the maternal inflammation".

‌



However the study authors stressed that they "do not identify rapamycin as a viable treatment for these symptoms in humans given its temporary effects and potential for toxicity from repeated doses". Instead, researchers said the drug’s effects "revealed new therapeutic targets for the development of future treatments".

Dr Harley Kornblum, the study's senior author, said: "It suggests the adult brain may be more adaptable than we assumed, even when the underlying structural changes from early development are still there. This points us toward the brain's functional circuitry, not just its physical structure, as a target for future treatment approaches."

Dr Janel Le Belle, an associate professor in the UCLA Department of Neurosurgery, added: "These results reframe how autism-associated symptoms might be treated. If the adult brain remains capable of functional normalisation, then some features of autism may be successfully addressed without needing to correct underlying structural differences."

‌



What is rapamycin?

Rapamycin is licensed and used in the UK. It is primarily used in specific cases like preventing organ rejection in transplant patients and to treat specific lung diseases. Related drugs are used for some targeted forms of cancer treatment. It is also being researched for its efficacy in helping longevity and chronic illnesses like ME.

What did the study do?

Researchers exposed pregnant mice to mild inflammation. Their offspring went on to develop "chronic brain and body-wide inflammation, mild brain overgrowth, overactive cell-signalling in the mTOR pathway, disorganised brain functional network connectivity and behaviours associated with autism".

When researchers gave the adult offspring a single dose of rapamycin, they found rapid improvement across nearly every measure: "neurons that had been firing abnormally calmed down, susceptibility to seizures dropped, brain regions that had been miscommunicating reorganised into more typical patterns and repetitive behaviours and sensory over-responsivity eased".

Article continues below

These changes occurred within roughly two hours. Researchers said that while previous studies have shown that offspring of mothers who experience inflammation while pregnant have a higher likelihood of developing "autism-associated traits" that continue into adulthood and that rapamycin has been previously shown in mouse studies to improve symptoms by suppressing an overactive pathway, it was less clear whether these brain changes could still be modifiable in adulthood.

What causes autism?

The National Autistic Society says evidence suggests autism may be genetic. It says: "Scientists have been attempting to identify which genes might be implicated in autism for some years. Autism is likely to have multiple genes responsible rather than a single gene. However, it is not caused by emotional deprivation or the way a person has been brought up. There is no link between autism and vaccines."

It also says that "the concept of a 'cure' is offensive for many autistic people and their families". It says "an intervention should never aim to 'treat autism'" but that there are "a range of interventions that can support autistic people in their daily lives."

News.title: Alex Jenkinson accused of threatening Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor faces new trial date
News.content:
Alex Jenkinson accused of threatening Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor faces new trial date

It is alleged Alex Jenkinson, 39, caused alarm or distress to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, at Marsh Farm on the Sandringham Estate

View 5 Images Alex Jenkinson had been due to go on trial at Westminster magistrates' court today (Image: Instagram)

A man accused of threatening Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor while he was out walking his dogs is now set to go on trial in December.

Alex Jenkinson, 39, allegedly caused alarm or distress to the royal, who reportedly fled to his car along with his security team during the incident, which took place while he was out walking his dogs near Marsh Farm, on the Sandringham Estate, in May. He had been due to stand trial over the alleged offence today at Westminster magistrates court, but a new date was set by Chief Magistrate Paul Goldspring.

The court heard Jenkinson is now set to go on trial on December 21, when Mr Mountbatten-Windsor is expected to give evidence via video-link from a location yet to be arranged. The defendant has been told he will not be allowed to personally question the former prince.

View 5 Images Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, previously known as Prince Andrew, arriving for the Requiem Mass service for the Duchess of Kent at Westminster Cathedral, central London, last September (Image: Jordan Pettitt/PA Wire)

The long-haired suspect previously appeared at Westminster magistrates court, via video link from King's Lynn Police Investigation Centre, in May, with his right arm in a sling. No details of the alleged offences were given during that hearing, which saw Jenkinson repeatedly rub his face and seem surprised when he saw on a screen that his case was being heard in London, exclaiming "Westminster?".

The hearing had originally been listed to be heard at Norwich magistrates court on the same day before being moved and then delayed until the afternoon. It came two days after police were called shortly after 7.30pm on May 6 to a report a man allegedly behaving in an intimidating manner in the village of Wolferton, where the King's brother has been living since earlier this year.

View 5 Images Alex Jenkinson was charged with two counts of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour to harass someone of cause alarm or distress (Image: Youtube)

Jenkinson was arrested before later being charged with two counts in relation to the incident, both of "using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour to harass someone or cause alarm or distress"; one against Mr Mountbatten-Windsor and another against a man called Stephen Terry on the same day.

The court charge sheet says he "used towards Stephen Terry threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause that person to believe that immediate unlawful violence would be used against him by any person, or to provoke the immediate use of unlawful violence by him whereby that person was likely to believe that such violence would be used, or it was likely that such violence would be provoked."

View 5 Images The alleged incident took place close to Andrew's home at Marsh Farm on the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk

He today pleaded not guilty to both vharges of "using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour to harass someone or cause alarm or distress". Jenkinson previously was handed an interim disqualification from driving after pleading guilty to a third charge - "failing to provide a specimen of blood in custody" - after officers suspected he had driven a vehicle on the same day.

As part of his bail conditions, Jenkinson was also told not to enter the county of Norfolk, not to contact Mr Mountbatten-Windsor directly or indirectly and not attend or attempt to attend any royal site, including the Sandringham Estate, Buckingham Palace, Balmoral, Windsor Castle and Highgrove.

View 5 Images Alex Jenkinson pleaded not guilty at a previous hearing in May (Image: Elizabeth Cook/PA Wire)

Chief Magistrate Paul Goldspring included measures naming Mr Mountbatten-Windsor by name, rather than imposing a ban on Jenkinson contacting members of the royal family in order to avoid any potential ambiguity about whether Mr Mountbatten-Windsor constitutionally remains a member.

Mr Mountbatten-Windsor has been living in the village of Wolferton since being forced to leave his former Royal Lodge residence in Windsor, which was surrounded by a ring of steel, due to his friendship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein

Article continues below

He lost his rights to state-funded police protection when he was stripped of his royal title in 2022 during a civil case with Epstein's late sex slave Virginia Giuffre, which he paid millions of pounds to settle, but admitted no wrongdoing in. Mr Mountbatten-Windsor, who has always denied any wrongdoing, has said he did not have sex with Ms Giuffre, who alleged she was trafficked to the UK by Epstein.

He was also stripped by the King of his right to be called a prince and his dukedom late last year over his links to Epstein and now pays for his own private security out of an allowance given to him by the King to meet his living expenses at Marsh Farm.

News.title: More than half of England in drought, Environment Agency declares
News.content:
Drought has been declared across more than half of England as hot, dry weather takes its toll on the country's water supplies.

The Environment Agency (EA) announcement covers much of central, eastern and southern England, and is a public sign that further restrictions on water use might follow.

It added that the impacts are already being felt, including low river flows, early harvests and high risk of wildfires. More than 20 million people are already under hosepipe bans.

North Wales and the Upper Severn river basin entered drought conditions last week, Natural Resources Wales said.

Scotland does not declare drought but monitors "water scarcity". Some parts of eastern Scotland are in the most extreme category of "significant scarcity", according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.

News.title: Burnham doesn't rule out tax rises to fix social care
News.content:
Asked about the threshold, Burnham said: "I think social care in England is as unfair as American healthcare. The vulnerable pay with everything and it can completely leave them with nothing.

"That floor has been in place for a long, long time and common sense says it cannot be fair."

Burnham said in "an ideal world" he would not want anyone to have to sell their home to pay for care, describing it as a "really awful process".

He added proposals he previously put forward were intended to stop that, saying: "If everybody on the NHS principle contributed a little, it would mean everybody could protect the majority of what they'd worked for."

Burnham said he did not know if people support that approach, adding this was for something for the consultation to consider.

On the cross-party talks, Burnham said there has been 22 failed attempts to make progress in almost 30 years.

The PM said: "We're going to have to find common ground here if this is to be a lasting solution."

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed said the first "constructive" discussion had left him feeling "hopeful" and more meetings will be required to find consensus.

He said: "Everyone will have to accept things we might not like in order to work together - but I think that's what the public want and expect us to do."

Sir Ed, who has a disabled son who needs round-the-clock care, said the system "just isn't working" and any solution must have family carers "at its heart".

Reform Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "Make no mistake, today Andy Burnham fired the starting gun on his scheme to raid the little money that hundreds of thousands of regular people have struggled to save over their lifetimes.

"That's why he can't rule out the new universal death tax."

Green Party social care spokesperson Ellie Chowns said: "If Andy Burnham is serious about doing things differently and tackling the crisis in care, he must work collaboratively with the Greens and other parties to do so."

News.title: Serial killer given whole life orders for murders of two men as police investigate four more deaths
News.content:
Serial killer James Desborough has been given two whole life prison sentences with no chance of parole - as police revealed they are looking into four unexplained deaths at the homeless shelter that housed him.

Desborough, already serving a minimum of 19 years for the murder of his prison cellmate, was given the whole life tariffs for killing 57-year-old Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman, 43, in Cornwall.

Aquilino and Coleman met Desborough at Newquay's Sandy Lodge homeless shelter, where police are now reviewing the unexplained deaths of two other men and two women.

Sentencing, Mr Justice Pushpinder Saini described Desborough as "a highly dangerous individual who had no regard for the life of those you think are worthless".

Desborough befriended the two vulnerable men and used "extreme violence" on both of them, before dismembering and concealing their bodies, the judge said.

He said the former builder used their bank cards and made journeys to give the impression they were still alive.

Their remains were discovered close to Desborough's woodland cabin near Sticker in Cornwall.

News.title: Boy, 7, dies in hospital after beach tragedy
News.content:
A seven-year-old boy has died in hospital after a beach tragedy that also killed his teenage cousin and her mother, his family has said.

Musa Ahmed was on a day trip to West Mersea, Essex, on 22 July, when he and five relatives got into difficulty in the water.

While he was pulled from the water and airlifted to hospital, Shelina Rahman, 41, and 15-year-old Sameeha, died at the scene.

Musa's family said he died "in a state of ease and peace" at the Royal London Hospital on Tuesday evening.

The family had travelled to the island, near Colchester, from Ilford in east London that morning.

Three others were also taken to hospital by ambulance after the incident, first reported to Essex Police at 17:35 BST, and were said by the force to be "recovering".

Musa's father, Shahin Ahmed, has said they were swept away by a "very strong" tide and police said they made "significant efforts to help each other".

News.title: Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan
News.content:
Uefa is not the only organisation unhappy with the situation.

Concacaf, which covers North and Central America and hosted this year's World Cup, said in a statement: "We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.

"We share the disappointment of many within our region and the game that this level of detail has been designed and shared publicly before any discussion with the relevant governance bodies and stakeholders has taken place.

"As leaders within football, we are the custodians of the game. Collectively, Fifa, the confederations and every member association have a responsibility to always act in the best interests of the sport."

The French Football Federation said: "It obviously raises many questions, particularly âsince we, the member federations, were not involved and we lack the specific information needed to weigh in on matters that are clearly fundamental to the future of football."

La Liga president Javier Tebas accused Infantino of trying to buy votes before the next Fifa Congress in March.

"It doesn't seem like a reform. It seems like an electoral campaign financed with the future of football," Tebas said.

"Development cannot be used to buy votes or silences. The competitions and commercial rights of Fifa are not the personal patrimony of Infantino.

"Whoever mixes politics, discipline, money and power without transparency cannot lead anything.

"Infantino is not the solution to Fifa's governance. He is the problem."

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said: "While the AFC recognises the importance of exploring innovative approaches that can strengthen the future of global football, initiatives of this scale and consequence must be founded upon the principles of good governance, transparency and meaningful consultation."

Hans-Joachim Watzke, vice-president of the German Football Association (DFB) and president of Borussia Dortmund, told Kicker magazine that Fifa's plans are an "absolute attack on football".

He said: "A line has been crossed here. If European football stands united against these plans, that carries a great deal of weight."

Infantino's predecessor Sepp Blatter said: "The close relationship between the Fifa president and the US president has reached a financial dimension that is deeply damaging football. No-one has the right to sell our game."

European Football Clubs (EFC), an organisation representing more than 850 clubs, said it would have been "appropriate" for Fifa to consult them on "a proposal of such magnitude".

It added: "We urge for calm and thorough consultation on all topics affecting the football ecosystem, together with more rigorous and transparent governance processes put in place to protect the game for the long term."

The Football Association of Wales (FAW) said it has "not yet received any substantial details from Fifa concerning the reported proposals" and that it "is concerned that such matters have become public prior to being shared with Fifa's member associations".

However, there was support for the plan from a Uefa member in the shape of Czech Republic FA president David Trunda.

He told Sky News he could "see the pragmatic benefits for Czech football".

"Of course we need more details but my personal point of view is that I can see the positive impact of Fifa's intentions," he said.

Global players' union Fifpro called on Fifa to "reconsider its proposal without further delay".

It said it had "noted with deep concern the proposal to transform the World Cup and other Fifa competitions into investable assets for private capital".

It said such a move "would fundamentally and irreversibly reshape the incentives underpinning the competitions" and that it was "particularly troubling that a project of this magnitude has been developed largely behind closed doors" when it had "potentially far-reaching implications for player welfare, the international match calendar and the future governance of the game".

News.title: BBC cancels Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live at the Apollo due to budget cuts
News.content:
Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live at the Apollo have been cancelled by the BBC, as the corporation makes further financial savings.

The main Mastermind series will continue, with Clive Myrie remaining as host, but the celebrity spin-off will end after the next series, which has already been filmed.

In a statement, the BBC said it was "incredibly proud of all three of these much-loved shows" and thanked the programmes' production teams.

"Unfortunately," it continued, "we have to make some really tough choices in light of our funding challenges, and these savings have been identified from the Entertainment genre."

Viewing figures for all three shows have fallen over recent years. Celebrity Mastermind has dropped from an average of 4m viewers in 2017, to 1.7m for its most recent series.

Blankety Blank, meanwhile, has gone down from 5.5m viewers in 2021 to 2.3m for the most recent series.

And Live at the Apollo has dropped from around 1.3m viewers in 2018 to around 660,000 on its most recent series. These figures include catch-up platforms such as iPlayer.

News.title: Prince Harry media battle legal bill expected to cost millions
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex and other high-profile claimants who lost their High Court privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail face a potential legal bill of millions of pounds.

The group - which includes Sir Elton John, Baroness Doreen Lawrence and Elizabeth Hurley - sued Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL) over claims of unlawful information gathering.

But earlier this month, all their claims were dismissed by Judge Mr Justice Nicklin following an 11-week trial.

At the High Court on Wednesday, the parties in the case began a two-day hearing to decide who will pay what legal costs for the mammoth trial.

In written submissions, lawyers for the Duke of Sussex and the other claimants described the costs incurred by the Daily Mail's publisher - almost Â£34.5m as of 9 July - as "eye watering".

They claimed that ANL had exceeded its approved costs by over Â£18.6m, and added the group was insured to cover some of the publisher's costs.

Nicholas Bacon KC for the claimants told the court the group took out insurance cover in the sum of Â£16.2m, and that ANL had "overspent what they'd told us they'd actually spent".

The total bill the claimants could face has not been decided.

But the "current level of cover would be insufficient to meet their total costs exposure, possibly to the tune of many millions of pounds.", the court was told.

ANL has argued the claimants should pay back full costs incurred by the publisher and has applied for the costs to be paid on an indemnity basis - a more favourable financial payout.

The publisher has argued the claimant's side acted unreasonably during the case - a conduct clause which could trigger indemnity cover.

In written submissions, lawyers for ANL said: "Where claims involve wide-ranging allegations of dishonesty and serious criminal conduct against named individuals, a focused, responsible and proper approach is required as the norm.

"The Claimants' conduct of this litigation wholly disregarded these key disciplines. In many cases this was in the face of repeated warnings by the court as to the proper approach to be taken."

News.title: Three ways that today's 20-somethings really do have it worse than their parents
News.content:
Young people in their 20s are facing a tougher start to adulthood than any generation in almost half a century, according to analysis of UK data on housing, employment and wealth, carried out for the BBC.

More than 40% of 25-year-olds are now living with their parents, their wages have stagnated and employment has fallen, show the figures which compare key metrics for different generations at age 25 stretching back to the early 1980s.

The findings are underscored by the experiences of young people themselves who, along with parents, have contacted BBC Your Voice about their circumstances, with many saying they were frustrated about being accused by older generations of not trying hard enough.

We asked the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) to gather and analyse government data, external, for the first time, to see if this generation really does have it worse.

The biggest change it found was where those in their 20s are living.

News.title: Teenage Norwegian 'hitman' guilty of UK murder plot
News.content:
A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for a Swedish organised crime group has been found guilty of conspiracy to murder.

An Old Bailey jury heard how Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025.

He pleaded guilty to possession of the firearms and ammunition but had denied the conspiracy charge.

Following a retrial, Natland showed no emotion as the jury brought in a unanimous guilty verdict after deliberating for just over 17 hours.

During the trial opening, prosecutor Alistair Richardson said the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

Natland had claimed rather than carry out the attack, he had planned to shoot himself in the foot, telling jurors he had found himself in "a major pickle".

The court heard how the Foxtrot Network had been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government.

The group is infamous for pioneering the relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS).

Natland flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March and was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden.

News.title: Fix palliative care before assisted dying debate, says PM
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that before assisted dying is considered in England and Wales, the funding of palliative and social care should be "fixed".

It is the first time Burnham has set out his position on the issue since becoming prime minister, as MPs prepare to debate it again when Parliament returns in September.

The government is likely to remain officially neutral, but Burnham's remarks suggest he personally will not back a bill being proposed by Labour MP Lauren Edwards.

The position is a shift from that of former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, who voted in favour of the previous attempt to legalise assisted dying and gave time for the issue to be debated in Parliament.

Sir Keir's support was privately cited by some Labour MPs as a reason they backed the bill last time.

Burnham told reporters: "I take the view that that debate - and I don't say that there shouldn't be a debate at some point about those issues - personally, I think there's something that needs to happen first.

"That is the fixing of the funding of palliative care and social care.

"I think it is very challenging to introduce that wider debate in a context of people not receiving that care and having the peace of mind about that care."

In 2025, MPs voted in favour of a bill proposed by Labour MP Kim Leadbeater to legalise assisted dying.

But the bill was not passed by the House of Lords, after an unprecedented number of suggested amendments delayed its progress until it ran out of time in April this year.

Its opponents argued it had substantial flaws that risked vulnerable people being pressured into ending their lives early.

The proposed law - known as the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill - would have allowed people over the age of 18 who were expected to die within six months to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

Labour MP Lauren Edwards plans to bring forward an identical bill in order to "finish the job" started by Leadbeater.

Following Burnham's comments, she said improving social care and legalising assisted dying was "not a case of either/or" and that the two things "can and must go hand in hand".

"The bill that has been before Parliament and thoroughly debated since October 2024 provides for a four-year implementation period - that means if my current bill becomes law next year, we would have until 2031 to fix the status quo that Andy Burnham rightly says is broken."

Jess Asato - a Labour MP and opponent of the bill - said MPs had "a responsibility to consider the safety of introducing such a flawed bill into a broken and failing care system".

"There can be no meaningful choice and no dignity at the end of life if we don't have a palliative care system that provides basic support for the vulnerable and an affordable social care system that gives everyone dignity at the end of their lives."

Burnham was asked about his views on assisted dying after he had announced plans to reform the social care system, with the view to create a national care service and to reach a political consensus on how to fund it.

In 2024, just before the first Commons vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill, Burnham told BBC Manchester he would "probably vote in favour of it" if he was in Parliament.

When he was previously an MP he abstained from a 2015 vote on another bill to legalise assisted dying because of concerns over safeguards and people feeling under pressure.

But he told the BBC in 2024 that he had had "family experience in the nine years since that has changed my view".

He said: "I think we do allow people to suffer and families to suffer too much."

He caveated his support as being for the principle of assisted dying and insisted he would want a requirement before any new law was implemented that hospices would be "properly funded and sorted out".

News.title: Man accused of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor threat faces December trial
News.content:
A man charged with threatening Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor near his home on the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk will stand trial in December.

Alex Jenkinson, 39, is accused of causing the former Duke of York to "fear unlawful violence" during an encounter as he walked his dogs on 6 May.

The trial - which will begin on 21 December - is expected to include evidence from Mountbatten-Windsor via videolink.

Jenkinson is accused of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour and had been due to stand trial on Wednesday. At Westminster Magistrates' Court, chief magistrate Paul Goldspring postponed proceedings over concerns about the defendant's mental health.

News.title: Body of Scottish woman found inside suitcase in Greece
News.content:
The body of a Scottish woman has been found inside a suitcase in an abandoned building in Greece, prompting a multi-agency investigation.

Police Scotland confirmed they are liaising with authorities after the woman was reportedly discovered by a homeless man in the Kypseli district in Athens last month.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, is thought to have travelled to Greece from Cyprus last month, state broadcaster ERT reports.

They said Interpol data had helped to identify the 38-year-old who is believed to have died between five and seven days before the discovery.

Greek police told BBC Scotland News the body of a British woman was found and fingerprint data from Interpol matched a woman born in 1988 and investigations are ongoing.

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) confirmed they are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We are aware of the death of Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece.

"Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland."

News.title: Chief constable resigns before misconduct tribunal
News.content:
The chief constable of Staffordshire Police has resigned, ahead of a gross misconduct hearing regarding his behaviour.

Chris Noble was suspended in August amid inquiries by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), with the watchdog confirming in March that it had opened two more investigations regarding his behaviour.

Noble resigned on Tuesday via a letter to the Police and Crime Commissioner for Staffordshire, Ben Adams.

The misconduct hearing began on Wednesday morning in Noble's absence and has since been adjourned.

He was chosen to lead Staffordshire Police after the retirement of the previous chief constable in 2021.

Prior to this, he was the assistant chief constable of Humberside Police.

In a statement, Staffordshire Commissioner for Police, Fire & Rescue and Crime, Ben Adams said: "I can confirm that yesterday [28 July], I received Chief Constable Chris Noble's resignation, which I have accepted with immediate effect.

"Becky Riggs will remain as Staffordshire Police's acting chief constable.

"The misconduct hearing will continue today as planned, under former officer provisions."

Staffordshire Police said that it would not be appropriate to comment due to ongoing misconduct proceedings.

In a recent statement, the IOPC said: "The chair of the panel has directed that no additional information relating to the detail of the allegations can be released at this time.

"We are continuing to investigate other allegations relating to Mr Noble. Given the sensitivity of those matters, for operational reasons, no further information can be provided at this time."

News.title: Pedestrian dies after being hit by several vehicles including police car
News.content:
A pedestrian has died after being hit by multiple vehicles including a police car.

Dyfed-Powys Police were called regarding concerns for the safety of a person seen on the A40 between the PC World roundabout and Abergwili roundabout, in Carmarthen, on Tuesday.

As officers reached the scene at about 21:50 BST, reports indicated several vehicles had crashed with the pedestrian, including a marked police car when it arrived.

The force described it as a "six-vehicle" crash.

No arrests have been made and the force has referred itself to the Independent Office of Police Conduct.

The force said inquiries to identify the pedestrian and next of kin were underway.

It added both carriageways of the road were likely to remain closed for a lengthy period of time while officers remained at the scene, and asked motorists to avoid the area.

Anyone with information is urged to contact Dyfed-Powys Police.

News.title: Woman accused of breaching Donaldson victims' anonymity
News.content:
A woman has been charged with breaching an anonymity order in relation to the victims of former DUP leader and convicted paedophile Jeffrey Donaldson.

Police said the 55-year-old was arrested in the Ballynahinch area on Tuesday.

She has been charged with a breach of a lifetime ban on reporting the identity of victims, and is due to appear before Downpatrick Magistrates' Court on 24 August.

Victims of sexual offences receive lifelong legal anonymity unless they waive their right to it.

Donaldson, who was an MP from 1997 until 2024, was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

He was told by the judge that the sentence would be a lengthy one.

It has since been confirmed he is to appeal his convictions.

News.title: Unauthorised airport car park grows despite stop notice
News.content:
Jane Fuller, from Hadleigh, Suffolk, said her daughter's car had been left unlocked for 22 hours in April.

"My daughter has an app on her phone and she managed to lock it from Croatia," she said.

"When we eventually got back to the car park, we had to hunt for it in the dark. We found it parked on top of rubble. It was a shocking experience," she added.

Deb Jordan, from Ely, Cambridgeshire, said the transport to the car park from the airport in May with her family had been "an absolute hazard".

She said passengers had been left stranded at Stansted Airport for more than three hours after landing.

"They piled two busloads of angry people onto one small transit minibus," she said.

"Luggage was piled on top of passengers. I had a pushchair wedged over my head."

On arrival at the car park, Jordan said the family had been given the keys to someone else's car.

Several customers said they had been charged an additional Â£20 on arrival at the car park to pay for transport to the Radisson Blu Hotel at Stansted Airport, from where they then had to walk to the airport.

They were also told to meet at the location at the airport on their return after ringing drivers at New Farm once they had landed.

Jurrien Timber has left Arsenal’s pre-season camp in Spain for a check-up on his long-standing groin injury.

Dutch defender Timber missed most of the final two months of last season due to the injury. He did make a substitute appearance in the Champions League final defeat to PSG, but then missed the World Cup.

Timber has now returned to London from Spain, though the BBC reports that it is part of his rehabilitation timeline and the 25-year-old has not suffered a fresh setback.

Timber played 30 Premier League games last year as the Gunners won their first title in 22 years. He also missed most of his first season, having signed from Ajax in 2023, due to an ACL injury.

Mikel Arteta has a few injury concerns with the new season just over three weeks away. Centre back William Saliba will be out for an extended period due to a back injury, while Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Noni Madueke look likely to miss the start of the campaign given their recent World Cup commitments.

In total, Arsenal had 15 players participating in the World Cup and after a lengthy 63-game campaign last season, the Gunners are not embarking on a big-scale pre-season tour this summer.

Arsenal’s first competitive clash is the Community Shield against Manchester City in Cardiff on 16 August before they host newly promoted Coventry City in the first match of the Premier League season on Friday 21 August.

Their first pre-season friendly is against Girona on Saturday. They also have matches against Real Betis, Borussia Dortmund and Como on their pre-season schedule.

News.title: Dexter fan serial killer handed two whole life orders for double murder
News.content:
For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Serial killer James Desborough has been given two whole-life orders for the murders of Claudio Aquilino, 57, and Daniel Coleman, 43, in Cornwall last year.

The former builder is already serving a life sentence for murdering his cellmate Steven Kempster, 65, at HMP Exeter, whom he killed while awaiting trial for these offences.

Passing sentence, Mr Justice Saini said Desborough would never be released.

“You are now aged 40. I cannot, of course, resentence you for the murder of Mr Kempster, but given you are already subject to a life sentence with a minimum term as I have specified, my concurrent sentences for the murder of Claudio and Daniel must reflect your overall criminality,” the judge said.

“Having seen and heard you give evidence, and considering the circumstances in which you murdered Mr Kempster, I am sure that you are a highly dangerous individual who has no regard for the lives of people who you think are worthless.

“You are a person who can kill in extreme violence, with no remorse or indeed reflection on your actions.”

open image in gallery Claudio Aquilino was murdered by Desborough ( Devon and Cornwall Police )

The killer and Aquilino and Coleman previously lived together at Sandy Lodge Hotel in Newquay, which housed homeless people and those suffering from addictions.

In light of the deaths of Aquilino and Coleman, police are reviewing the deaths of four others who lived there at the same time as Desborough.

Desborough lived at Sandy Lodge Hotel between December 2024 and April 2025, during which time two men and two women died unexpectedly.

Aquilino and Coleman, who both suffered from long-term addictions, had previously lived with Desborough at the homeless hostel, and the last time they were both seen alive was in his company.

open image in gallery Daniel Coleman was murdered and dismembered by James Desborough ( Devon and Cornwall Police )

After their disappearances, the powerfully built Desborough, who is 5ft 10in and weighs nearly 18st, went on to spend their money on drugs and alcohol, and claimed they had both left Cornwall.

Their bodies were dismembered in an area of Sticker Woods, near St Austell, where Desborough lived in a wooden cabin.

It was there that police discovered, deposited in a stream, 1,900 burned bone fragments from the body of Aquilino.

Parts of Coleman’s body, including his torso, legs and feet, were found in a shallow grave nearby. His genitals have never been found and deliberate removal could not be excluded.

Prosecutors said Desborough was jealous of Coleman because he had developed a sexual interest in his friend’s ex-wife, Hannah Creswell.

open image in gallery The cabin where James Desborough lived ( Devon and Cornwall Police )

Desborough told a forensic biologist who was searching the woods for Coleman’s body that he “particularly enjoyed the dismemberment scenes” in the television series Dexter.

Police found several handwritten notes inside Desborough’s cabin, including one headed: “Bug out list” and another: “Hostiles.”

He had also made plans to leave the UK before he was arrested.

The father-of-one denied both murders and told the jury it was a “series of unfortunate circumstances” that the two men died on his land within a short space of time.

He accepted then spending their money on beer and drugs, but told jurors: “They were friends, I got on well with them.”

On Tuesday a jury at Winchester Crown Court found Desborough guilty of murdering Aquilino and Coleman following a five-week trial.

Desborough, of Old Oak Woods, Lower Sticker, Cornwall, had previously pleaded guilty to preventing the lawful burial of the two men’s bodies.

News.content:

Some people swear by a cool flannel. Others pop their pillow cases in the freezer. And more still are spending hundreds of pounds on portable air conditioning units. But there’s one method to help you cool down and sleep during this relentless summer of heatwaves that is so counterintuitive you’ve likely not tried it yet. How about a hot bath before bed?

Yes, it may sound mad. Surely an icy shower would be a better way of cooling off before hitting the sack? The answer to that question is a resounding “no”, according to science. Even though it might feel nice at the time, “if the water is too cold, the skin blood vessels constrict, preventing dissipation of heat from the skin and delaying cooling,” says GP Dr Deborah Lee.

Essentially, a cold shower is tricking your body into thinking it doesn’t need to use the mechanisms it has at its disposal to cool your core temperature – it thinks it has to conserve heat instead.

open image in gallery Shock: A cold shower isn’t the best way of cooling down in the heat ( Getty/iStock )

By contrast, though having a warm bath will slightly raise your body temperature, it causes the blood vessels to dilate so that they’re closer to the surface of the skin, better able to radiate out and get rid of excess heat.

In its advice on how to sleep well when it’s hot, Bupa recommends having “a hot or lukewarm bath (not cold). Your body temperature will go down when you get out of the bath; this will help you to sleep.”

This cooling down process is not just welcome to make us more comfortable when the mercury rises – it also promotes sleepiness, making it easier to drop off.

As your body cools, that drop in temperature helps stimulate the release of melatonin from the brain

“Immersing yourself in a warm bath temporarily raises your core body temperature,” says Dr Tom Cullen, a senior lecturer in high-performance physiology at the University of Hull. “The important part happens when you get out. As your body cools, that drop in temperature helps stimulate the release of melatonin from the brain. Melatonin is the hormone that promotes sleepiness, and under normal circumstances it's released in the evening as body temperature naturally declines.”

Having a bath mimics this natural temperature reduction and aids the temperature regulation process, leading to improved sleep. Researchers have dubbed the phenomenon, for obvious reasons, the “warm bath effect”, according to the Sleep Foundation.

In a recent survey of 2,000 UK adults conducted on behalf of Drench, over half (52 per cent) of respondents had experienced this effect first-hand, reporting that having a warm bath before bed improved their sleep quality.

38C - 40C The optimal temperature for your hot bath, according to research

One separate meta-analysis of 17 scientific studies discovered that taking a warm evening bath or shower improved self-reported sleep quality and sleep efficiency – the percentage of time you actually spend asleep while in bed. It also found that immersing oneself before bed resulted in a “significant shortening” of sleep onset latency – the exact amount of time it takes to transition from full wakefulness to the first stage of sleep. In other words, participants fell asleep much faster after taking a bath. The researchers hypothesised that warm water stimulates blood flow to the hands and feet, which allows body heat to escape more quickly.

Timing and temperature are crucial in all this, though. Just as freezing water is not conducive to sleep in a heatwave, so a scalding tub could do more harm than good. The research has flagged that between 38C and 40C is a good temperature – warm enough to feel comfortable, but not so hot that your heart rate is significantly raised or you start to sweat heavily.

open image in gallery It might not look appetising, but it works – just make sure you time it right ( Getty/iStock )

The optimal time to hop in the tub, meanwhile, is one to two hours before bed: “You need to leave enough time to allow the body to cool afterwards, reinforcing the signals that tell the brain it's time to prepare for sleep,” says Dr Cullen.

And, though wiling away several hours in the tub with a book and scented candles might be presented as the epitome of “wellness”, shorter is better for the purposes of sleep; 15 to 20 minutes is ideal.

Finally, throw some good sleep hygiene into the mix. Swerve that bathtime glass of wine – it will likely hinder, rather than help, sleep – and no doomscrolling during or after if you want to avoid an overstimulated brain.

From his vineyards in Bordeaux wine country, Edouard le Grix de la Salle can sometimes smell the burning forests far away. The smoke brings a whiff of hardship for the region's economic fortunes.

Wildfires that have burned an area four times the size of Paris and driven 220,000 people from homes and some of the region's tourist attractions promise to sting France's already squeezed economy.

“It’s a physical apocalypse when you see all these sites where there’s nothing left aside from burnt homes and forests, and then there’s the economic apocalypse,” said Patrick Seguin, president of the regional chamber of commerce, his voice choking with emotion in a phone interview.

It's “going to be a stab in the back for what remains of our economy.”

Le Grix de la Salle is among entrepreneurs bracing for pain. French government appeals for people to avoid the region are causing consternation.

“It’s incredible that they’ve said such a thing, especially when wine tourism is becoming more and more important,” Le Grix de la Salle said.

Bordeaux’s legendary wine has seen consumption plunge as young people turn to other beverages and competition from vineyards abroad has grown. U.S. President Donald Trump ’s tariffs have given winemakers — and much of the global economy — an added hangover.

“The wine business has been in crisis for several years now and it’s worsening with the geopolitical problems, the now widespread problems of inflation and the fact that wine is falling out of fashion among younger people,” Le Grix de la Salle said.

“Tourism was really the only dynamic part of the business that was still growing, both for us and, more generally, for Bordeaux wines,” he said. “And now this comes along as a brake.”

His family's Grand Verdus wine estate is roughly 35 kilometers (20 miles) from the fires that have raged since last week on the other side of the Garonne River that runs through Bordeaux. Bordeaux's Gironde region is mainland France’s largest by area and the fires have hit only a small percentage of it. But the mark on its reputation is sizable.

“How did they not think about protecting that sector? And the cultural sector, too. There’s so much to visit in Bordeaux. There are so many museums, there are châteaux. It’s unbelievable,” Le Grix de la Salle said.

The region in southwest France is replete with vacation spots for tourists lured by soft-sand beaches, winemaking châteaux, some of France's largest pine forests and the historic city of Bordeaux, a UNESCO World Heritage site. The oyster-rich Arcachon Bay draws foodies. But the fire and evacuations have emptied some prime spots.

The chamber of commerce says 39,000 businesses have been affected in the region that's a hub of defense and aerospace industries, including Airbus, Dassault and Thales.

Even before the fires, the chamber of commerce said rising energy costs were squeezing profits. Some 94% of businesses responding to a poll of regional enterprises in mid-July said they face difficulties.

“We’re getting more and more calls from heads of small- and medium-sized businesses, tiny businesses and craft businesses that are calling for help and saying, ‘What am I going to do tomorrow?’” Seguin said.

Two commercial courts in the cities of Bordeaux and Libourne reported a 37% increase in business liquidations from June 2025 to the same month this year, he noted.

Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said some restaurateurs told him that reservations have plummeted. He is pushing back against other officials' pleas that people avoid the region. He repeatedly has noted that the city hasn't been evacuated and isn't closed for business.

“The museums are open, the cafes and restaurants are open,” he said. “Life also goes on in our beautiful city.”

___

Keaten reported from Lyon, France, and Leicester reported from Paris.
