On Wednesday morning, an FA spokeswoman added: "We were completely unaware of this proposal and have no substantive details, including what the proposition actually is, and what conditions are attached.

"Based on the limited information, we are deeply concerned about the lack of process and governance to get to this point, and the apparent substance and principles involved.

"When the proposal is shared in the full and transparent way now promised by FIFA, we will make our views clear, and comment further."

The Football Association of Wales (FAW) later said it had "not yet received any substantial details from FIFA concerning the reported proposals.

"Consequently, the FAW is concerned that such matters have become public prior to being shared with FIFA's Member Associations. We await receipt of FIFA's full proposal before commenting further on this matter."

An Irish FA spokesperson said: "Like others, we have yet to receive any meaningful detail on these proposals. From what we have seen so far, we have questions about both the way it has emerged and the issues it raises.

"Once FIFA provides the full proposal, as it has indicated it will, we will review it carefully before commenting further."

'None of us are the owners of football'

Relations between UEFA and FIFA were already under severe strain, with UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin not attending the World Cup final in protest at a series of FIFA governance issues, including its handling of the Folarin Balogun case.

But the way the plans emerged, as well as the proposal itself, provoked fresh fury on Tuesday, with FIFA not raising the landmark strategy during meetings with football associations in New York on the eve of the World Cup final.

It is understood the FA was completely unaware of the plans - first reported in the Financial Times and The Times. Sky Sports News has contacted the Scottish FA for comment.

UEFA said in a statement after those reports emerged that the "soul and governance of football are not assets to trade".

"This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross. UEFA takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association.

"So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game.

"The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade - especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA's to sell."

UEFA added: "Having held discussions with many stakeholders across the game, UEFA knows there is significant and growing opposition to FIFA's scheme. FIFA cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends. We can grow the game correctly. It's time to prioritise associations, clubs, leagues, players and fans."

LaLiga president Javier Tebas said: "FIFA's competitions and commercial rights are not (FIFA President Gianni) Infantino's ⁠personal property. Anyone who mixes politics, discipline, money and power without transparency is not fit to lead anything. Infantino is not the solution to FIFA's governance problems."

Glenn Micallef, the European Commissioner for Intergenerational Fairness, Youth, Culture and Sport, said: "This isn't baseball. The FIFA World Cup remains the greatest sporting tournament on ​the planet, despite FIFA exploiting every commercial opportunity.

"But enough is enough. The relentless commercialisation of football has become corrosive. It's threatening the things that made football the world's ⁠most popular sport."

'Remarkable commercial value' in football - FIFA explains proposal

FIFA later moved to clarify the proposed new structure, with a spokesperson saying it was beginning a consultation process after receiving a proposal that is currently under review.

FIFA confirmed to Sky Sports News that JP Morgan is acting as financial advisor on the project, with Thrive Capital - whose chief executive is Josh Kushner, brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared - expected to lead the proposed investor group.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gianni Infantino labels the 2026 World Cup as the greatest of all time

FIFA insists it would retain sole control over football governance, competitions, the international match calendar and all sporting and regulatory decisions, with any outside investment in a FIFA subsidiary rather than FIFA itself.

Infantino said the proposal would help "democratise football worldwide" and ensure more of the game's commercial success is reinvested into development projects around the globe.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol looks back at the World Cup and debates whether or not it will be regarded as a success

"Football is the world's most popular sport and an extraordinary engine of human and social development," said Infantino.

"Parts of the game have turned that popularity into remarkable commercial value - and we celebrate that success and want it to continue, because it lifts the whole game ... our next stage of growth needs a structure built for it, one where the commercial side of the game operates as a focused, dedicated business, with its value shared more and better all around the world."

The governing body also dismissed suggestions that Infantino could become chief executive of the new entity when his final term as president ends, saying such a move has "never been discussed".

But FIFA said both the president and the administration would need to play leading roles in any new entity to ensure FIFA retains control of any subsidiary in line with its statutes and regulations and for the benefit of member associations.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player How many goals, red cards and penalties? Take a look at the World Cup in 2026 in numbers

FIFA is a not-for-profit organisation owned by the 211 associations that make up its membership. As an association of associations, it enjoys a tax-free status in Switzerland where it is based.

Its revenue for the 2022-26 cycle is expected to be $15bn (£11.26bn), the majority of which comes from TV rights, sponsorship and ticket and hospitality sales from the men's World Cup this summer.

The next World Cup is the women's tournament in Brazil next year.

What happens to Infantino if plans collapse?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports correspondent Kavel Solhekol breaks down Gianni Infantino's latest plans after the World Cup.

Latest from Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol:

"It’s shocking how nothing is shocking any more. I should be surprised, but I’m not surprised at all. I’ve just come back from the World Cup. According to FIFA, it was the most successful World Cup ever. They made more money than they know what to do with. Fans were paying outrageous prices for tickets.

"Gianni Infantino and those close to him have looked at this and said ‘this is the future.’ One way to make sure you have more tournaments like the one you’ve just had, is to set up a subsidiary of FIFA that will look after FIFA’s tournaments and to invite private investors to invest in that company.

"In the short term, there’s going to be a big pot of money potentially available for the 211 member associations of FIFA. The big question is, are they going to accept what Infantino is proposing? What happens to Infantino if these plans collapse? Are we seeing a tipping point on the horizon where a lot of people in football are saying they don’t like the way Infantino has been running football?

"I think there is such a groundswell of opposition to these plans that if I had to put money on it, I think they won’t succeed. It reminds me of what happened to the European Super League where plans came out, there was outrage and pretty quickly the plans didn’t come to fruition.

"Infantino knows everyone has got a price. FIFA have written to all 211 member associations and have said you have until September 19 to accept this plan. If you do, there is going to be a pot of £7.5bn for us to share. If you don’t, that pot will drop from £7.5bn to £2bn. How many of these member associations are going to turn down that money?"

Sports.title: F1 season to end in Europe if Middle East unable to host final rounds
Sports.content:
The 2026 Formula 1 season will end in Europe in the event the final two scheduled races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi need to be relocated because of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, F1 president Stefano Domenicali has confirmed.

The sport's bosses were previously forced to cancel April races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, and announced over the weekend that the Bahrain Grand Prix will now be hosted by Malaysia in October.

Bahrain's inability to host the event in October has raised doubts over whether the final two rounds of the season - in Qatar (Nov 27-29) and Abu Dhabi (Dec 4-6) - will be able to go ahead in their planned locations.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Domenicali insisted he is still hopeful of the calendar remaining as it currently stands, and that F1 will wait until its mid-September deadline before making a decision.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Formula 1 has added Malaysia to its 2026 schedule to host the Bahrain Grand Prix that was postponed earlier in the season

"With regard to the end of the season, we are in touch with all the other championships," Domenicali said. "And I know that, for example, WEC (World Endurance Championship) has announced that they will not go at the end of the year in the Middle East and they will stay in Europe.

"The way that we are structured is that we will take the maximum time for us to see how the situation will develop, and we will take the decision at the right time. That moment would be not before the middle of September.

"For us, today, the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are confirmed. But, of course, if the situation will not be clearer, the way that we believe it should be, before the middle of September, we will take the decision."

Formula 1 2026 remaining races Netherlands* August 21-23 USA October 23-25 Italy September 4-6 Mexico Oct 30-Nov 1 Madrid September 11-13 Brazil November 6-8 Azerbaijan September 24-26 Las Vegas November 20-22 Malaysia October 2-4 Qatar November 27-29 Singapore* October 9-11 Abu Dhabi December 4-6 *denotes Sprint weekend

Domenicali explained that the challenges of "Brexit-connected documentation" make Europe the only alternative venue for the final two races, but says there are multiple options within the continent.

"I just want to confirm to you that if this [races in the Middle East] will not be possible, the end of the season will be in Europe, because we cannot go in other places," he said.

"There are some possibilities on the table, but I don't think it's right to make some promises or anticipate certain things, but that's the situation of today.

"Even if I really hope that it will not be the case, if the situation will not allow for us to be there, we're going to finish the championship in Europe."

Imola 'an option' | Second Las Vegas race was considered

There has been speculation that Italy's historic Imola circuit is the front-runner to host if needed, but Domenicali said the track is "an option, but is not defined" as a would-be replacement venue.

It remains possible that Imola and another venue could act as replacement hosts, with Formula 1 keen to get as close to the originally planned 24-round schedule as possible. As it stands, the calendar has been reduced to 23 races with the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix lost.

Racing in Europe in late November or early December would come with the risk of cold weather, but Domenicali pointed out that expected temperatures are actually colder for the Las Vegas Grand Prix earlier in November than they are in Europe at that time of year.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the 2025 Emilia Romagna Grand Prix from Imola

The Italian revealed holding a second race in Las Vegas had been considered but overlooked given the risk of undervaluing the event and going up against the hugely popular NFL.

He said: "The fascinating side is that if I look at the statistics of the temperature in Europe in that time, it is less cool than Las Vegas' average temperature while we are racing.

"It's definitely something that no one knows where the temperature will go and what the weather will be like. I think that actually we see in this situation of how the pollution of the climate change is happening. There's no certainty or anything about that.

"There was a possibility of having two races in Las Vegas, but we don't want to ruin a jewel that is growing by undervaluing what we are doing there.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Anthony Davidson and Jenson Button talk you through the Las Vegas Grand Prix Strip Circuit

"And of course, we don't have to forget that in that period of the year, we are fighting in the US against NFL. That is a major sport that is, I don't want to say detracting, but a lot of fans are watching that, so we need to avoid any kind of situation that would put us in front of something that of course is quite still very big in the US."

Any further changes to the calendar could have implications on the title race, which Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli currently leads by 50 points from Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, with 12 scheduled rounds remaining.

Sports.title: Welbeck to have medical as Chelsea set to pay first fee for over-26 since 2022
Sports.content:
Chelsea have agreed an undisclosed fee with Brighton for Danny Welbeck.

The 35-year-old has been given permission to undergo a medical in the next 24 hours ahead of his imminent move to Stamford Bridge.

Chelsea have turned to Welbeck as they look to add experience to manager Xabi Alonso's squad.

The last time the west London club paid a transfer fee for a player over the age of 26 was four years ago, when they signed Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang from Barcelona.

Image: Welbeck is set for a medical ahead of a move to Chelsea

It has been two years since Chelsea selected a player over the age of 30 in any game.

Sky Sports News reported earlier this week that initial positive talks had been held regarding a move for Welbeck who has one-year left on his contract at Brighton.

Welbeck has continued to be a reliable goalscorer in the Premier League at 35 years old. Last season he scored 13 times, after scoring 10 in the previous campaign.

His potential arrival would be another example of Chelsea prioritising physically imposing players with Premier League experience this summer.

They have already signed Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa for £117m - a record fee for a British player - and are close to bringing in Crystal Palace defender Maxence Lacroix.

It would also place further doubt on the futures of strikers Nicolas Jackson, Liam Delap and Marc Guiu.

Chelsea have signed several players from Brighton in recent seasons including their main striker Joao Pedro, plus Moises Caicedo, Marc Cucurella and Robert Sanchez.

A number of Brighton staff members have also moved to Stamford Bridge over the past four years, including sporting directors Paul Winstanley and Sam Jewell.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jay Bothroyd discusses why Jordan Henderson and Welbeck would be good signings for Chelsea and will add the experience the team has been needing

Neville backs Chelsea decision to sign PL experience

Gary Neville has said signing players like Welbeck and Jordan Henderson is exactly what Chelsea's young players need in order to gain more guidance.

The former Premier League-winning captain insists the decision to bring the veterans in is not a "magical" one, but rather an example of what all top teams need to compete.

"If you watched Chelsea for the last three, four or five years you'd say there's inexperience right throughout the football club," he said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Gary Neville says Chelsea have been crying out for Premier League experience in their squad, backing any decision to sign the likes of Welbeck and Henderson

"I think putting a spine in of good, senior professionals who act as guardians of good behaviour, responsibility and discipline in the dressing room is something that's not magic. It's something all top teams have had for many decades.

"Putting in Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck who know how to win Premier League titles, their jobs will be as much off the pitch as it will be on it. They're still good players who can contribute 25-35 games a season, but they will make sure the young players turn up every single day and give their all.

"I didn't think the young players at Chelsea have any real leadership or guidance on and off the pitch. They've now got people who can do that."

BlueCo's drastic change in transfer policy

Analysis from Sky Sports' Callum Bishop:

The BlueCo era at Chelsea has been defined by hoarding some of the best young talent on the planet and developing them in-house. That method has had some successes, but overall, it has not panned out.

Image: Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang was the last player over the age of 26 who Chelsea paid a transfer fee for

There is clearly some recognition and accountability from the top brass about that. In bringing in Alonso as manager, they know they have lucked out in getting one of the most highly-sought-after tacticians in the game. The Spaniard has clearly identified the need for experience and the club are following his lead.

The interest in Granit Xhaka earlier in the summer was among the first signs of the shift. Even making a move for Lacroix is evidence of a change in approach.

The Welbeck move is surprising, but there is some logic that can be applied to it. Is he going to start every week? No. However, Chelsea's four senior strikers have an average age of just 23. Combined, they have made 269 Premier League appearances and scored 74 goals.

Image: Thiago Silva was the last player over the age of 30 to play for Chelsea

The Brighton veteran has 400 appearances and 90 goals on his own. To have that as your back-up to the young guns you want to develop makes sense.

Henderson? That's a complete 180 degree turn. Caicedo and Enzo Fernandez are two of the more experienced players Alonso has. If you had to pick anywhere Chelsea needed a wise head, you would not say midfield.

Yet, they wanted Xhaka. They now want Henderson. Alonso may have been the man to oversee the blossoming of players like Florian Wirtz at Bayer Leverkusen. However, he clearly sees the values of opposite characters and knows Chelsea, and perhaps more importantly, he needs people ready now.

Sports.title: Langer hints at interest in England Test job
Sports.content:
Justin Langer says he hasn't heard from anyone at the ECB over the vacant England Test head coach role which he has been linked with, but the Australian hinted at being interested.

Speaking on the Stick to Cricket podcast, the former Australia head coach labelled that job, as well as India and England as the biggest in the sport, adding: "It's a career and everyone looks at all opportunities."

Brendon McCullum was removed as England's Test head coach earlier this month after a run of seven defeats in nine, while the early favourite to replace him, Andy Flower, turned down the role citing his current coaching commitments with Royal Challengers Bengaluru in the IPL and London Spirit in The Hundred.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking to Michael Atherton on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, former Australian white-ball captain Aaron Finch gives his thoughts on why Tom Moody or Justin Langer would be great candidates for the England Test coach role.

Langer, who is also involved in the The Hundred, leading the Manchester Super Giants, has also been touted as a possible successor, although The Telegraph have reported that he's not one of the ECB's shortlisted candidates and he himself insists he has yet to be contacted.

"I haven't, no," he said. "I haven't heard from anyone. It's all paper talk, all hypothetical."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Southern Brave and Australia all-rounder Marcus Stoinis says Justin Langer's work ethic would make him a good choice if selected to be England's next men's Test head coach.

Langer, who earned 105 Test caps for his country from 1993-2007, added: "I'm passionate about the game of cricket, but particularly Test cricket.

"I see now with franchise cricket, it's awesome, but we've got to have Test cricket. It must keep thriving for the health of the game - and so that's why I say about the three big countries [Australia, India, England] and why it's important they keep going strong.

"When it comes to coaching, it's a career and everyone looks at all opportunities."

Ben Stokes' retirement? I've heard all the counter arguements, but I thought 'respect'. I think when you're a player who has done what he has for England, a great warrior, I think go out however you want. That's my honest view.

McCullum has been retained as England's white-ball head coach, meaning the job will again be split from the Test team.

"My personal view has always been that if you're the head coach of Australia you should oversee all of it," Langer said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Stuart Broad shares his thoughts on who could take over from Brendon McCullum as head coach of the England Test team.

"It can work [split jobs] if you have the right people. They've got to get on very well, be on the same page and have the same thinking. And alongside the director of cricket [Rob Key], they've got to fit like a glove.

"We've seen that with Andy Flower and Ashley Giles [for England], and McCullum and Matthew Mott to a degree.

"It's complicated, with T20 cricket, white-ball cricket. I would say there will be some teething issues for Baz and whoever he does it with.

"If they work well together, it could work, but there haven't been too many examples where it has."

Langer recorded 15 wins, 11 losses and 5 draws in his time in charge of Australia, which included retaining the Ashes in England in 2019 with a 2-2 series draw, before a 4-0 triumph in the Covid-impacted return Down Under in 2021-22.

He resigned in acrimonious circumstances in February 2022, just a few weeks after the comprehensive win over England, amid claims he fell out with senior players.

Sports.title: Harrington picked as Europe's third vice-captain for 2027 Ryder Cup
Sports.content:
Luke Donald has named Irishman Padraig Harrington as his third vice-captain for the 2027 Ryder Cup which will be played at Adare Manor in Ireland in September next year.

Harrington joins the Molinari brothers, Edoardo and Francesco, in Donald's backroom team for next year's contest, as Team Europe seek a third consecutive Ryder Cup victory following wins at Marco Simone in 2023 and Bethpage Black in 2025.

The three-time major champion, one of Ireland's most decorated and popular sporting heroes, was a player in the only previous Ryder Cup to be played in his home country in 2006.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look back at Harrington's heroics en route to his Open title defence in 2008

He represented Europe six times in total as a player - including being part of four triumphs - and was previously a vice-captain on three occasions before becoming captain for the 2021 Ryder Cup at Whistling Straits.

"Luke and I arranged to meet up at The Open and chatted about it, and we felt we could strike up a good team again," said Harrington.

"Obviously, he was my vice-captain in 2021, and we have worked together as vice-captains in the past. And certainly, I feel I've something to give.

"Luke has a very strong team around him already and he felt that we would work well together.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports Jamie Weir explains why Luke Donald has been chosen as captain of Europe Ryder Cup team for a third time.

"It's something I didn't expect. I honestly didn't think I'd ever wear the European Ryder Cup logo again. So I'm very happy to be part of it.

"The Ryder Cup has been a special part of my life. Representing Europe has always been one of the highlights of my golfing career, and to be able to do it again in this situation, especially in Ireland, is special.

"You wouldn't want to miss out with it being in Ireland, so I'm very pleased.

"I think it will be a spectacular occasion and one of the great sporting events to be played in the country. The whole of Ireland will be behind it, watching it, enjoying it and living it.

"The fans are going to be fantastic, and I think the atmosphere will be second to none."

Donald said: "Padraig is someone I thought about quite a lot, especially with it being in Adare.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Donald expresses his gratitude to his fans, family and team-mates after being recognised in the King's Birthday Honours list with an OBE for his success with Team Europe.

"I've been around Padraig in many Ryder Cup team rooms, as a player, as a vice-captain to his captaincy, and he's been a vice-captain before in the past as well.

"So he brings a wealth of experience, and I do love the fact that there's a connection. He understands the Irish crowds and all that goes with having a Ryder Cup in Ireland. I think it's going to be very special for him.

"He's loved in Ireland with what he's achieved in the game, and that will only bring more energy to our team. We'll get the fans even more behind us, and you know I think that can only be a good thing. I'm very excited to have his expertise."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ryder Cup captain Jim Furyk is hopeful Tiger Woods will be able to play a role in the team in 2027.

Harrington made his Ryder Cup debut at The Country Club in Brookline in 1999 and was ever-present for the next five editions, helping Europe to victory in 2002, 2004, 2006 and 2010. He contributed a total of 10½ points to the European Team during that period.

He was named as vice-captain for the first time by fellow Dubliner Paul McGinley for the victory at Gleneagles in 2014, a role he returned to in 2016 at Hazeltine National under Darren Clarke and in 2018 for the victory at Le Golf National in Paris under Denmark's Thomas Bjorn.

Harrington then led Team Europe at the 2021 Ryder Cup at Whistling Straits, which was postponed by 12 months due to the Covid pandemic in 2020.

Sports.title: Uefa has to show backbone: concrete action can make Fifa’s World Cup plans untenable | Nick Ames
Sports.content:
As the World Cup neared its conclusion, one leading figure in European football pondered how Gianni Infantino might attempt to rinse away the damaging stain of the Folarin Balogun scandal. It all came down to money. “He will just announce more funds for everyone,” was the gist, although the tournament passed without any explanation of how Fifa would carve up its record $15bn (£11.2bn) haul.

That was the tip of the iceberg. Infantino’s plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors, announced on Tuesday, nine days after the final, has sent shockwaves around the sport and left senior personnel scrambling. There is little time for a coordinated response given Fifa, at the height of what passes for football’s holiday period, has given FAs until 19 September to decide whether to accept the initial $20m payment that would effectively count as endorsement of the new scheme.

The reaction must come quickly. Perhaps, when Uefa assesses its next move, it will look back to 2021 and remember the credit it happily banked in blocking the proposed European Super League. Fifa’s plan, which could allow private investors a say in how and when its tournaments are run, is potentially more seismic and global in scale. If football’s future has been on a ticking clock under Infantino, the time is one minute to midnight.

Uefa’s speed in responding to the plan was of a piece with its renewed appetite, honed over a number of run-ins over the past 15 months, to stick the boot into Fifa. “This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross,” it said, although anyone feeling a sense of deja vu needed only to scroll back three weeks. On 6 July, another Uefa statement said the shelving of Balogun’s suspension “crossed a red line”. These are strong, accurate words, but they can be wielded only so many times.

Infantino can rush his proposals through by counting on votes from the overwhelming number of FAs, primarily based outside Europe, who pledge fealty to his administration. But a show of backbone from football’s most powerful continent, a sporting behemoth that has eaten up any competition on the pitch and through the financial clout of its institutions, would be a major blow to Fifa. It would only take concrete action from a few of Europe’s major nations, with their governments in lockstep, to render any plan to sell off football’s crown jewels untenable.

View image in fullscreen Fireworks go off at New York New Jersey Stadium as Spain’s Rodri lifts the World Cup. Photograph: Mike Segar/Reuters

Who will put their heads above the parapet? This is a moment to remember that, as the Guardian revealed in mid-July, more than 200 of Fifa’s 211 members have already submitted letters in support of his candidacy for re-election early next year. Most of those resisting significant pressure to offer backing are from Europe, with Germany the highest-profile holdout. But England’s FA, which is hoping to rubber-stamp its hosting of the 2035 Women’s World Cup, was quick to offer its endorsement well before this summer.

Then there are cases such as Finland, whose FA president, Ari Lahti, said in June that his country aimed “not to be an eyesore” by refusing to back Infantino. It is a common stance, even among federations who are vocal in private about their disgust for Fifa’s trampling over norms and proximity to the Trump administration. Countries of all sizes have a duty to put the beauty contest on hold.

Any talk of boycotting future World Cups, which would surely have to include the women’s edition in Brazil next year, is complicated by a section of Fifa’s statutes that says its members are obliged to take part in its competitions. The only way to avoid financially prohibitive sanctions may be to threaten the most radical step of all: a withdrawal from Fifa and the creation of a new governance model for football.

Uefa’s position may be made trickier by its close relationship to the thus far taciturn European Football Clubs (EFC), which would like to set up a joint venture with Fifa to run the Club World Cup. EFC and Uefa already run a joint venture, UC3, that operates the commercial aspect of Uefa competitions, but one of the key differences from Fifa’s proposal is that it does not involve private capital.

Somehow, everyone must be corralled together if Infantino is to be tackled. Another way would be to remove some wind from Infantino’s sails by putting up a serious electoral opponent. After the Balogun affair, conversations with figures at all levels of the sport speculated whether Uefa might endorse its own candidate to run for the Fifa presidency in March. Consensus suggested it would be too soon; that this will be a period of positioning for 2031 when, according to Fifa’s current rules, Infantino must stand aside.

But there is no time to play a long game when Infantino plans to carve up football’s future among private interests in rapid order. Nor is there the opportunity to wait for any European Commission response to the complaint by FifPro, the global players’ union, and the European Leagues organisation about Fifa’s grip on the international match calendar, which was lodged in October 2024. A favourable outcome could place obstacles in front of any plans by Fifa, or its friends in private investment, to expand its tournaments, but no resolution appears in sight.

Uefa and Europe must take a lead and reject the status quo. Doing so might reveal friends in unexpected places. There are certainly countries in Asia, among other confederations, that would be open to clear suggestions of a better path. The fear is that a rush of nebulous statements such as that by the Danish FA, which responded to Infantino’s plan by emphasising the need to “gain a complete understanding of the proposal and the process behind it” will result in nothing bar the standard procrastination and tacit acceptance.

Bravery and sturdy spines are required now, more than ever, if football is to survive in anything resembling its present form.

Sports.title: Defence promises to be a central issue for Carrick and Manchester United
Sports.content:
In Leny Yoro, Ayden Heaven, Harry Maguire, Matthijs De Ligt, and Lisandro Martínez, Michael Carrick can talk of high potential: seasoned operators who will patrol the Manchester United backline safely.

Except the 44-year-old privately harbours concerns about the five central defenders, especially as there is no plan to strengthen in the position unless one or more departs. Are they an ideal blend of youthful zest and experienced winners? Or a unit that may prove vulnerable and injury-prone across the long months of the campaign?

Carrick approaches his first full season as manager with the prospect of leading United on four fronts for a first time: Premier League, FA Cup, Carabao Cup and, after a two-year absence, the Champions League.

When taking temporary charge last January, after the sacking of Ruben Amorim, Carrick had 17 league matches to negotiate with United out of the other competitions. Carrick impressed, wiping away the angst and chaos left by the Portuguese’s removal. United finished last season in seventh place with 32 points, nine behind Aston Villa in third.

The coming season, though, is the acid test and may expose Carrick’s callowness with only 20 games as United’s manager behind him. In those 17 matches last season, United lost only twice – 2-1 defeats by Newcastle and Leeds – and conceded 18 times. He made United hard to beat. But closer scrutiny of the five players tasked to secure central defence – the full-backs Noussair Mazraoui, Diogo Dalot and Luke Shaw can operate there too – throws up uncomfortable questions.

Yoro, at 20, and the 19-year-old Heaven are yet to progress beyond showing potential and must mature into sure-footed defenders this season.

View image in fullscreen The Manchester United manager Michael Carrick will be fighting on four fronts this season. Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters

Yoro, with 66 appearances since joining from Lille, for £52m, in 2024, is the more senior but has been prone to the occasional error. After two seasons, the hope is that Yoro’s 6ft 3in frame, serious turn of pace, and calm style will elevate his game.

The 6ft 2in Heaven, who signed in February 2025 from Arsenal for a nominal fee, made 11 league starts last season and is blessed with technique, speed and a more robust build. He says: “I’m young and I’ve got to be patient, especially in my position. You don’t see a lot of 19-year-olds playing week in, week out. I know it’s nothing personal. I’m waiting for my opportunity.”

At 33, Maguire is at the opposite end of the career spectrum. The former England defender possesses guile and commitment yet is one-paced and may be exposed. Left out by Thomas Tuchel for the World Cup, the former United captain offers leadership, and was part of the 2024 Carabao Cup triumph, so knows how to win.

Under Carrick he would expect to begin the season as first-choice, alongside Martínez, except the 28-year-old Argentinian remains plagued by injury. He was forced off before half-time in the World Cup final defeat by Spain with a muscle problem, and his fitness for the season opener at Hull is in the balance.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

After a starring role in United’s 2-1 defeat of Manchester City in the 2025 FA Cup final, Pep Guardiola rated him “a top five centre-back in the world”. But regardless of The Butcher’s merits, Carrick cannot rely on him staying fit.

De Ligt’s robustness may be of even greater concern for the manager. The 26-year-old has not played since the 2-1 win at Crystal Palace on 30 November with a back injury that was finally operated on in May. Speaking after the procedure, he said: “Since November I have done everything, pushing myself in every session and exploring every option, to get back to doing what I love, playing football.”

The aim is for De Ligt, who boasts league-winners medals from with Ajax, Juventus and Bayern Munich is to be back early in the season. Yet the uncertainty over De Ligt, Maguire, Martínez, Yoro and Heaven is mirrored by the club’s so far unconvincing summer recruitment, particularly compared with their rivals.

Manchester City signed Eliott Anderson for £116m, while Chelsea (Morgan Rogers, £117m), and Tottenham (Sandro Tonali, £100m, Mateus Fernandes, £85m) have all made big investments. United’s major signing, by contrast, the 29-year-old Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa, plus Andrey Santos, a 22-year-old with just 11 league starts last season for Chelsea.

There are still five weeks of the transfer window left so the picture may change significantly by 1 September. But at the moment, it’s difficult to make a case for a fit-for-purpose defence at Carrick’s United.

Sports.title: Liverpool prepare opening offer for Paris Saint-Germain’s Bradley Barcola
Sports.content:
Liverpool are preparing an opening offer for Bradley Barcola following talks with the Paris Saint Germain forward’s representatives.

Barcola is a leading target for Liverpool as they look to add a proven winger to Andoni Iraola’s squad ahead of the new season. Yan Diomande had been wanted but is set to join Real Madrid after PSG pulled out of a deal for the Leipzig winger.

PSG have placed a value in the region of £145m on Barcola, which would represent a British record sum. He has two years left on his contract with the European champions but is believed to have turned down the offer of an extension, having falling down the pecking order in Luis Enrique’s gifted team.

Liverpool have been exploring whether the 23-year-old is open to leaving PSG for Anfield. Having received encouragement that he wants to move to the Premier League, Liverpool are expected to bid for the France international in the coming days. Whether they are prepared to meet PSG’s valuation remains to be seen, but the club will attempt to make Barcola their statement signing of the summer.

Liverpool have signed versatile forward Víctor Muñoz from Osasuna this summer and finalised Jérémy Jacquet’s transfer from Rennes for an initial £55m but are looking to strengthen further in attack and defence, with Iraola concerned about his defensive options in particular.

Sports.title: Manchester City leading opposition to Premier League’s £1.5bn EFL proposal
Sports.content:
Manchester City are leading the opposition to the Premier League’s plans to offer £1.5bn to the English Football League in a landmark financial settlement, which will be discussed at a meeting of the 20 clubs on Thursday.

The Premier League wants to put its proposed offer, which would be spread over 10 years, to a vote on Thursday in the hope of getting the matter resolved before the start of the season, but City are understood to have come up with a counterproposal amid concerns about how the package will be funded.

A number of City’s concerns are shared by other members of the so-called Big Six, who will be asked to pay more than other Premier League clubs towards the New Deal for Football, but it is unclear how many of them are prepared to back their rivals.

City remain short of allies within the top flight as they wait for the much-anticipated judgment of an independent tribunal after being charged with 115 breaches of Financial Fair Play rules, despite settling a long-running legal dispute with the Premier League over its Associated Party Transaction rules last year.

Quick Guide How do I 

The Guardian has learned that City irritated several clubs by submitting a series of late amendments to proposed rule changes before the Premier League’s Annual General Meeting at the 11th hour in June, which were defeated by 19 votes to one.

City and other big clubs are understood to be unhappy with the Premier League’s proposal to fund the financial redistribution package by increasing the levy on transfer fees from 4% to 6%, which would leave the bigger spending clubs with a large bill.

The Premier League will only ballot clubs on Thursday if they are confident of getting the 14 votes required for the proposal to pass, with sources describing them as cautiously optimistic despite facing some opposition.

At an average of £150m-a-year the Premier League’s proposed contribution has not altered significantly since a similar offer of £750m over five years was proposed in September 2023, although they have doubled the length of the deal.

If approved by the clubs and accepted by the EFL an initial payment of £100m would be made this season, with larger contributions to be made in subsequent years until the 2035-36 season.

It is unclear whether the EFL would accept the Premier League’s first offer however, with its chair, Rick Parry, believed to be holding out for a bigger deal.

If approved the EFL would allocate 80% of the New Deal to the Championship clubs, 12% to League One and 8% to League Two.

City and the Premier League declined to comment.

Sports.title: Where all 20 Premier League clubs should strengthen before the season
Sports.content:
Arsenal: central midfielder

Declan Rice was worked to the bone by Arsenal last season, playing 4,456 minutes in all competitions. This showed at points during the World Cup, when the midfielder’s body looked on the verge of breaking down. Arsenal need high-quality reinforcements in the centre of the pitch so Rice can occasionally have a rest. Christian Nørgaard struggled to get on to the park last season, with Mikel Arteta seemingly not trusting the former Brentford captain. An extra midfield option could prove crucial to Arsenal retaining their crown.

Aston Villa: left-back

Aston Villa have finished in the top seven for the last four years and they won the Europa League last season. They need more depth in the squad to establish themselves among the Premier League’s elite permanently, but may lose the left-back Lucas Digne to Paris Saint-Germain. Ian Maatsen is a fine player but he cannot play every week in a season that includes a Champions League campaign, hence Villa’s interest in signing Pervis Estupiñán from Milan.

Bournemouth: right-back

Adam Smith is a Bournemouth legend who has made more than 400 appearances for the club but he is 35. Max Aarons and Julián Araujo were signed to replace him but, for one reason or another, things have not worked out for them. And Álex Jiménez has gone out on loan to Fiorentina. Marco Rose needs to make a statement signing at right-back so Smith can finally rest.

View image in fullscreen Adam Smith puts in some work in the gym during Bournemouth’s pre-season testing. Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty Images

Brentford: left-back

Brentford have already addressed their biggest weaknesses, but they could do with an upgrade at left-back. Rico Henry has struggled for fitness and form since suffering a horrific injury three years ago. He played 30 games in all competitions last season but made four errors leading to shots – the joint most of any Brentford player. Reinforcing the left flank would also free up Keane Lewis-Potter to play further forward if Keith Andrews wants to utilise him more on the wing.

Brighton: central midfielder

Brighton will have been planning for James Milner’s retirement and Pascal Gross’s ageing legs for a long time. Only six midfielders over the age of 34 played in the Premier League last season, and two of them did so for Brighton. They are thin in the middle of the park and there’s also the possibility of more departures. Carlos Baleba is frequently linked with a move and Yasin Ayari’s impressive performances at the World Cup may have caught someone’s eye. Nobody scored more goals from outside the penalty area at the tournament than the Sweden midfielder. Brighton could do with someone else in there even if Baleba and Ayari stay.

Chelsea: goalkeeper

Chelsea have spent more than £200m this summer – £117m of it on Morgan Rogers – but still have several problem positions. They seem keen to sign a centre-back and should add depth in central midfield and on the left wing, but a goalkeeper is where the most urgent attention is needed. Robert Sánchez has never truly convinced. Since he joined in August 2023, he ranks second in the Premier League for errors leading to shots (17) and errors leading to goals (seven). Of the worst 10 culprits in both metrics, Sánchez has made the fewest appearances and played the fewest minutes. Mike Penders has arrived from Strasbourg but, at 20, he is one for the future. Xabi Alonso does not want to start his tenure worrying about the reliability of his first-choice goalkeeper.

Coventry: goalkeeper

There are a lot of unknowns for Coventry as they return to the Premier League after 25 years, not least how well the centre-forwards Haji Wright and Ellis Simms will take to leading the line against the best defences in England. But the biggest unknown of all is who will be between the sticks, because Coventry do not have a first-choice goalkeeper. They want to make Carl Rushworth’s loan deal permanent, but have not been able to agree a fee with Brighton. Only Bristol City keeper Radek Vitek (+8.5) prevented more goals with his saves in the Championship last season than Rushworth (+8.2). Without him, there’s a big hole that needs filling.

Crystal Palace: centre-back

Pierre Sage used a back three in all of Lens’ league games last season, so it’s likely that Crystal Palace will continue to employ the 3-4-2-1 formation that served them so well under Oliver Glasner. They will need more depth at centre-back, though. Having lost Marc Guéhi to Manchester City in January, their Premier League win rate last season dropped from 35% with the England international starting to 22.2% without him. Jaydee Canvot is an adequate replacement, but Palace are still short on numbers at the back. If Maxence Lacroix also leaves the club, their need for another centre-back will become even starker.

Everton: right-back

Séamus Coleman’s 17-year stay at Everton has come to an end and Nathan Patterson is also expected to depart, meaning Jake O’Brien is likely to be their only remaining recognised right-back. Well, we say “recognised right-back”, but the consensus among Everton fans is that the hulking Republic of Ireland international is not dynamic or technical enough to be a full-back. James Garner has also filled in there from time to time. It has been a problem position for a while now.

Fulham: centre-forward

Fulham need more players who can score goals. Raúl Jiménez (nine) and Harry Wilson (10) accounted for 19 of their 43 Premier League goals (excluding own goals) last season and they have both left on free transfers. No one else scored more than four league goals last season. More will be expected from Rodrigo Muniz (one goal), Samuel Chukwueze (three goals) and Kevin (one goal), but Fulham clearly need greater depth in attack. Álvaro Arbeloa, the new manager, is keen to sign Gonzalo García from Real Madrid but Fulham need at least two fresh faces.

Hull: wide forward

Hull City desperately need to add a few splashes of quality to their attack. Oli McBurnie has the physicality to lead the line, but the 30-year-old needs players to run off him to be effective. Hull have sold Kyle Joseph to Middlesbrough and have not tried to re-sign Joe Gelhardt after his loan, meaning they are light in attack.

Ipswich: striker

Most promoted sides are let down by a lack of precision in both boxes. By signing Issa Diop, Ipswich have secured a proven defender to play alongside Dara O’Shea. But they need more firepower up front. George Hirst has reached double figures for goals in a season only twice and the £24m signing Emersonn has never scored more than six league goals in a single campaign (though he is only 22). Daizen Maeda is a much-needed addition from Celtic.

View image in fullscreen The signing of Daizen Maeda is a boost to Ipswich’s attack. Photograph: Steve Welsh/PA

Leeds: goalkeeper

Leeds signed Lucas Perri from Lyon last summer for £15.6m in the hope he would solve what had become a problem position. He didn’t. Karl Darlow, originally acquired as backup to Illan Meslier in 2023, ended up playing more games in the league last season. But Darlow then left on a free transfer, ultimately joining Manchester United. Leeds also opted to let Meslier’s contract expire. Their remaining goalkeeper options are Perri, who underwhelmed in his first season, and the 33-year-old Alex Cairns, whose most recent competitive appearance was for Salford in the 2023-24 season. They need another keeper.

Liverpool: right-winger

Mohamed Salah’s final season at Liverpool was his most underwhelming, but he still had a hand in 22 goals across all competitions. In terms of what he achieved in nine years at Anfield, Salah is one of the greatest players in Liverpool’s history and close to irreplaceable. His output last season is not irreplaceable, though. A dynamic wide attacker who provides goals and creativity – such as Bradley Barcola – is on the agenda, and Andoni Iraola has a good track record developing such players.

Manchester City: winger

Enzo Maresca has addressed one hole in the Manchester City squad by signing Elliot Anderson, but he could do with another option on the flanks to give City more attacking variety. At the end of last season, City lacked strength in depth on the wing. Antoine Semenyo struggled during the run-in and City did not have a quality replacement to turn to on the bench. Savinho regressed in his second season in England, starting only seven league games and scoring one goal, and Phil Foden and Rayan Cherki are better in the middle.

Manchester United: central midfielder

Michael Carrick’s central midfield options have been enhanced by Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. It’s a pretty good start, but they need more. If we categorise Bruno Fernandes and Mason Mount as No 10s, Manchester United had only three senior central midfielders last season: Kobbie Mainoo, Casemiro and Manuel Ugarte. Casemiro has joined Inter Miami and Ugarte would probably have left too had he not suffered an anterior cruciate ligament injury at the World Cup that will keep him out for most of the season. United still need an athletic, ball-winning midfielder.

Newcastle: full-back

We could have picked a few positions for Newcastle but have chosen full-back as they need one for each flank or, failing that, someone who can play on both sides of the defence. Tino Livramento and Lewis Hall are two of the best full-backs in the Premier League, but they have had injury problems and Newcastle lack depth now that Kieran Trippier, Emil Krafth and Matt Targett have departed. Dan Burn can fill in at left-back but that is not ideal; they have Leo Shahar at right-back but he is an unproven teenager; and Alex Murphy can fill in at left-back but he is more of a central defender.

Nottingham Forest: centre-back

Let’s assume replacing Elliot Anderson is a given for Nottingham Forest. The other area they need reinforcements is centre-back. Oliver Glasner, their new coach, swears by a back three; he lined up with three or five at the back in every game during his two seasons at Crystal Palace. Forest have several centre-backs already – Nikola Milenkovic, Murillo, Morato and Jair Cunha, plus a couple of prospects – but bringing in at least one more defender with experience of playing in a back three would not go amiss.

Tottenham: winger

When Mohammed Kudus and Dejan Kulusevski are fit again, Tottenham will have a couple of good options on the right flank. However, they are not on the club’s pre-season tour to New Zealand and Australia, and may not be available for the start of the season. On the left, Spurs have only Mathys Tel and Wilson Odobert, neither of whom can be relied upon for consistent output. Between them, Tel and Odobert racked up just four goals and three assists in a combined 55 league appearances last season. Odobert is also recovering from a serious knee injury and will miss at least the first few months of the season. That leaves Tottenham with almost no options out wide. They need at least one winger.

Sunderland: creative midfielder

After a very busy transfer market last summer and an extremely successful first season back in the top flight, Sunderland have been quieter this time around. That is understandable but, with a first European campaign since 1973 coming up, they need more depth, and that could mean reinforcement across the pitch. They could really do with a little more creativity, having generated just 23.2 expected goals in open play in 38 league games last season – only relegated Burnley and Wolves fared worse.

This is an article by Opta Analyst

Sports.title: Awakening giants: Dortmund add stardust to their rise through leagues
Sports.content:
Located in Austria during a pre-season training camp, the Borussia Dortmund women’s team, squad as well as staff, are plotting how to reach the 2. Bundesliga after missing out on promotion during their rapid rise last season.

Dortmund finished two points off the top and a place in the regional playoffs despite a goal difference of +101, and the club have wasted no time in signing big names to make sure there is no such near-miss this time around.

The team’s managing director, Svenja Schlenker, says: “We have great new players, we have a great environment, Manuela, wouldn’t you agree?” Manuela refers to Manuela Zinsberger, the Austria goalkeeper who played previously for Bayern Munich and Arsenal. Alongside the Germany legend Alexandra Popp, Zinsberger is one of two major summer signings for the third-division side, and a statement of Dortmund’s intent.

“Definitely,” Zinsberger says. “I’m looking forward to the new season and the first matches, so it couldn’t be better right now.” Her decision to leave Arsenal at the end of last season for life in the third tier of German football was a surprise to many, but the 30-year-old had reasons for doing so. “They were partly family decisions, but also my conversations with Svenja,” she says.

View image in fullscreen ‘We have great new players, Manuela, wouldn’t you agree?’: Svenja Schlenker is pleased to have Manuela Zinsberger at Dortmund. Photograph: Alexandre Simões/BVB

“The vision of the club, where they are now, where they want to be, what my role would be in that, and coming out of my comfort zone was a big part of it, to challenge myself on another level.

“The conversations were good. We spoke about the DNA of the club, what I can bring with my experience to the group of players, and to help achieve what we’ve literally put on paper. Dortmund is doing really well. The level from a club perspective, staff, infrastructure, is already high for a third-division club. We’re setting the bar high, it’s showing what the club is putting into women’s football, and that makes me happy.”

Dortmund are not shy in their ambitions, and really it is not a surprise a club of their size have aspirations of joining the likes of Bayern, Wolfsburg and Eintracht Frankfurt in the Frauen-Bundesliga. Their success can also help push women’s football in Germany as a whole, with no team from the country having won the Champions League since 2015.

“It means we will have to spend a lot of money, and that’s OK on one end, but I don’t know what will happen in the next few years,” Schlenker says. “Other countries are a bit further on than we are, we just concentrate on the third division and then we think about what we have to do in the next few years.”

“If you put Bayern versus Borussia on paper people want to watch, but we have to work hard to get there,” Zinsberger says. “We’ve made the first steps, now it’s down to us to connect as a team and get the results. We are a little behind England in general, we have to push it.”

View image in fullscreen Borussia Dortmund are eyeing a meeting with Bayern Munich one day. Photograph: BVB

The arrival of Zinsberger and Popp, as well as that of the longtime Wolfsburg sporting director, Ralf Kellermann, to the same role, are all key markers of the club’s ambitions, according to Schlenker. “We’re so happy to have both of them, as well as Ralf. They bring huge experience to Borussia Dortmund,” she says. “We started in the seventh division, so we have a lot of firsts every year and we don’t all have the experiences they do, so we use that to improve every day.”

“Svenja and Ralf are really close to the team, which is really nice,” Zinsberger says. “They try to have conversations on a daily basis about what we can improve. It’s really nice to see, because if you’re not close to the team, it’s hard to make those decisions.

“We have internal goals, but we look game by game. We have a job to do and that’s to win every single game, that’s the aim of the club. We can’t take any game less seriously than the other, we have to go into every game wanting to win, and what comes out at the end is hopefully positive.”

Dortmund’s ambitions are wide-ranging, as Schlenker explains: “We will build our own training facility next to the men’s campus. I’ve spoken to so many players and [for them] it’s about that – facilities, infrastructures. That’s what I’m working for and have worked really hard for it because I want to build a great second home for all our players.”

“We all need money, we all need to pay our bills, but we need the right infrastructure to build for the next generations,” Zinsberger says. “I’m so happy we’re doing that here.”

Sports.title: Abusive chanting against immigrants in English football on rise, new data reveals
Sports.content:
Abusive chanting against immigrants has become a feature of football matches in England, according to new data from Kick It Out.

Last season 39 reports of anti-immigrant chanting were made to the anti-discrimination charity, more than the previous two seasons combined. Phrases such as “stop the boats” and “send them back” were reported as being heard “at all levels of the game”, Kick It Out said.

The growth in anti-immigrant rhetoric was consistent with a broader rise in reports of discrimination, at matches and online. Kick It Out received 1,744 reports of discriminatory behaviour in total during the 2025-26 season, a record and a 25% increase on the previous campaign.

The number of reported incidents increased across every type of discrimination to new highs. Reports of racism remained the most common, rising 19% year-on-year, the 792 reports making up 45% of the total. Complaints of sexist behaviour rose 12% to 216, homophobia rose 46% to 203, antisemitism rose 43% to 93, ableism rose 20% to 89, and Islamophobia rose 88% to 60. Kick it Out said all six areas had seen their biggest totals in five years.

Reports of abuse in grassroots football rose for a fifth consecutive year, up by 33% in 2025-26 to a record 248 reports. Equally, the 98 reports of abuse against match officials was the same as the past three seasons combined.

Samuel Okafor, chief executive at Kick It Out, said such behaviour at matches and in online spaces was matched by a rise in hateful rhetoric elsewhere in British society, but he praised the willingness of supporters – and players – to speak out.

“These figures show that discrimination remains deeply embedded across the game at a time when we’re also seeing rises in hate crime and divisive political rhetoric in Britain,” he said. “But they also show that people are more willing to stand up to abuse when they see it, and it’s encouraging to see professional players set that example last season.”

For example, in March, a 60-year-old man was given a suspended sentence for sending offensive messages to the England Women defender Jess Carter, who went public over the attacks during the European Championship last year. In the men’s game, Antoine Semenyo drew attention to the racist abuse he had received over the course of the season, with a charge of racially aggravated behaviour against one man scheduled to go to trial in September.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Kick It Out’s findings concur with those reported by the UK Football Policing Unit last week. The police said that some of the increase could be explained by improved reporting mechanisms, with misogynist abuse only introduced as a separate category of discrimination at the start of last season. Both police and Kick It Out have called on online platforms to do more to stop abuse.

Okafor said: “We will continue to work with football authorities, clubs, leagues, regulators and government to ensure we match the courage shown to report abuse with clear and consistent action so that football is welcoming to everyone.”

Sports.title: Is Kazuyoshi Miura the oldest goalscorer in competitive football history? | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“Kazuyoshi Miura recently scored in the Emperor’s Cup at the tender age of 59 – is he the oldest goalscorer in football history?” asks Terry Winter.

If we were picking an all-time Knowledge XI, ‘King Kazu’ would be in the mix for a place. He’s appeared in various age-related queries over the years, and tales of his exploits always give us hope as we wheeze through middle-age. On Saturday, Miura scored his first competitive goal ⁠in nearly four years as ⁠Fukushima ​United thrashed Iwaki Furukawa 7-0 in the Emperor’s Cup.

Miura’s goal extended his record for the oldest goalscorer in professional football. These are the oldest goalscorers we could find, but drop us a line if you can beat them.

59 years 149 days, Kazuyoshi Miura: Fukushima United 7-0 Iwaku Furukawa, Emperor’s Cup, 25 July 2026

51 years 5 days, Innocent Benza: Herentals College FC 1-2 Hwange Colliery, Zimbabwe Premier Soccer League, 25 May 2023

49 years 208 days, Billy Meredith: Brighton 1-5 Manchester City, FA Cup, 23 February 1924

49 years, 14 days, Stanley Matthews: Stoke City 2-2 Swansea City, FA Cup, 15 February 1964

Innocent Benza, aka IB9 and no we didn’t make that up, was on target when Herentals College FC lost 2-1 to Hwange Colliery in the Zimbabwe Premier Soccer League three years ago. He’s believed to be the oldest top-flight goalscorer. In fact he may have scored a more recent goal, as he was still going strong last season when he reached 200 games for Herentals College FC.

Benza has got another 20 years to go if he wants to become the oldest goalscorer on record, though. In March 2020, Ezzeldin Bahader scored a penalty on his debut for 6th of October SC in the Egyptian Third Division. He was – and you’ll like this – 74 years, 125 days old. For the sake of Portugal’s future World Cup chances, Cristiano Ronaldo should not be made aware of this record.

Top of the tree in women’s football appears to be Formiga, who scored for Brazil against Canada in November 2019 at the age of 41 years, 249 days. She retired soon after, having amassed 234 caps over a 26-year international career.

View image in fullscreen Formiga before the 2019 World Cup. Photograph: Naomi Baker/Fifa/Getty Images

With Andy Burnham succeeding Keir Starmer as Labour leader, the UK now has an Everton-supporting prime minister. (A few years ago, he appeared on our own Daniel Harris’s podcast to discuss the 1995 FA Cup final.)

We’ve made a list of PMs who have publicly spoken about being a fan of a particular team or have shown an allegiance in some other way, and, from our initial research, it looks like the balance of power is spread thinly, with no team belonging to more than one prime minister.

Boris Johnson once stated he “supports all London teams” but we are counting none of the capital’s clubs as belonging to him. Before the second world war it was very rare for a prime minister to talk about football, so our list doesn’t go beyond 1945. If you can add to it, or find a team supported by more than one of the country’s leaders, please get in touch.

View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham showing some retro support. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA

Andy Burnham (2026-) Everton

Keir Starmer (2024-2026) Arsenal

Rishi Sunak (2022-2024) Southampton

Liz Truss (2022) Norwich City

David Cameron (2010-2016) Aston Villa (definitely not West Ham)

Gordon Brown (2007-2010) Raith Rovers

Tony Blair (1997-2007) Newcastle United

John Major (1990-1997) Chelsea

Edward Heath (1970-1974) Burnley

Harold Wilson (1964-1970 and 1974-1976) Huddersfield Town

Clement Attlee (1945-1951) Fleet Town (mainly because he played for them)

View image in fullscreen Labour leader Tony Blair takes part in a heading contest with Newcastle United boss Kevin Keegan in Brighton during a break at the 1995 party conference. Photograph: PA/PA Archive/Press Association Images

B teams and W teams

“Alphabetically, Tottenham Hotspur are the last club in this season’s Premier League,” notes Robert Johansson-Mars. “That feels weird as there are usually a couple of clubs below them (West Ham, West Brom, Watford, Wolves, Wigan, Wimbledon and whatnot). When was the last time the Premier League (or First Division) didn’t include any W team? However, a league without clubs beginning with the letter B would be truly shocking. Has that ever occurred?”

Prepare to be shocked, Robert. An English top-flight without a B-team is reasonably-common. It last happened in the Premier League just over a decade ago. Blackburn Rovers and Bolton Wanderers were relegated in 2011-12; Burnley rejoined the Premier League in the 2014-15 season. (If you list AFC Bournemouth thus, rather than Bournemouth, it also occurred in 2015-16 while Burnley were yo-yoing.) Those are the only examples in the Premier League era – but the last six years of the old Division One were similarly bereft after Birmingham City were relegated in 1985-86.

The answer to your first question depends on how pedantic you are feeling. This season will be the first in which the men’s English top flight has included no teams whose name begins with W, but there is one historical example where the only W-team subsequently changed their name. Between 1906-11, Woolwich Arsenal flew the flag for the Ws in the English top flight.

In women’s football it’s a more familiar sight – there were no W-teams in the top flight between Watford (2009-10) and West Ham (2018-19).

Knowledge archive

“Apart from Newcastle United how many other clubs using United in their name are actually two teams who merged together to form one?” wondered Keith Gilroy in 2011.

Unsurprisingly, the Magpies aren’t the only United formed by the merger of two clubs (in Newcastle’s case Newcastle West End and Newcastle East End), though there are surprisingly few in the Football League. Plenty of Uniteds seem to have simply plumped for the name – Lincoln Amateurs, for example, were forced into a name change once they began to pay players in the 1950s. With Lincoln City already taken, United just beat Rangers in the club’s vote for a new suffix.

Some that aren’t strictly united Uniteds are: Sheffield (formed from Sheffield United Cricket Club), Leeds (formed following the demise of Leeds City FC in 1919), Manchester (name change from Newton Heath LYR FC), West Ham (formerly Thames Ironworks) and there are plenty more. But here are a few clubs in the pyramid who truly are united Uniteds:

View image in fullscreen The Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding Company Limited was a shipyard and iron works straddling the mouth of Bow Creek at its confluence with the River Thames, at Leamouth Wharf (often referred to as Blackwall) on the west side and at Canning Town on the east side. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian

Scunthorpe United: The Iron’s website reports, slightly mysteriously that “in 1899 Brumby Hall joined forces with another team to call themselves Scunthorpe United”. Who this anonymous other team was is unclear, but in 1910 the new club merged with nearby Lindsey United just to make sure.

Hereford United: According to the club: “Before the formation of Hereford United there were four leading amateur clubs in Hereford and it was believed that a higher class of football could be sustained if they were to amalgamate. After a meeting in the city, both Hereford City and Hereford Thistle decided to remain independent while St Martins and RAOC (Rotherwas) decided to merge, and thus Hereford United was formed in 1924 with Dr E.W. Maples as chairman.”

Torquay United: A slightly labyrinthine one this. The original Torquay United merged with Ellacombe in 1910 to become, slightly counter-intuitively, Torquay Town. The new club took Ellacombe’s Plainmoor ground, sharing with Babbacombe FC, with whom they then merged in 1921, becoming Torquay United once more.

Maidenhead United: The wonderfully-named Maidenhead Norfolkians joined forces with Maidenhead FC in 1904. Initially Maidenhead Town, they became a United in 1920.

Sutton United: Formed in March 1898 by the amalgamation of two leading junior sides, Sutton Association and Sutton Guild Rovers.

Ebbsfleet United: A United formed of two Uniteds. Gravesend United and Northfleet United merged to form Gravesend & Northfleet FC in 1946, before becoming Ebbsfleet United in May 2007.

Hayes and Yeading United: One of the newest Uniteds, Hayes and Yeading were formed in May 2007 after the merger of Hayes and, yes, Yeading.

Chesham United: The merger of Chesham Town and their neighbours meant the football world was deprived of the brilliantly monikered Chesham Generals from 1917. United are currently flying high in the Zamaretto Premier.

Aylesbury United: The former Conference side “were founded in 1897 when three local sides: Night School FC, The Printing Works and Aylesbury Town decided to merge”.

Can you help?

“Malachi Fagan-Walcott’s final game of last season was for York City against Rochdale in the National League. His first competitive game of 2026-27 season was for Hearts against Sturm Graz in a Champions League qualifier. Has a player ever made a bigger leap in competitive levels between consecutive club games?” asks Tom Reed.

“On Sunday, Sean Murdoch was the referee for St Mirren v Dunfermline in the Scottish League Cup. Murdoch was previously a goalkeeper and played for Dunfermline. Are there any other examples of a former player refereeing a match for a club they had played for?” asks Ian Golightly.

“My beloved Kilmarnock have won only four of their 21 penalty shootouts, a 19% success rate,” writes Andy Kerr. “Does any professonal club have a worse record?”

“Seeing the picture of Omar Sivori in last week’s Knowledge, I noticed the referee in the background dressed in black, as was the norm. Were there any instances of colour clashes with the likes of Notts County, Newcastle, etc, causing problems during matches before referees went full spectrum?” wonders Paul Huby.

Sports.title: Real Madrid open talks over Rodri deal and Man City signing of wonderkid could allow for sale
Sports.content:
Real Madrid open talks over Rodri deal and Man City signing of wonderkid could allow for sale

Real Madrid have opened initials talks with Manchester City to sign Rodri, talkSPORT understands.

The Spanish midfielder has already made it clear he wants to join Real.

1 Rodri could secure a return to his homeland this summer Credit: Getty

City would like to keep Rodri this summer, even if the midfielder does not sign a new contract.

The 30-year-old's current deal is due to expire at the end of the season.

However, should City sign Morocco international Ayyoub Bouaddi, or another midfielder, they may be more inclined to let Rodri leave.

Should Real elect to press ahead, they will likely have to fork out a pretty penny for Rodri.

It is understood City value Rodri significantly higher than the reported numbers of €50million (£42m).

A move to Los Blancos would complete somewhat of a homecoming for Rodri, who was born and raised in Madrid.

He honed his craft in Atletico Madrid's academy for six years, only to return following a five-year stint at Villarreal.

But Rodri was only on Atleti's books for one season as City elected to trigger his £62.6m release clause in 2019.

The eight-figure fee has proved to be a shrewd investment from City.

Rodri has won an impressive 11 major trophies over the course of his time at the Etihad Stadium, including the Champions League and four Premier League titles.

Sports.title: Harry Kane backed to win prestigious award only eight players have won in 20 years
Sports.content:
Harry Kane backed to win prestigious award only eight players have won in 20 years

Harry Kane has been tipped to become the first Englishman to win the Ballon d'Or for 25 years.

The Bayern Munich striker is amongst the favourites to win the prestigious award at a ceremony in October.



3 Kane has been backed to win the Ballon d'Or after a stunning season for club and country Credit: Getty

World Cup winner Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe, who won the tournament's golden boot, are also in the running.

However, Kane has now received the backing of a former Tottenham Hotspur team-mate.

Kane's Ballon d'Or backing

Toby Alderweireld endorsed the England captain for the award during an appearance on Wednesday's Breakfast show.



The ex-Belgium defender joined Andy Goldstein and Andy Townsend live on air.

When asked if he thinks Kane should win the Ballon d'Or, Alderweireld replied: "For me, yes.



"I’m going to tell you why. Because before, it was always people who were quick, good dribblers and stuff like this. Of course, the (Lionel) Messi’s and (Cristiano) Ronaldo’s, but Harry is so good.

"Of course, he’s a goal scorer, but on the other hand, he’s a real team player. He makes the team play better.



"Everyone’s talking about that he’s dropping more into midfield, but his positioning is so good when you are under pressure and you want to get some breathing time.

"You put the ball to him, he uses his body so good. He’s a very good striker. I think he’s one of the best in the world. He’s very complete."

Kane's stunning season

Kane scored 61 goals in 51 appearances in all competitions for Bayern last season.

3 Kane's goals fired Bayern to a league and cup double as he scored 61 times for the club Credit: Getty



Those include 36 in the Bundesliga as he won a third successive golden boot as well a second European Golden Shoe.

Alongside their title triumph, Bayern completed a league and cup double by lifting the DFB Pokal, in which Kane also finished as top scorer.

As well as his goals, Kane also provided seven assists for his Bayern team-mates.

Meanwhile, his six goals for the Three Lions at the World Cup took his overall tally for club and country last term to 73 goals in 65 matches.



Elite company

Kane would become just the ninth different player to win the Ballon d'Or since 2006 if he is successful this year.

The award has been dominated by Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo over the last 20 years, with eight and five wins, respectively.

3 Ousmane Dembele became only the eighth different Ballon d'Or winner in 20 years in 2025 Credit: Getty

Ballon d'Or winners since 2006 2006: Fabio Cannavaro

2007: Kaka

2008: Cristiano Ronaldo

2009: Lionel Messi

2010: Lionel Messi

2011: Lionel Messi

2012: Lionel Messi

2013: Cristiano Ronaldo

2014: Cristiano Ronaldo

2015: Lionel Messi

2016: Cristiano Ronaldo

2017: Cristiano Ronaldo

2018: Luka Modric

2019: Lionel Messi

2021: Lionel Messi

2022: Karim Benzema

2023: Lionel Messi

2024: Rodri

2025: Ousmane Dembele

However, neither of them have received the honour since Messi's last triumph in 2023.



Instead, Rodri and Ousmane Dembele are the two latest recipients, with the former in the running again this year.

The Spain captain was named World Cup player of the tournament after his nation's second triumph in Canada, Mexico and the USA.

Kane would also be the first Englishmen to win the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001 and only the fifth ever.

His current best finish in the award's rankings is 10th, which he achieved in 2017, 2018 and 2024.



Last year's ceremony saw Kane ranked 13th overall between Paris Saint-Germain pair Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Desire Doue.

Sports.title: Toby Alderweireld reveals best ever teammate – and it’s not Harry Kane or Eden Hazard
Sports.content:
Toby Alderweireld reveals best ever teammate – and it’s not Harry Kane or Eden Hazard

Toby Alderweireld has told talkSPORT that people are surprised when he names Mousa Dembele as the best player he's played with.

The retired Tottenham and Belgium defender shared a dressing room with the 39-year-old for both club and country across his career.

5 Alderweireld made a total of 236 appearances for Spurs between 2015 and 2021 Credit: Getty - Contributor

Alderweireld spent six years with Spurs after joining from Atlético Madrid in 2015 following a season-long loan at Southampton.

The 37-year-old, who ultimately played 236 times for the club, helped the Lilywhites record three top-three finishes in the Premier League and reach their only ever Champions League final in 2019.

Spurs also had the best Premier League defensive record in each of the seasons between 2014 and 2017 under Mauricio Pochettino.

The majority of which saw Alderweireld partner compatriot Jan Vertonghen in central defence, with World Cup winner Hugo Lloris in goal, and England pair Kyle Walker and Danny Rose at full-back.

'Pochettino made us very, very fit'

"I think we were scary, like the names you said," Alderweireld reflected to talkSPORT Breakfast duo Andy Goldstein and Andy Townsend.

"But then in front of us, we had Mousa Dembele, Victor Wanyama, Eric Dier. That was a proper team. We were physically so strong.

"Pochettino made us very, very fit. And all the guys had a good mentality. They worked hard. They didn't complain.

"We did everything the manager asked us to do. And yeah, and that's what you saw from the first second.

"We were pressing, we were fighting. We were physically strong. And of course, we had the quality as well. Think about Jan Vertonghen, Mousa Dembele, Christian Eriksen. Those are very, very good players."

5 Alderweireld's Tottenham team are among the greatest Premier League sides to have never won the title Credit: Getty

Despite their undoubted quality, Tottenham were unable to get over the line and win a trophy during Alderweireld's spell at the club.

The Belgian was part of the team who set a Premier League record for most points in a single season with 86 in 2016/17.

For reference, that is one more point than rivals Arsenal accumulated to win the title last season, but in Tottenham's case, they were pipped by Chelsea's epic 93-point haul.
