The 25-year-old heptathlete won world silver in Tokyo last year, and a showdown with Katarina Johnson-Thompson was set to be one of the highlights of the Commonwealth Games athletics programme.

In the absence of the double world champion, who decided to prioritise next month's European Championships in Birmingham, O'Connor found herself comfortably clear of England's Jade O'Dowda after four events, despite struggling with appalling weather conditions at Scotstoun. It's a new feeling coming into a major championship with all the pressure on," she said.

Article continues below

"I'm not the newbie anymore who can surprise people. I normally really thrive under pressure, so hopefully that continues. It wasn't my best day, but I'm still leading and I'm in a good position. I was really nervous before the hurdles, but it was solid, nothing more.

"I didn't execute as well as I can in the high jump, and my shot was atrocious. It was just miserable. You can't blame the weather – you have to cope with the elements in this sport. My 200m was a lot better, but I can't be complacent or I'll get beaten."

Sports.title: Chelsea’s dream final month of transfer window as Alex Scott and World Cup wonderkid sign
Sports.content:
Chelsea’s dream final month of transfer window as Alex Scott and World Cup wonderkid sign

Chelsea have wasted little time splashing the cash this summer but the Xabi Alonso rebuild at Stamford Bridge is far from complete with several key pieces still needed

View 7 Images Xabi Alonso is looking to hit the ground running as Chelsea boss (Image: Getty Images)

Chelsea are entering the final stretch of the summer transfer window with plenty still to solve. Xabi Alonso has wasted little time putting his fingerprints on the squad, with the Blues beginning a significant reshaping process designed to reflect the Spaniard's tactical demands.

But while formations and recruitment remain central to the rebuild, there is another area Chelsea must address - adding more experience, personality and leadership to a group that has often lacked those qualities under the current ownership.

There have already been signs of the new era taking shape. The arrival of Morgan Rogers for a club-record £117million was a major statement of intent, particularly after many had expected Arsenal to secure his signature. Chelsea have also moved to strengthen their defensive options by bringing in Atalanta wing-back Marco Palestra for £43m.

‌



However, the biggest challenges of the window may still lie ahead. Chelsea need further additions if they are to build a squad capable of competing on all fronts. And it isn't just spending that will get them there, it's careful squad management, with arrivals and departures and internal man-management needed.

With that in mind, we're examining what a dream end to Chelsea's summer transfer window might look like.

FOLLOW OUR CHELSEA FB PAGE! Latest Blues news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Xabi Alonso drops telling hint over Chelsea’s Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck transfers READ MORE :

Xabi Alonso left with easy transfer decision as Chelsea win Western Sydney Wanderers goalfest READ MORE :

Get Lacroix over the line

The immediate priority should be finalising the £52m acquisition of Maxence Lacroix. The Crystal Palace centre back has been Chelsea's leading defensive target throughout the summer and would bring a level of physicality, composure and experience that has been missing from their backline.

Reports suggest an agreement has already been reached with Palace, with Lacroix completing his medical earlier this week. The French defender, who represented his country at the World Cup, has established himself as one of the Premier League's most dependable defenders since arriving at Selhurst Park from Wolfsburg in 2024.

His arrival would hand Alonso the perfect profile to anchor a back three alongside Levi Colwill. The 26-year-old is also capable of operating in a conventional four-man defence, offering Chelsea greater adaptability depending on the tactical challenge ahead.

‌



View 7 Images Maxence Lacroix is on the verge of joining Chelsea (Image: Jared C. Tilton - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)

Secure Welbeck and Henderson

For a squad built around emerging talent, adding experienced veterans such as Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson - both of whom Chelsea are now expected to bring in - would provide an immediate injection of maturity. Their combined experience at club and international level is exactly what the dressing room has lacked during difficult spells.

Welbeck would give Alonso a dependable attacking option who can perform multiple roles and understands the demands of Premier League football better than most. Henderson, meanwhile, would bring relentless professionalism, high standards and a commanding voice to help guide Chelsea's younger midfielders.

‌



Landing both players on short-term contracts would represent a relatively small financial commitment compared to Chelsea's usual spending, while potentially delivering huge benefits behind the scenes. More importantly, it would demonstrate that the ownership can recognise weaknesses within their project - a criticism that has followed them because of their consistent focus on developing young players.

View 7 Images Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson look set to join Chelsea (Image: Getty)

Sign a left wing-back

Following Marc Cucurella's move to Real Madrid, finding a starting-quality left wing-back remains essential to completing Alonso's tactical vision. Rayo Vallecano's Pep Chavarria has become the leading candidate after impressing in La Liga with his energy, defensive discipline and willingness to constantly push forward.

‌



However, Vallecano are refusing to budge on their valuation, insisting Chelsea activate the player's £42.4m release clause, leaving the Blues to consider alternatives if talks stall. Whether Chavarria or another target arrives, Alonso needs a player who can stretch opponents, deliver consistently from wide areas and offer a constant attacking outlet.

Completing this deal would allow Chelsea to fully embrace Alonso's preferred 3-4-2-1 shape, creating balance across both flanks after already adding Palestra on the opposite side.

View 7 Images Chelsea are still working on a deal to sign wing back Pep Chavarria (Image: Aitor Alcalde Colomer)

‌



£70m Alex Scott deal

Chelsea have reportedly already tested Bournemouth's resolve with an initial £64m offer for Alex Scott, but increasing that bid towards £70m could be enough to secure the midfielder. He has developed into one of the Premier League's most complete young central midfielders, blending the ability to escape pressure with outstanding progression of the ball.

With Andrey Santos gone and Romeo Lavia continuing to battle injury problems, Chelsea cannot afford to enter the new season lacking options in the middle of the pitch. Scott's ability to carry possession, control matches and inject energy would provide Alonso with another valuable midfield weapon.

A midfield featuring Moises Caicedo and Enzo Fernandez behind Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers would already boast exceptional quality, but depth remains a concern. Bringing in Scott would solve that issue while also underlining Chelsea's ambition, especially if they beat off competition from other Premier League clubs chasing his signature.

‌



View 7 Images Chelsea have submitted an opening bid for Alex Scott (Image: James Gill - Danehouse/Getty Images)

Sign wonderkid winger

Chelsea are also looking to strengthen their attacking depth by pursuing Bayer Leverkusen teenager Kerim Alajbegovic. Alonso knows the youngster well from his spell in Germany and will have followed his impressive development through Leverkusen's academy system.

With Alejandro Garnacho completing a loan switch to Aston Villa, signing Alajbegovic would ensure Chelsea still possess serious competition and explosiveness out wide. The Bosnian winger combines electric pace with creativity, making him the type of high-upside prospect who could develop alongside Jamie Gittens, Geovany Quenda and Estevao.

‌



Convincing Leverkusen to sell such a promising talent will not be straightforward, but the teenager is believed to be available for around £30m. Considering his potential, that figure could eventually look like excellent business.

View 7 Images Kerim Alajbegovic impressed at the World Cup (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

Keep Enzo Fernandez

Retaining Enzo Fernandez is arguably the most important task Chelsea face before the transfer deadline. Questions over his future have intensified after the midfielder made indications - both subtle and obvious - that he wants to move elsewhere. Losing him would represent a huge setback.

‌



Alonso will need to speak with the Argentine once he returns from his post-World Cup break and convince him that Stamford Bridge remains the ideal environment for the next stage of his career. Since arriving from Benfica in a then-British record £105m transfer in 2023, Fernandez has become one of Chelsea's central figures. Yet after three-and-a-half years without the club establishing itself as a serious title challenger, it is understandable why the 25-year-old is questioning his future.

Chelsea remain in a strong position, however. Fernandez is tied down until 2032, while their £120m valuation would likely scare away all but the richest clubs. Real Madrid, once considered the most likely destination, have also reportedly eased their pursuit in recent weeks.

View 7 Images Enzo Fernandez has made it clear that he wants to leave Chelsea (Image: Harry Langer/DeFodi Images/DeFodi via Getty Images)

‌



Even so, Alonso cannot allow the uncertainty to continue. Restoring Fernandez's faith in Chelsea's direction and ensuring his attention remains fully focused on the club should be one of the manager's biggest priorities.

Shift deadwood

New arrivals must be matched by departures, and Chelsea still need to reduce the size of their squad before the window closes. They have already made progress by selling Cucurella, Santos and Tyrique George for substantial fees and sending Garnacho to Aston Villa on loan, but the clear-out is far from finished.

Welbeck's arrival would create further congestion in attack. Joao Pedro is expected to begin the season as Alonso's first-choice striker, leaving Welbeck, Liam Delap, Nicolas Jackson and new arrival Emmanuel Emegha - signed from Strasbourg last year - competing for limited opportunities.

‌



With Emegha likely to leave on loan, Chelsea should consider permanently moving on either Delap or Jackson. Jackson would probably attract the higher fee following his productive loan spell at Bayern Munich last season, but after Delap's underwhelming debut campaign at Stamford Bridge, selling the English forward could arguably be the cleaner solution.

The defence also requires attention. Benoit Badiashile, Wesley Fofana and Axel Disasi all have uncertain futures, and removing at least two of them would lower the wage bill, raise additional funds and leave Alonso with a more streamlined squad capable of challenging across every competition.

Sports.title: Sir Geoff Hurst and England fans recall 1966 World Cup glory exactly 60 years on
Sports.content:
Sir Geoff Hurst and England fans recall 1966 World Cup glory exactly 60 years on

Sir Geoff, 84, told the Mirror: "I still get stopped all the time by fans who tell me what they were doing on the day we won the World Cup"

View 4 Images The moment we will never forget - England captain Bobby Moore holds the Jules Rimet trophy aloft (Image: Mirrorpix via Getty Images)

It is 60 years since the greatest moment in our footballing history - and one man can remember it like it was yesterday.

‌



Hat-trick hero Sir Geoff Hurst says he is still stopped everywhere he goes with people keen to share their memories of the World Cup final - July 30, 1966 - when his life changed forever. They remember Kenneth Wolstenholme's iconic commentary line: "Some people are on the pitch! They think it's all over... it is now!"

‌



Fans, the families of the '66 heroes, and legends of the game have told the Mirror of their memories of the epic encounter against our old rivals. Sir Geoff met with fans from that era who are now living in Hendon Hall, a residential home, at a Budweiser event in London. Hendon Hall was the hotel where the England team stayed before the final back in '66.

‌



Sir Geoff, 84, told the Mirror: "I still get stopped all the time by fans who tell me what they were doing on the day we won the World Cup. I have such great admiration and feeling for those who remember the game and the day. I meet people on a regular basis and see how significant the day was.

View 4 Images Sir Geoff Hurst in 1974 with England team mates Martin Peters (left) and Bobby Moore (Image: Mirrorpix)

"It is an honour to meet the fans who were at Wembley on the day. You realise, even now, what a huge part it played in their lives and how they remember it."

‌



Jack and Bobby Charlton were feted with an open top limousine ride when they returned to their hometown, Ashington, Northumberland. Their dad Bob was working a shift down the pit for both the quarter-final against Argentina and the semi-final against Portugal.

For the final, the Mirror paid for Bob and his wife Cissie - the football-loving mum of the Charltons - to travel to Wembley to see the match. But their late brother Gordon, a merchant seaman, listened the final on a ship in Singapore.

View 4 Images (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire)

‌



Manchester Utd legend Nobby Stiles was convinced he was going to be dropped for the game, before Sir Alf Ramsey assured him that he was in the team. His wife Kay, who still lives in the family home in Manchester, was worried about him missing out right up until the day before the final.

Nobby's son John, 62, of Doncaster, said his dad saw a sign held up by fans saying 'Nobby for Prime Minister' on the way to Wembley, which team mate Alan Ball pointed out to him.

He recalled: "He told my mum that he was convinced he was going to be dropped. The TV pundits were all saying that he should be dropped after the Argentina game. He thought the country was against him.

‌



"Then at training Sir Alf came up to him, and Dad was convinced he was going to be dropped. But he just said: "You are playing tomorrow.' He later discovered the FA had called him in and told him to drop my dad, but he refused and said he would resign.

View 4 Images Sir Geoff says he is stopped everywhere he goes by people wanting to share their memories of 1966 (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire)

"On the way to Wembley, Alan Ball nudged him and about 100 Cockneys held a sign that read, 'Nobby for Prime Minister'. So he felt 10ft tall when Alan pointed that sign out to him."

‌



John added: "Wherever dad went on the after-dinner speaking circuit, people wanted to tell him what they were doing on the day that he danced with the World Cup trophy. They would say 'do you know where I was?', as if my dad was supposed to know. But he never left without signing an autograph or posing for a picture for the fans who wanted to meet him."

Peter Laurence, now a resident in Hendon Hall, was on a Dover to Calais ferry listening to the final on a transistor radio.

He recalled: "We were driving to southern Italy. I never thought that they were going to get to the final and Geoff said: 'You bloody coward!' I was very peeved when they got there." England scored the winner as they got into port in Calais.

Article continues below

"We jumped up and down like dervishes, got into a local hostelry where we proceeded to get hammered and we met some Germans. We put our arms around each other. It was the German equivalent of entente cordiale."

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino is out of control and a danger to football - he has to be stopped
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino is out of control and a danger to football - he has to be stopped

Gianni Infantino has shown his true colours in setting out his plan to sell a stake in the global game to private investors - the time has come to topple him as FIFA's president

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino wants to take FIFA's commercial powers to a new level (Image: Eva Marie Uzcategui/FIFA via Getty Images)

FIFA is a not-for-profit organisation which has made $13billion (£9.6bn) in the last four years.

‌



Under Gianni Infantino’s leadership, world football’s governing body has leaned into that contradiction, pursuing all-out expansion and commercialisation.

‌



Growing the game. That has been Infantino’s oft-stated goal. More, more, more. Bigger, more frequent tournaments. Higher ticket prices. Half-time entertainment. Celebrities, influencers, dignitaries and heads of state in the stands.

‌



It has won him plenty of friends and supporters. A fourth term as FIFA president had been expected, with the various controversies of the World Cup – a denied visa for a Somali referee, Iran’s travel struggles, Donald Trump’s meddling in disciplinary proceedings – water off a duck’s back.

The Guardian reported recently that more than 200 FIFA members had endorsed Infantino for re-election. On Tuesday it became clearer why that might be.

UEFA nations could BOYCOTT World Cup in light of FIFA's plot to sell tournament READ MORE :

Gary Lineker shows FIFA disgust in four-word response to Gianni Infantino bombshell READ MORE :

Infantino wants to create a subsidiary worth $20billion (£15bn) and then sell off 20 per cent of FIFA Forward Enterprise to investors to raise $4.2bn (£3.16bn). The idea was communicated in a press release so boring, perhaps deliberately, an effort to obscure the stark reality: that he wants to sell off chunks of the global game for profit.

‌



Profit for Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared, who is leading the proposed investor group. Profit for Infantino himself, who according to The Times, could become commissioner of the company once he steps down as FIFA president. And profit for FIFA’s 211 members.

Infantino has sent a letter to FIFA’s member associations telling them they will each receive $40m (£30m) by January if they agree to the proposal by September 19. A source told The Times on Wednesday that it amounted to “pure bribery”.

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino is using methods from Donald Trump's playbook (Image: Eva Marie Uzcategui/FIFA via Getty Images)

‌



It is a brazen attempt to get his way and something straight out of the Trump playbook. Infantino has ingratiated himself with the US President, inventing the farcical FIFA Peace Prize to appeal to his ego. Bizarrely, he recently received an endorsement to become the next United Nations chief in return.

Infantino has somehow created a cult of personality, which for a career lawyer and administrator from Switzerland, is impressive. The white trademark trainers with a suit. The ludicrous “today I feel” speech. The recent rambling letter imploring his haters to “meditate or pray".

He is completely self-obsessed and, having spent the last six weeks flying around on a private jet to hold court with the world’s leaders, his ego has run out of control.

‌



For many, that could be forgiven or overlooked. But now we are seeing the dangers of having such an egomaniac in charge of world football.

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino had been expected to win re-election for a fourth term (Image: Florencia Tan Jun, Getty Images)

Infantino has pressed launch on the biggest shockwave in football since the European Super League debacle five years ago. That self-interested power grab collapsed embarrassingly almost straight away, overcome by the sheer immediate force of the backlash.

‌



FIFA’s smaller members will no doubt be wooed by the promise of cash. But the bigger, more powerful nations must take a stand against Infantino’s ludicrous plot to sell off the crown jewels. The response from UEFA, the FA and Concacaf is promising.

The plot must be foiled – and it could have the added benefit of toppling Infantino from power if a rival for the presidency steps up. Football is at the top of a slippery slope. His megalomania must be challenged.

Sports.title: Geoff Hurst finally finds out how he was spotted as England potential by Alf Ramsey 60 years later
Sports.content:
1966 legend Geoff Hurst has just learnt for the very first time how he was spotted as a potential England player by manager Sir Alf Ramsey.

Incredibly, it was in a League Cup second round game for West Ham against Division Three minnows Mansfield Town on October 13, 1965 in front of just 11,590 people. Hurst said he was “completely unaware” that Ramsey was even at the game.

The match was played five months before Hurst made his England debut and, of course, later that year he became the first man to ever score a hat-trick in a World Cup final - exactly 60 years ago.

View 7 Images Eton Manor legend Graham Phillips (right) with respected author and historian Grant Bage (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

‌



England icon was left penniless and forced to sell jumpers from his 1-bed flat READ MORE :

The extraordinary revelation was uncovered by Ramsey’s biographer Grant Bage in a series of new interviews. Ramsey told one of his closest friends, respected amateur team manager Charlie Phillips how he was impressed by how Hurst handled long balls from Bobby Moore that night.

Two of Hurst’s goals at Wembley in the 4-2 win over West Germany came from long passes from Moore. Now Bage, who spent six years researching and writing his biography The Unseen Sir Alf, has informed Hurst who had no idea Ramsey was even at that particular match.

Hurst replied: “I was completely unaware that this happened, which completely changed not only my football life, but my life. October 13th was obviously a very lucky day as I got married on that day 64 years ago. Thank you again.”

View 7 Images Geoff Hurst in his West Ham days (Image: Popperfoto via Getty Images)

‌



Bage said: “Even sixty years on, we keep unearthing new information about Sir Alf Ramsey and the 1966 World Cup. It’s incredible that these ‘nuggets’ are coming out so many years later. It’s amazing that, on an October night at Upton Park at a League cup match against Mansfield, that Alf formulated his thoughts and plans for the World Cup.

“Football was rarely filmed in the 1960s, so the England manager slogged his way round watching hundreds of games, just to work out who the best English players were. And Hurst wasn’t even the player he was going to watch. But now we know that what he saw that night sowed the seeds of World Cup glory.

View 7 Images Geoff Hurst gave Mirrorman Andy Lines exclusive interview before World Cup (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

‌



"Alf Ramsey conquered world football through hard work and attention to detail. Just imagine if he hadn’t bothered to go to that game. Geoff Hurst didn’t even know about it which makes it all the remarkable.”

Bage found the new information after meeting Graham Phillips - son of Charlie Phillips the manager of East London non-league side Eton Manor. Hurst, who played 499 games for West Ham, has little memory of the match which was played almost 61 years ago. Ramsey was coaching them at the time and Charlie became a great friend and trusted confidante.

Bage said: “I can’t thank Graham enough for coming forward with all this detailed extra information. It helps us learn more about how Alf slotted together the only England team to ever win the World Cup."

View 7 Images Eton Manor legend and stalwart Graham Phillips (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

‌



Graham said: “Alf and my dad Charlie had two long telephone conversations, both instigated by Alf, in the immediate aftermath of the 1966 triumph. It was in these telephone discussions that Alf conveyed stories about the World Cup to Charlie.

“There were other conversations, but these were the main ones. But you have to understand that Charlie didn't sit us down after his chats with Alf and brief us on what had been said. The information came out from him gradually, on different occasions, like when we were sitting watching TV, or some relevant story had been in the paper.

“What I recall above all else is my father describing how Alf had, under the Upton Park floodlights, told me that he had witnessed ‘the second coming of Tommy Taylor’. That was a deeply significant comparison, which needs explaining for a modern audience.

“In March 1953 Tommy Taylor had signed for Manchester United, aged just 21. His 112 league goals, in a total of 166 league appearances, helped United win successive league championships in 1955-56, and 1956-57. In 19 senior appearances for England, he also scored 16 goals. Tragically, Tommy Taylor was then one of eight Manchester United players killed in the Munich air disaster of February 6, 1958, his 26th birthday having been reached the week before he died.

‌



View 7 Images Eton Manor legend Graham Phillips with respected author and historian Grant Bage (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

“Alf Ramsey was not prone to hyperbole, so for him to compare Geoff Hurst to Tommy Taylor was amazing: especially as Hurst was not even the main reason Ramsey had gone to watch this particular game. Alf told Charlie that Ronnie Boyce was the ‘intended’ prime target, and perhaps to take another look at Johnny Byrne.

“What must also be remembered by modern football fans, to make sense of this, is that in the mid-1960s there was very little filming of football. Most league games were also played either at 3pm on a Saturday, or on Tuesday or Wednesday evenings early in the season, before cup competitions had got going.

View 7 Images Geoff Hurst scores England's controversial third goal (Image: Getty Images)

‌



“Consequently, if Alf Ramsey wanted to review any promising English player, he needed to attend hundreds of games himself: which is why the England manager undertook this particular scouting mission to West Ham’s unpromising midweek, early-stage league cup game against lower-league opposition.

“Alf told his friend Charlie that, as it happened, Alf had phoned West Ham out of courtesy to tell them he would be attending. Unfortunately, he did not manage to speak to their manager, Ron Greenwood, so did not know whether his message had got through. “Ironically, HAD Ramsey talked to Greenwood, he may not even have made the trip! As things turned out, neither Ronnie Boyce nor Johnny Byrne would play that night, against Third Division Mansfield Town, in round three of the League Cup. Luckily though, Alf went anyway.”

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino's heinous plan must be stopped - but the FA should take a hard look at themselves first
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino's heinous plan must be stopped - but the FA should take a hard look at themselves first

The FIFA president's plans to sell the World Cup off to private investors has provoked widespread condemnation but the European governing body might want to take a long hard look at itself and its own commercial dealings

View 2 Images FIFA President Gianni Infantino exchanges gifts with The Football Association President Debbie Hewitt (Image: 2026 FIFA)

There is, of course, a quite stark irony in UEFA and all of us in these parts taking the high moral ground over Gianni Infantino’s proposal to sell the World Cup off to private investors. When it comes to selling out to the highest commercial bidders, UEFA and the Premier League and the Football Association and the rest of the elite European nations have been the trailblazers.

‌



Remember when the European Cup was a thing of single-tie knockout beauty? Probably not. That was before UEFA sold its name and birthright to Russian oil companies and the like, and turned it into a bloated, corporate mess with its own phoney anthem.

‌



Remember Gazprom? UEFA were not so moralistic then. Don’t forget, UEFA executives love a VIP gig and a freebie as much as FIFA executives do.

‌



On Aleksander Ceferin’s watch, the Champions League has become a commercial monstrosity. And as much as Infantino is a power-obsessed egotist who needs dethroning, he is only following a template set by those in Europe who rinse football followers for everything they’ve got.

In professional terms, Infantino is a wrong ‘un, of that there is absolutely no doubt. But since when have we been able to sermonise about the sanctity of football?

Gary Lineker shows FIFA disgust in four-word response to Gianni Infantino bombshell READ MORE :

UEFA nations could BOYCOTT World Cup in light of FIFA's plot to sell tournament READ MORE :

The Premier League has had - and continues to have - a quite spectacular disregard for the traditional match-going fan who might be a bit hard up. How about putting our own house in order? We sold our game to television.

‌



Perhaps politicians could do something meaningful instead of jumping on a bandwagon. Intoxicated with his carefully-acquired power, Andy Burnham, the professional Evertonian, has waded in.

“Football does not belong to investors,” he posted in one of his many social media missives. Really, Andy? So how come you want the Glazers and the great Sir Jim Ratcliffe to benefit in their hundreds of millions by having a new 100,000-seater stadium facilitated by local and central government?

As uncomfortable as Infantino’s plans sound, how about you concentrate on making sure your constituents can afford or have a chance to go to a game? Burnham’s social media message was truly laughable.

‌



“Dress the deal up however you like,” he said. “Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.”

Mate, the World Cup was sold out an age ago. It was sold out when it went to Russia. It was sold out when it went to Qatar. Didn’t hear a peep from you then.

‌



English football has sold out, lock, stock and barrel. Look at the FA Cup, for goodness sake, a competition that has sold its birthright and traditions for a fast buck.

Do something about that, Prime Minister. Have a word with those at the FA who thought it was a good idea to present the FIFA president with an England shirt with his name on the back recently.

View 2 Images Gianni Infantino has been praised by Donald Trump for the commercial success of World Cup 2026 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Look, Infantino’s ruse is reprehensible yet entirely predictable. And sadly, understandable. Hopefully, the backlash will be sufficient to get rid of him, but you doubt it.

After all, his idea of selling the World Cup off to private investors will have players and their agents licking their lips. Imagine how much a star player will be able to charge for a few weeks work on the grand stage.

And the chances are that the fans - ripped off at every turn by the current set-up - will not really care that much. It is still a proposal that demands opposition. Vehement opposition.

Article continues below

But maybe UEFA and the European footballing bigwigs - including our own - should have a long, hard look at themselves first. Because they have paved the way for FIFA’s greed.

Sports.title: Luis Diaz hands Liverpool Bradley Barcola transfer boost as final decision made
Sports.content:
Luis Diaz hands Liverpool Bradley Barcola transfer boost as final decision made

Liverpool are targeting PSG winger Bradley Barcola this summer, and their chances of a deal have been boosted by former Reds forward Luis Diaz

View 2 Images Former Liverpool forward Luis Diaz has made a decision over his future (Image: David Ramos, Getty Images)

Bayern Munich winger Luis Diaz may have provided a boost to Liverpool's hopes of signing Bradley Barcola this summer. The Reds have been heavily linked with the PSG forward as they continue their search for a Mohamed Salah replacement.

‌



Salah left Anfield at the end of the season, leaving Liverpool searching for a way to replace his goals and assists. Barcola seems to be the player who has come out as the number one target, although a deal is expected to cost over £100 million.

‌



Our sister title The Liverpool ECHO reports that it is unlikely to put Andoni Iraola's side off making a move. They do, however, face competition from both Bayern Munich and Arsenal, and this is where Diaz comes in.

‌



Liverpool chief provides FSG investment update after Jeff Bezos talks READ MORE :

Jurgen Klopp given strict instruction about managing Germany days after making quit threat READ MORE :

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

The Colombian has been a resounding success at the Allianz Arena since completing a £66million switch from Liverpool last summer. During his debut season in Germany, he netted 26 goals and laid on 23 assists across 51 appearances in all competitions.

That impressive form has attracted attention from Saudi outfit Al-Hilal. French publication L'Equipe claimed that the club were preparing to table an opening bid of at least €70million (£60m) for the wide man.

‌



However, Sky Germany reports that Diaz has informed Bayern that he wishes to remain at the club. The German champions are therefore unwilling to enter into negotiations with any club regarding a potential transfer, and have not placed an asking price on Diaz.

The 29-year-old still has three years left to run on his contract at the club. With Diaz's future appearing to be settled, this should bring Bayern's pursuit of Barcola to a close. With all of their attacking options remaining in place, they are unlikely to venture into the transfer market to bolster that area of their squad.

View 2 Images Bradley Barcola is emerging as a key transfer target for Liverpool (Image: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista, Getty Images)

‌



Arsenal are also said to be prioritising a move for Real Madrid forward Vinicius Junior over Barcola. This could potentially leave Liverpool with a clear path to the PSG star.

The French club may have been more receptive to a transfer amid their pursuit of RB Leipzig's Yan Diomande, who had also attracted Liverpool's attention. They have, however, been pipped to the post by Real Madrid.

PSG have since taken the remarkable step of issuing a statement confirming they have withdrawn from the race for the Ivory Coast international. "PSG has this evening officially withdrawn its interest and its bids for Yan Diomande," the statement read.

‌



"The asking transfer fee and salary demands were completely disproportionate and distortive - and PSG will not break its principles of rational financial management and squad balance.

"As a two-time consecutive Champions League winner and the most successful club in recent years, PSG will also not engage in the inflationary and manipulative games of certain player agents - and will instead calmly and confidently continue its transfer planning."

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
