World.title: Wildfire smoke: A health emergency beyond the flames, WHO warns
World.content:
Fires are sweeping southern Europe in what is now one of the worst wildfire seasons in years. The situation has forced mass evacuations, damaged infrastructure and claimed lives.

 

Their toll on people's health and on healthcare systems is also rising across the region.

“These are not merely fire episodes affecting livelihoods and creating this immediate danger; it's a true health emergency”, Dorota Jarosinska, Programme Manager at the World Health Organization’s European Centre for Climate Change, Environment and Health, told Euronews Health.

She added that the impacts may continue long after the fire is out, and can be felt at considerable distance from where the wildfire took place.

“This smoke coming from wildfires may travel hundreds, if not thousands of kilometres, impairing air quality in places very distant from the fire itself, including urban areas that are heavily inhabited, affecting potentially many people,” Jarosinska added.

“It's not necessary to see the flames or to see a plume of smoke to experience the health risk”.

What wildfire smoke is, and why it’s harmful

Wildfire smoke is a mix of toxic pollutants, particulate matter and gases. The health risks can vary depending on what is burning, as fires often consume plastics, electronics and paints that release toxic chemicals into the air.

“These small, fine particles can really penetrate from the lungs to our blood and trigger a response in our organism, activating our immune system and causing inflammation,” Jarosinska said.

While symptoms among healthy people can be mild, such as throat irritation and a runny nose, Jarosinska noted that those with underlying health conditions can suffer a far greater impact.

People with asthma or chronic pulmonary disease are particularly vulnerable, as are those with heart disease, along with children and older people.

"The symptoms are diverse and can range from mild to very severe, even life-threatening," Jarosinska added.

Public health advice must not leave anyone behind

Yet, Jarosinska noted that public health advice tends to be general, aimed at the broader population rather than tailored to those most at risk.

Beyond recommendations such as staying indoors and limiting exercise, guidance that benefits everyone, even if the need varies with air quality, Jarosinska called for more nuanced advice that better accounts for vulnerable groups.

“Advice is also given to use air conditioning and these high efficiency filters and that's very good advice for those who have these devices,” Jarosinska said.

However, she warned that some of these guidelines can leave behind people who lack access to such equipment, or to air-conditioned or clean-air spaces.

According to Jarosinska, part of the authorities' responsibility is to provide spaces where people can cool down and access clean air, and to ensure these are available to everyone in the community.

“[Authorities must] take care also of those who are more disadvantaged, who cannot access health care, who don't know the local language, who have no access to information,” she added.

A growing strain on healthcare systems

This drive towards resilience and preparedness for climate emergencies also includes reinforcing the capacity of healthcare systems, Jarosinska noted.

“When we talk about exposure to wildfire smoke and health impact, we think of individuals, their individual suffering and problems. But it's also really a huge strain on the health sector.”

She stressed that healthcare professionals need to be trained and equipped with the right information: they need to understand what poor air quality means, how to communicate it, and what advice to give to each patient.

"The immediate priority is to strengthen the position of the health sector: to train people, to equip them, so that the health argument is communicated more strongly and factored into local action," Jarosinska added.

World.title: Ireland unveils blueprint to electrify economy by 2050
World.content:
Ireland has announced a sweeping review of its electricity system, with the government promising a blueprint to reshape the country's power sector by 2050 as it races to meet climate targets and electrify its economy.

 

Irish Climate, Energy and Environment Minister Darragh O'Brien said on Wednesday that work is underway on a long-term strategy to set out how Ireland plans to generate, transmit and regulate electricity through to 2050.

The move from Dublin comes as Ireland has taken the helm of the rotating EU Council Presidency and vowed to make electrification a priority.

The disruption in the Middle East has also revealed how the EU's dependence on imported fossil fuels is leading to higher energy bills and inflation, with roughly an extra €50 billion spent on fossil fuel imports in just 111 days during disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz.

"Ireland's energy transition represents a momentous opportunity for us all, to help make our economy and industries more efficient and competitive, to open new opportunities for businesses, and create tangible benefits for our communities across Ireland," O'Brien said.

The new "Power Sector White Paper" is expected to become the cornerstone of future energy policy, guiding legislation, investment decisions and grid development as Ireland shifts away from fossil fuels towards an electricity-based economy.

The review comes as electricity demand is forecast to surge over the coming decades, driven by electric vehicles, heat pumps, industry and rapidly expanding data centres, putting growing pressure on the national grid.

Data centres, in particular, consumed 23% of Ireland's total metered electricity in 2025, scaling up from 5% in 2015. According to the Irish Central Statistics Office, total usage almost matched the electricity used by all urban and rural households combined (28%).

At the EU level, political talks are underway to agree on how to modernise the bloc's ageing power grid. More than a technicality, revamping the EU's grids is paramount for EU countries to fully utilise the vast amounts of renewable energy produced and ultimately electrify the bloc's economy.

Adding pressure to the race towards electrification, the European Commission has recently announced a 46% electrification target by 2040, in a bid to encourage EU countries to boost related investments.

A holistic approach to electrify Ireland's economy

The White Paper will examine some of the biggest questions facing the energy transition, the Irish government said. This includes how much electricity Ireland will need, where it will come from, how the grid should evolve and how the country can balance the competing priorities of affordability, security of supply and decarbonisation.

A statement from the Irish Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment said the strategy will be backed by detailed modelling of future energy scenarios, including risk assessments, demand forecasts, infrastructure needs and governance arrangements.

"This White Paper will be a key part of guiding the energy transition to clean, secure, affordable electricity. It will set a path to deliver — for this generation and future generations," O'Brien added.

"It will require national conversation and collaboration. Starting today, I invite all stakeholders across government and the public, private and voluntary sectors to work with us on this initiative."

The initiative forms part of Ireland's commitment to achieve climate neutrality by 2050 under EU law, with electrification remaining the government's central strategy for cutting emissions across transport, heating and industry.

France was the first EU country to announce its own electrification plan aimed at cutting reliance on fossil fuels. Other EU countries are likely to follow suit.

However, for the EU to fully succeed in electrifying the bloc's economy, the current high electricity prices must be addressed, or households and businesses won't have sufficient incentives to switch.

The Commission recently asked member states to ensure that electricity is not taxed more heavily than gas, while leaving governments free to determine the structure of their national tax systems under the EU's energy taxation rules.

Eva Schwab, energy poverty policy officer at the European Federation of National Organisations working with the homeless, said that electrification will only succeed if everyone is included.

Schwab regretted that the Commission plan, seen as a model for EU countries to emulate, makes no mention of energy poverty.

"Without targeted support, the households that stand to benefit most from lower energy bills will remain locked into expensive fossil fuels while better-off households capture most of the gains.”

World.title: EU coordinates wildfire aid for France and Spain amid warnings heatwave could spread
World.content:
Europe had its share of wildfires recently, and there is still no clear end to it, as the disaster continues to ravage swathes of France and Spain.

 

Experts in the European Union are monitoring the latest developments at the emergency coordination centre in Brussels, while crews on the ground battle to contain the blazes.

These EU officials are playing a vital role, as they are responsible for reallocating limited resources across Europe to ensure the right equipment is delivered on time to where it is needed.

"The team is monitoring the situation, monitoring the risk in France, how it will develop, and is in continuous contact with the French authorities to see whether they need additional support," Maria Zuber, the head of the unit, explained on Wednesday.

The EU's emergency response capacity pools assets like water-bombing aircraft, helicopters, and fire engines from across the bloc's 27 member states and 10 partner nations, including the Western Balkans and Turkey.

When disasters break out, from wildfires in France to an earthquake in Venezuela, officials in Brussels help coordinate available aid to match requests from affected countries.

Since France requested EU assistance last week, aircraft from countries ranging from Slovakia and Slovenia to Portugal and Turkey have deployed to the southwest of the country.

"We still have some gaps, so we are looking," Zuber said. "Just last night, Serbia offered additional helicopters."

EU urges member states to place additional equipment on standby

The fires raging in France and Spain this year are the latest to sweep across parts of Europe, as scientists attribute intensifying heatwaves to human-driven climate change.

This year's heat extremes have dried out vegetation that had flourished during previous wet spells, creating tinderbox conditions.

As this annual threat escalates, the EU is bolstering its resources by purchasing its own aircraft and urging member states to place additional equipment on standby.

In Brussels, dozens of officials work on a rotating roster to maintain 24/7 oversight of emerging crises worldwide.

Throughout the summer, they are joined by around 25 weather and fire specialists from EU member states, who assess how blazes may spread and identify where new ones could erupt.

"We have implemented mechanisms that have been improved over time, as we recognised that forest fires were becoming an increasing challenge in recent years," said Borja Miguelez, the deputy head of the emergency centre.

"We have increased the availability of aerial resources and enhanced the technical capacity of the teams managing the emergency response."

Although concurrent fires in France and Spain are placing heavy strain on ground crews and equipment, Miguelez notes that the EU has so far fulfilled every request for aid.

However, with further extreme heat expected over the coming days, fire warnings are surging in other regions, which could push demand higher.

"Today we're seeing two forest fires on a very, very large scale, but we're also remaining very vigilant for the future, because summer isn't over yet, and we're now set to experience another heatwave," Miguelez said.

"So we're remaining very alert about what might lie ahead as well."

World.title: French wildfires affect 40,000 businesses as disruption spreads
World.content:
As Spain lifted an evacuation order in a wildfire-hit region near Madrid, France was still battling one of its worst wildfires in decades on Wednesday, with businesses suffering mounting disruption.

 

The Bordeaux-Gironde Chamber of Commerce and Industry told Euronews that 40,000 businesses were directly or indirectly affected by the fire and associated evacuation orders. Patrick Seguin, president of the CCI Bordeaux-Gironde, estimated that they represented approximately 200,000 affected jobs.

“We are experiencing an unprecedented situation. A mini-Covid. An economic catastrophe for our businesses, already penalised by the current economic climate,” Patrick Seguin, president of the Bordeaux-Gironde Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told Euronews Business.

Separately, the French Economy Ministry estimated that around 130,000 employees were unable to work because of the fires.

The chamber has established a crisis helpline for businesses, which is receiving a growing number of calls. Companies are primarily seeking help with cash-flow problems, deferred loan and tax payments, insurance claims, social-security contributions and placing employees on France’s partial-unemployment scheme.

Euronews Business previously reported on the initial economic damage caused by the fires, including the closure of strategically important defence sites, which disrupted operations at ArianeGroup and Dassault Aviation, among others.

Related French wildfires threaten defence sites and hit regional economy

Although the overall economic cost has yet to be calculated, the chamber warned that tourism businesses generating as much as 80% of their annual turnover during the summer season could face severe difficulties.

Thirty-eight campsites and other camping areas have been evacuated and four have been affected by the flames, according to La Tribune. Around 4,000 holidaymakers were evacuated from accommodation in Lacanau on Tuesday.

The Bordeaux-Gironde Chamber of Commerce and Industry said that a Facebook group called Gironde Solidarité Entreprises had also been created to enable companies to offer one another temporary offices, warehouse space, logistics and other practical assistance.

“The entire image of the Gironde region and its tourism market is taking a hit, but that's not all. A whole sector of our economy has been affected,” Seguin said.

Seguin also urged the rapid deployment of resources to provide initial support to affected businesses, in coordination with government services, saying that “business leaders need strong signals”.

The French government announced emergency support on Monday for businesses affected by fires in Gironde, the Landes and the Var. Companies affected by evacuation orders will be able to use the state-supported partial-unemployment scheme.

A meeting will be held at the Economy Ministry on Thursday to provide “more precise answers” to affected companies, Industry Minister Sébastien Martin told BFMTV-RMC.

Meanwhile, the region’s power grid required adjustments by France’s national transmission system operator, RTE. The company said in a statement that its maintenance teams had joined the fire-service command centre to coordinate actions to protect electrical infrastructure essential to powering homes, fire stations, reception centres, telecommunications networks and other critical infrastructure.

RTE said it had switched off certain lines and electrical substations to allow firefighters to work safely.

“In parallel, our teams are adapting the operation of the electricity network in real time, in constant coordination with Enedis, to limit the consequences of any unavailability,” RTE said.

No wildfire-related outage on the electricity transmission network had been reported by local media as of Wednesday afternoon. RTE’s latest official update, issued on Tuesday, said no transmission-network outages were underway at that time.

As of Wednesday afternoon, the fire remained stabilised but had still not been fixed, meaning that renewed outbreaks remained possible. Around 42,000 hectares had burned, and more than 220,000 people had been evacuated since the blaze began. Approximately 60,000 residents were authorised to return to their homes, although several flare-ups were reported as temperatures and winds intensified.

World.title: Archaeologists find oldest library in Iberian Peninsula in Puente Genil
World.content:
The archaeological site of Fuente Álamo, in the Cordoban town of Puente Genil, may contain a proto-library that would be the oldest found to date in the Iberian Peninsula, according to a study published in the Journal of Mediterranean Archaeology by researchers from the universities of Córdoba and Granada.

 

Until now it was thought that room number 10 at Fuente Álamo had been a shrine to Mithras, a deity of Persian origin that was incorporated into the Roman pantheon at a relatively late stage. The complex began life as a spa in the 1st century BC, which was later abandoned and converted into a villa around the 3rd century. The specialists do not give a precise date for when the room was used as a library, but say the house reached its peak over the following two centuries, before being remodelled again in the 6th century.

To clear up this question, the researchers used a technique known as shape grammar, which makes it possible to analyse how the different architectural elements of a room fit together. In the case of Fuente Álamo, the room has a layout that matches the structure of Roman libraries: an apse, rectangular niches that may have held shelving, semicircular niches, a podium and adjoining rooms that could have served as workspaces or storage areas.

The discovery is exceptional, experts argue, because the architecture of Fuente Álamo preserves a particular combination of clues that allows them to go beyond a simple hypothesis and push the research further. The library at Fuente Álamo would thus be not only the oldest in the Iberian Peninsula, but also the westernmost in the entire Roman Empire and one of the best preserved.

World.title: World Cup sell off: Has FIFA finally gone too far?
World.content:
A new FIFA proposal to sell off a stake in the World Cup has been met with fury in the football world. Under Gianni Infantino’s presidency, FIFA has become increasingly profit-driven, but is this too much?

"While you divide, we unite," Gianni Infantino wrote on social media on Monday, in a long missive aimed at his detractors. By Tuesday, he had united the football world — albeit in opposition to his latest scheme.

Shortly after reports emerged in UK newspapers The Times and the Financial Times on Tuesday, FIFA confirmed its plans to create a new subsidiary, named FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). This would enable it to sell a minority stake in the World Cup's operations to private investors for an estimated $20 billion (roughly €17.5 billion).

Chief among FIFA's proposed investors is the investment vehicle, Thrive Eternal, headed by Joshua Kushner — younger brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

Why is FIFA's new World Cup plan controversial?

Other than the potential conflict of interest connection to Trump, with whom Infantino has grown close, there are significant concerns about transparency, corruption and whether FIFA has the remit to make such a move unilaterally.

"The World Cup is one of the few truly global sporting events, and that comes with a responsibility beyond maximizing revenue," Bret Myers, a professor of sports business practices at Villanova University in Pennsylvania, USA, told DW.

The US connection is important, with the model echoing the way that many US sports operate. Formula 1 too went through a similar process when it was bought by Liberty Media in 2017. Greg Maffei, a former Liberty CEO, has been a "key commercial adviser" to FIFA on the FFE plan.

"North American sports have long operated within a more commercial framework, where private ownership, franchise valuations, and investor involvement are widely accepted," Myers added.

"Football, particularly in Europe, has a much stronger tradition of clubs and competitions being viewed as cultural institutions rather than purely commercial assets."

USA striker Folarin Balogun's red-card ban during the World Cup was suspended after Infantino got a call from Trump Image: Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire/IMAGO

More fundamentally, the concern is that this is the first step towards the World Cup, football's biggest prize, becoming privately owned.

"A minority investment is very different from relinquishing control," Myers said. However, it does represent a significant shift in how the World Cup is financed and managed commercially."

World football's global governors are a nonprofit organization but sit on cash reserves of an estimated $8 billion after a World Cup that saw ticket prices skyrocket.

Given FIFA's remit lies in developing football, rather than purely profiting from it, there is a sense that this is a move designed to shore up Infantino's power and, perhaps, encroach on the turf of the continental football federations he failed to include in the planning.

How do Infantino and FIFA aim to sell the plan?

FIFA has promised to invest profits back into the game, mostly by offering all 211 member associations a flat fee of $20 million in 2027, rising to 24 million by 2035. Associations must decide whether to accept those payments by September 19 or risk them being reduced or retracted.

"The president controls this huge pot of money and uses it to reward those that are loyal to him, that support him, and punish those that are not supportive of him," Miguel Maduro a former chairman of FIFA's Governance, Audit and Compliance Committee, told DW.

"FIFA could do lots of good things with money. But there is no system of checks and balances and accountability to make us sure that the money is actually going to be well spent by all national football associations. Everything that that's happened in the past makes me suspicious of how this money will end up being spent."

What has the reaction been from the footballing world?

Almost universally negative. National federations, world leaders and fan groups have all come out against the idea, with federations particularly peeved about the lack of consultation.

But perhaps the most surprising reaction came from the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), who released a statement confirming it was "not consulted on the proposal and is disappointed" by the way in which it was released. Asia and Africa, are where Infantino's main power base lies, as together they have 101 of the 211 national associations – with each getting a vote on the president.

The close friendship between Infantino and Trump has raised alarm bells for some Image: Kai Pfaffenbach/REUTERS

Similar misgivings were expressed by a number of powerful national football associations, including Germany's DFB.

"A line is being crossed here. There is a strong consensus among the member associations on this matter, as evidenced by several conversations I have had in recent days with Aleksander Ceferin (president of Europe's football governors UEFA) and other colleagues," said Hans-Joachim Watzke, a DFB vice president.

"If European football stands united in opposing these plans, it carries significant weight."

Who might oppose FIFA's World Cup plans?

UEFA seems in the best position to lead any revolt – and has hit out at the plans, saying football is "not FIFA's to sell." It was a strongly worded statement of the type UEFA has released several times in recent months as its battle with FIFA plays out in public. Reports suggest UEFA will meet as soon as Wednesday to discuss their options.

Maduro backs UEFA's stance but said he'd like the current climate to serve as an opportunity for broader reform.

"I don't think UEFA has the same severity of problems that we find in FIFA, but I do think it also suffers from serious governance problems and that they need to be addressed," he said.

"Simply getting rid of Mr. Infantino but leaving the entire structure and model of governance of sports will be removing a couple of bad apples but leaving the tree that produced them in place."

Aleksander Ceferin's UEFA has been a strong critic of FIFA in recent years Image: Mike Egerton/PA/picture alliance

How could this change football?

That the AFC and the CONCACAF (which governs North, Central America and Caribbean football) have criticized the way the latest plans were released, may have strengthened UEFA's hand in any thoughts of breakaway or boycott.

It may also lead to the continental federations uniting to find someone to oppose Infantino in next year's presidential election or in threats of boycotting next year's Women's World Cup.

But Maduro thinks such talk is often designed to appease the public before intentions are quietly shelved.

"What we've seen so far for the most part is that these statements, where they distance themselves from these kinds of initiatives of FIFA, are made under the pressure of public opinions. But then they actually never follow through."

Maduro went on to say that UEFA's increasingly strident opposition to FIFA is, at least in part, a reaction to an increased threat to its own highly lucrative Champions League. Should the proposed changes go through, Maduro expects World Cups to be more frequent and a further expansion of FIFA's recently expanded Club World Cup.

"They will want to transform that into the big international football competition of clubs instead of the Champions League. That's what they will try to do because it will be in their commercial interest," he said.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: Germany news: Temperatures to soar amid new heatwave
World.content:
07/29/2026 July 29, 2026 German official defends deportation of non-criminal to Afghanistan

The German government on Wednesday defended its decision to deport an Afghan back to their homeland despite not being convicted of any crime.

On Tuesday evening, the latest in a series of deportation flights from Germany to Afghanistan took off, carrying 31 Afghan people.

But unlike previous flights, which saw only criminals deported to the Taliban-run country, Tuesday's flight was the first to include a person not convicted of a crime.

On Tuesday, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that those on the latest flight were mostly "serious offenders who had committed crimes such as murder, rape and acts of violence," but admitted that "the designation of 'convicted offender' does not apply" to one of the passengers on board.

The government has said that it prioritizes deporting individuals convicted of serious crimes.

An Interior Ministry spokesperson told reporters on Wednesday that the government aimed to "begin with deporting people who have been convicted and those who pose a threat" but that it was also possible "to put people on deportation flights who are not criminals."

Dobrindt said on Tuesday that "people who have no right to stay in the country can also be subject to deportation if there are no signs they have integrated in Germany."

As a member of Chancellor Merz's conservative party, Dobrindt defended the government's actions and said it would continue to pursue a strict immigration policy with a "firm stance."

Refugee rights groups sharply criticized the deportation, and Tuesday's flight, which set off from Leipzig, was accompanied by protests of about 250 people, according to officials.

World.title: BMW to cut up to 8,000 jobs
World.content:
Nearly half of BMW's German staff will receive a voluntary redundancy offer in the carmaker's bid to reduce staff by about 8,000 people.

BMW aims to cut staff by up to 8,000 positions by the end of 2027, according to company sources.

The German carmaker said the reduction would primarily target office jobs, while production line workers will be spared from cuts.

"The workforce will ultimately be reduced by around 8,000 people by the end of 2027," an anonymous source told the AFP news agency. "We're planning on the basis of that."

The Munich-based automaker hopes to achieve the cuts through natural staff turnover as well as a voluntary redundancy scheme. The latter would be aimed at all employees in Germany not directly involved in production, who could choose to accept severance packages in a period from October 2026 to the end of 2027.

The company currently employs 84,000 staff in Germany, and roughly 154,000 globally.

The latest German carmaker to announce job cuts

BMW is the latest German car company to announce job cuts, following similar moves by rival brands Volkswagen, Mercedes and Volkswagen-owned Audi.

Germany's prestigious car industry is struggling amid stiff competition from Chinese carmakers, US tariffs, and narrower profit margins from electric cars.

BMW was long considered one of the sector's more resilient players. The planned cuts come after the company warned last month that its sales in China were falling sharply.

Last year, BMW's vehicle deliveries in China were already at their lowest level since 2017, and they fell 30% year-on-year in the three months to June.

On Thursday, BMW is due to announce its earnings for the first half of 2026.

World.title: Europe wildfires: Spain lets people return, France faces extreme heat
World.content:
Spain lifted evacuations for Avila province, a day after doing so in parts of the Madrid area. To the north in France, temperatures rose again, with extreme heat warnings in much of the country, including Gironde.

As Spain battled its largest wildfire on record and France struggled to contain a blaze four times the size of Paris, scientists warned that extreme wildfires were becoming more frequent worldwide.

Europe wildfires continue as new heatwaves hit France, Spain To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Evacuees allowed to return in Spain

Spain started lifting evacuation orders for various places in the Avila province on Wednesday, having taken similar steps in the Madrid province on Tuesday.

Interior Minister Francisco Martin Aguirre announced progressively reduced restrictions for a variety of places after conditions overnight allowed firefighters to make gains, saying tens of thousands had been able to return home.

Sanchez: 'Next 12 hours will be very important'

"Today, I believe we are closer to that final objective" of "defeating the fire," Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez told reporters in televised comments at a command center in the town of Navalarnero near the fire zone.

"Things are progressing favorably, with the greatest of caution," he said, predicting that "the next 12 hours will be very imporant — they will be decisive for consolidating the work that has been done."

For a week, Spain has been fighting two large fires that had at times come close to merging into a single blaze in wooded hills west of Madrid.

However, authorities remain on alert, with highs consistently above 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit) forecast every day in the Madrid area this week.

Spain's meteorological agency AEMET warned of a new stretch of high temperatures starting on Wednesday Image: Cordon Press/picture alliance

Heat warnings across most of France, including fire flashpoint Gironde

On France's southwestern Atlantic coast, temperatures and winds picked up once more on Wednesday, threatening to fan the flames.

Temperature warnings were in place for most of the country, with the most severe on the eastern border and in the southwestern areas hardest hit by fires, including the Gironde region. The Meteo France weather service forecast highs of 40 Celsius in the Bordeaux area in the afternoon.

Thousands of French firefighters, with support from elsewhere in Europe, are trying to control the fires in Gironde Image: Mohamad Salaheldin Abdelghani Alsayed/Anadolu/picture alliance

French authorities have been forced to relocate around 220,000 people in total amid the fires, many of them from holiday resorts on the coast — like Lacanau and Grand Cohot on Tuesday.

More than 2,200 firefighters and over 20 aircraft remained mobilized, backed by crews from across France and European partners.

"We strike quickly and strike hard at any new smoke emissions," Gironde fire commander Matthieu Jomain said.

The Gironde wildfire has burned an area four times the size of Paris, and resisted the firefighting efforts of a dozen countries.

While new fires were reported in France's Gironde, authorities in Landes said the advance of the wildfires had stopped Image: Jeanne Accorsini/SIPA/picture alliance

Climate change exacerbating wildfires

Scientists say climate change is fueling hotter, drier summers that are intensifying wildfires across Europe. The warmer temperatures are also extending fire seasons and making these blazes harder to control, straining the resources of European nations.

Currently, the European Union only coordinates the deployment of extra resources pooled from its member states when a ​country requests emergency help. As fires on the continent grow more extreme, however, the bloc called for greater investment in forest management and wildfire prevention.

Has Europe lost control of its wildfires? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Brussels is purchasing its own permanent firefighting fleet.

"Climate change ​is accelerating. So, our response must evolve just as quickly," Hadja Lahbib, the EU's Crisis Management Commissioner, told Reuters.

World.title: How a Ugandan lost 20 years of her life to xenophobia
World.content:
After decades of building lives in South Africa, renewed anti-immigrant tensions in 2026 forced hundreds of African migrants to leave. A Ugandan who spent two decades in South Africa shared with DW how she's coping.

When Winniefred Kabiri boarded a flight from Johannesburg to Kampala, she was leaving behind much more than a country. The Ugandan entrepreneur spent 20 years legally living in South Africa. During that time, she earned two university degrees and a postgraduate qualification, raised her children and established several businesses. "Initially everything was very successful. I created a life for myself and educated my children," Kabiri told DW.

But as anti-foreigner campaigns intensified in parts of South Africa this year, she no longer felt safe. "There was always a threat," she said. "But this year they gave ultimatums."

Kabiri is among more than 1,100 Ugandans evacuated from South Africa by their government following months of escalating xenophobic tensions, protests and intimidation targeting mostly African migrants. Uganda completed the first phase of its repatriation exercise in July, bringing home 1,102 nationals through six evacuation flights from Johannesburg.

Thousands leave S. Africa over threats of xenophobic attacks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

South Africa has experienced recurring outbreaks of xenophobic violencesince the late 1990s, with migrants often blamed for unemployment, crimeand poor public services. Analysts say persistent inequality and economic frustration have continued to fuel anti-immigrant sentiment despite evidence that migrants contribute significantly to local economies . This year, however, many migrants say the atmosphere became markedly different.

Groups demanding tougher action against migrants organized public demonstrations and campaigns, while reports of intimidation, evictions and sporadic violence heightened fears among foreign communities. Many immigrants interviewed by DW said they felt vulnerableregardless of whether they possessed legal documentation.

Leaving behind years of investment in South Africa

For many returnees, like Kabiri, departure meant abandoning years of investment. She left businesses in commodities trading, mining, real estate and perfume manufacturing. She also left behind a professional network built over two decades. "Obviously,when you are told to leave and you're unprepared, you leave things behind," she said.

Another Ugandan returnee, Mathias Baguma, said he lost a business he spent years developing in Johannesburg. Baguma moved to South Africa in 2017 and later invested in a guesthouse, restaurant and retail operation. During the unrest, he says the property was attacked and looted.

Operation Dudula, March and March and other anti-foreigner protesters have been staging regular protests calling on migrants to leave Image: Rogan Ward/REUTERS

"My business was vandalized. The shop was robbed, the restaurant broken into," he told DW. "I had to run for my life." Like many migrants across the continent, Baguma had viewed South Africa as a place where hard work could provide opportunities unavailable at home. Instead, he returned to Uganda with little more than personal belongings and memories of the life he had built.

Starting a new life in Uganda after fleeing xenophobia

Back in Uganda, the challenge for returnees is no longer escape, but rebuilding. Authorities say returning migrants were received at Entebbe airport and taken through orientation and reintegration programs, including counseling, health assessments and information sessions on government support initiatives.

Officials also introduced returnees to programs in agriculture, tourism, technology and small-business development aimed at helping themrestart their lives .

Xenophobia in South Africa: Who’s really paying the price? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

DW correspondent Frank Yiga said the Ugandan government moved quickly to organize transport, reception centers and psychosocial support for those affected. "The government helped prepare them for reintegration and informed them of the opportunities available," Yiga said.

Kabiri praised the initial response but acknowledged that rebuilding after 20 years abroad would be difficult. "I have to rebuild myself. I need to rebuild a new home and a business," she said.

She says family members have offered emotional support, but the financial reality remains daunting. For now, her focus is on creating a new future in Uganda. "East or West, home is best," she concluded.



This article was adapted from an AfricaLink Podcast . You can listen to the podcast here

Edited by: Chrispin Mwakideu.

World.title: Iran signals gas price hike as fuel crisis looms
World.content:
Iranian authorities want to dampen fuel consumption, but a sudden increase in gasoline prices risks social unrest as many Iranian households are already under severe economic pressure.

Iran is moving closer to politically sensitive changes in gasoline pricing as the government struggles with a widening gap between domestic fuel production and consumption, exacerbated by the ongoing conflict with the US.

On July 25, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said changes to fuel prices or rationing are "certain and unavoidable," although officials have yet to confirm whether the response will come through new quotas, higher prices or both.

Iran uses a tiered subsidized fuel price system with monthly quotas currently ranging from 1,500 tomans ($0.008) per liter at the lowest rung, to 5,000 tomans ($0.026) at the top. Iranian media have reported the new top rung for gasoline could jump to 10,000 tomans ($0.053) per liter, which would be nearly a 100% increase. The figure has not yet been officially confirmed.

Compared to the rest of the world, gasoline in Iran seems very inexpensive. But after years of sanctions and economic malaise, Iranians are also earning a lot less. Fuel may look exceptionally cheap in dollar terms, but the incomes used to pay for it are asi exceptionally low.

For example, the basic monthly minimum wage in 2026 was set at around 16.6 million tomans, or about $87. Any hike in gas prices comes down hard on households.

The last major sudden increase in fuel prices in November 2019 triggered nationwide protests and one of the bloodiest crackdowns in the history of the Islamic Republic.

Protesters blocked a Tehran highway after a fuel price hike in 2019 Image: Babak/MEI/SIPA/picture alliance

This time, the government faces another complication. Iran was already consuming more gasoline than it produced before the US launched the war in February. Damage to fuel infrastructure and restrictions on imports have made that imbalance harder and more expensive to manage.

All Iranians need fuel

Iranian officials argue that they need to suppress demand for gasoline with higher rates. But critics say that gasoline is a necessity and higher costs will not dampen demand.

A resident of Karaj, a small city near Tehran, said that said higher gasoline prices would quickly work their way through the economy, making everything more expensive.

"It will cause a chain reaction in the prices of goods and services, and the greatest pressure will ultimately fall on middle and lower-income households," he told DW anonymously for safety reasons.

A car that consumes roughly12 liters per 100 kilometers (19 miles per gallon) will not suddenly become more efficient because gasoline costs more, he said. Without better vehicles or effective public transport, motorists have few alternatives.

"Transport fares will go up when fuel becomes more expensive," he added.

In March 2026, there were reported strikes on fuel tanks at an oil refinery in Tehran Image: Majid Asgaripour/WANA/REUTERS

Umud Shokri, an energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University in the US, told DW that pricing could still play a role in reducing fuel consumption, but only as part of a much wider policy.

"Higher prices could discourage unnecessary driving and make fuel smuggling less profitable, but they would not solve the crisis by themselves," Shokri said.

A gradual increase for consumption above monthly quotas could help control demand, he said. But it would need to be combined with financial support for poorer households and substantial improvements in public transport.

Otherwise, he warned, higher prices could add to inflation and provoke social unrest.

How is oil powerhouse Iran short of gasoline?

Iran has some of the world's largest oil reserves, but crude oil production and gasoline production are two different things.

Shokri estimates that Iran currently produces around 121 million liters of gasoline per day, including blended fuel, while daily consumption is about 129 million liters. During holidays and peak travel periods, demand can rise even further.

The deficit has been developing for years.

Since 2019, domestic consumption has risen faster than production. Estimates cited in Iranian discussions suggest daily gasoline use has increased by around 39 million liters since 2019, while production capacity has risen by only around 16 million liters.

A country that once had surplus gasoline available for export has consequently become increasingly dependent on imports.

Shokri believes one of the quickest alternatives could be greater use of compressed natural gas, or CNG. Iran already has an extensive CNG network, but much of its capacity remains unused. Converting more vehicles to dual-fuel systems could reduce gasoline consumption relatively quickly.

Stronger rationing, measures against fuel smuggling and tougher efficiency standards could also help, he added.

Over the longer term, Iran would need to replace inefficient vehicles, improve public transport, electrify motorcycles and taxis, modernize refineries and increase strategic fuel storage, he said.

Imports could normally help compensate for shortages, but sanctions complicate payments, shipping and insurance. The war has added another layer of risk around maritime routes.

Russia might appear to be an obvious alternative supplier because of its close political relationship with Tehran. But Moscow has its own gasoline problem, with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, pipelines and fuel storage sites disrupting production and contributing to shortages.

"Russia may be politically willing to help Iran, but currently it has less fuel available to export," Shokri said.

Iran's Kharg island is the country's main oil export hub (file photo from 2016) Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Iran's fuel problems predate US war

The war with the US has damaged fuel depots, storage tanks and parts of the distribution network, particularly around Tehran and Alborz. Shipping disruption also made imports more difficult and expensive.

However, Shokri cautions against overstating the physical destruction of Iran's fuel infrastructure.

He said there is currently no reliable evidence that Iran has permanently lost a large share of its gasoline production capacity. Refineries appear to have returned close to full operation.

"The war did not create Iran's gasoline crisis, but it made an already serious shortage more difficult and expensive to manage," he said.

It is unclear how the Iranian public will respond to another sharp fuel shock. The war has added another layer of anger, insecurity and frustration to grievances that were already building over living costs and declining purchasing power.

In that environment, a fuel price increase would not take place in an economic vacuum. It could become a trigger for wider discontent, making the government's decision over gasoline as much a political calculation as an economic one.

World.title: Lebanon's pilot zone plan: Can it work?
World.content:
The Israeli army has handed so-called "pilot zones" back to the Lebanese, The move is meant to facilitate an end to fighting between Hezbollah and Israel, and to Israeli occupation. But locals and experts are skeptical.

It has been just over a week since the so-called "pilot zone" plan was launched in Lebanon and the gap between the plan's ambitions and the reality on the ground remains stark.

According to the June 26 agreement between Lebanon, the US and Israel, the pilot zone plan is meant to see the Israeli military gradually redeploying out of parts of southern Lebanon it currently controls, which then allows the Lebanese army, or LAF, to move in.

After the armed wing of Lebanon's Hezbollah group fired rockets at Israel in March this year, Israel invaded Lebanon and now occupies a large swathe of the country’s south. The pilot zones are meant to end that. Once the LAF controls the zone, then Hezbollah can supposedly no longer operate from there. And once one zone has been secured, then the next will be actioned.

However there have been a number of troubling incidents already. The Israeli army shot at the vicinity of Lebanese soldiers as they approached one area last week and Israeli demolitions of homes and buildings in Lebanon continue, as do attacks with drones and bombs elsewhere in southern Lebanon.

The Israeli army's behavior jeopardizes the agreement from which the pilot zone plan originates, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun told the UN's human rights chief Volker Türk this week, when the latter visited Lebanon.

UN human rights chief Türk said that Israel's 'overall conduct resulting in large scale displacement and denial of returns could amount to international crimes' Image: Mohamed Azakir/REUTERS

Pilot zone residents not impressed

Locals that DW spoke to, who live in the pilot zones, were also skeptical.

Hussein Kamaleddine, the mayor of Srifa, told DW he didn't understand why his village or the village of Froun had been made a pilot zone because Israeli soldiers had never even been stationed there.

"This is something that was forced upon us," Kamaleddine said. "It still doesn't make sense to us why these villages were considered pilot zones."

Other commentators have pointed out that lack of Israeli presence may be exactly why these towns were chosen as the first pilot zones: They don't directly impact northern Israel's security and it's a kind of soft launch for the plan.

Kamaleddine said he was happy to be back home in Srifa even though, he noted, he was surrounded by rubble. But he credited that homecoming to his community's resilience, not state support.

"Being back in Srifa now feels like a dream," he said. "But it's not thanks to the government. These so-called pilot zones are nothing but a scheme by the US and Israel."

Srifa: Lebanese soldiers were already operating here prior to the start of the pilot zone scheme Image: Hassan Ammar/AP Photo/picture alliance

Authorities from the village of Froun sent DW a written statement, expressing similar opinions. The town supported the LAF and that soldiers coming there had "preserved security and stability," they said.

But at the same time, they also completely rejected the pilot zone plan and described it "as serving the enemy [Israel] by prolonging its presence on Lebanese territory and creating a rift between the army and the people."

One of the major concerns about the pilot zone plan is that the LAF will be forced to confront Hezbollah fighters eventually, which could cause unrest, or even civil war. Hezbollah is thought to be as strong, or even stronger than, the Lebanese army.

Villages destroyed by Israeli army

Locals from another pilot zone village Zawtar al-Gharbieh (or West Zawtar) have been trying to get back home for several days now, mayor Abed Ezzeddine told DW.

And Israeli soldiers had definitely been there, Ezzeddine said. Almost all of the village has been destroyed.

"After seeing it, I can't describe it any other way: It's catastrophe upon catastrophe," Ezzeddine continued. "In principle, we cannot allow everyone to return at once, we're letting people in gradually. The plan is that once the army finishes clearing all the roads, God willing, everyone will be able to return."

The mayor has told other media this week that, despite being a pilot zone, the village doesn't feel safe. Another nearby village, Zawtar al-Sharqiyah (or East Zawtar) is still occupied by Israeli soldiers and the road going into his town runs through there, which makes it difficult to move around. When journalists from the Associated Press visited Zawtar al-Gharbieh this week, they heard explosions nearby and saw Israeli drones overhead.

The Israeli military can still shoot into 'pilot zones' and has said it reserves the right to return in order to combat Hezbollah — if they do, the Lebanese (pictured) must withdraw Image: Ali Hashisho/Xinhua/picture alliance

How to tell if pilot zones work

Beyond the current problems on the ground, there are also major theoretical issues with the pilot zone plan.

"The framework Lebanon signed does not specify a withdrawal timetable and there is still no clarity on how disarming Hezbollah is defined, what the success criteria for disarmament are, and which party is responsible for determining whether these benchmarks are being met," explains Randa Slim, lead for the Middle East program at the US-based Stimson Center.

"Until the pilot zones include areas inside Israel's 'yellow line' and we see tangible evidence of Israeli forces withdrawing gradually from these areas, they serve, in my opinion, as Israeli smokescreens for an indefinite occupation in southern Lebanon," Slim argued.

This week Israeli prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seemed to confirm that , saying Israel would not be withdrawing soldiers from Lebanon anytime soon.

"I'm not sure many people have much confidence that the agreement is a pathway to a constructive endgame here, whether in terms of facilitating the disarmament of Hezbollah or advancing an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon," Julien Barnes-Dacey, director of the Middle East program at the European Council on Foreign Relations, or ECFR, told DW. "The terms have been shaped by Israel and give Netanyahu the space to … facilitate the country’s ongoing occupation of southern Lebanon."

Positives about pilot zones?

It's a bad deal but now that Lebanon has signed it, it must make the pilot zones work, Michael Young, a senior editor at the Carnegie Middle East Center in Beirut, argued in a July 21 commentary for UAE-based media outlet The National .

The Lebanese government must insist locals be allowed to return to their homes. Without it, the scheme is useless, Young wrote. And if the LAF does manage to control the pilot zones they move into, "this could serve as leverage to compel the Israelis to widen the areas of Lebanese control, since it is unlikely Hezbollah would seek a confrontation with the Lebanese army," Young concluded.

Also still being debated is which neutral party could monitor whether the pilot zones have been successful. In late June, France and Italy said they would be willing to lead an "international coalition to support Lebanon."

But the Europeans "are not going to deploy forces so long as we keep seeing conflict conditions on the ground," the ECFR's Barnes-Dacey pointed out. "If Europeans want to make a real difference at this stage, they could focus on pressuring Israel to pull back militarily while stepping up support to strengthen the Lebanese government."

Edited by: Andreas Illmer

World.title: Bayreuth Festival: Ceremony and commemoration
World.content:
"I would like to state explicitly that Katharina Wagner is changing the culture of remembrance in Bayreuth." With these words, spoken from the stage of the Bayreuth Festival, German-Jewish author Michel Friedman encapsulated the central message of the festival's two-day opening celebration.

Friedman spoke during a commemorative event titled "Silenced Voices," dedicated to Jewish artists who worked at the Bayreuth Festival and were later murdered or oppressed under the Nazi regime. Despite initial organizational turbulence, his talk became one of the key events of the opening celebrations on July 26, alongside the concert on the eve of the festival and the premiere of a new production of the opera "Rienzi."

Katharina Wagner (center) with Michel Friedman and guests during a tour of the exhibition “Silenced Voices” Image: Daniel Löb/dpa/picture alliance

Friedman also visited the exhibition with Bayreuth Festival director Katharina Wagner and several members of the local Jewish community. In the park surrounding the Bayreuth Festival grounds, directly beside the bust of Richard Wagner, a series of gray memorial steles stands as a powerful reminder of the Jewish artists whose lives were lost. A cantor from the Jewish community recited a prayer for the victims, and their names were read aloud.

'Democracy is in danger'

Friedman's speech in the Festspielhaus, which lasted more than an hour, encompassed far more than the omissions and blind spots of Germany's culture of remembrance. For the 70-year-old, whose family was almost entirely murdered during the Holocaust, the focus was on something more fundamental — the mechanisms that foster hatred and injustice, and the passivity of society that allows them to flourish. His message was about the present as much as the past.

Friedman criticized what he called a "bored, decadent democracy" and urged everyone present and everyone listening — as well as those outside the hall who remain "silent and grumbling”— to become active witnesses to their own time, before it is too late once again.

"My country, Germany, is a community. This community is defined by diversity, and diversity has once again become a concept that is under heavy attack. Yet this community and this diversity are the only future we have," he said.

A long history

Few places in Germany bring together history, culture and politics as strikingly as Bayreuth. The opening of this year's festival demonstrated that once again. To mark the festival's 150th anniversary, the red carpet was rolled out and graced by many of Germany's celebrities and politicians, including Chancellor Friedrich Merz, former Chancellor Angela Merkel as well as many international guests.

Inside the Festspielhaus, visitors were greeted by Bayreuth figures from the past century and a half, represented in a large mural by Hungarian street artist Adam Heat that dominates the auditorium.

A large mural by Hungarian artist Adam Heat showed many involved in Bayreuth's past Image: Enrico Nawrath/Bayreuther Festspiele

At the center is King Ludwig II of Bavaria presenting Richard Wagner with a Grail overflowing with money — a vivid metaphor for the founding of the festival. Surrounding him is an illustrious cast of Bayreuth figures from the past 150 years — members of the Wagner family, who have guided the festival for generations; conductors ranging from Wilhelm Furtwängler and Arturo Toscanini to Oksana Lyniv and Nathalie Stutzmann. Also depicted is Wagner admirer and longtime Bayreuth guest Adolf Hitler, portrayed in elegant attire and holding a small glass.

Nike Wagner, the composer's great-granddaughter, summed up the message behind the work in her festival address: As visitors to the festival's grand hall, we become part of "Wagner's artistic ritual. Whoever takes a seat here now, sits with all those who have sat here before."

Katharina Wagner warns against the far-right

Katharina Wagner, Richard Wagner's descendant and the festival's artistic director spoke candidly about her family's Nazi ties. "Given my family's close and, in some cases, deeply personal ties to the Nazi regime, and given the role of the festival as a cultural showcase of the Third Reich, but also bearing in mind that our German democracy today is once again threatened by forces seeking to make antisemitism, racism, chauvinism, and nationalism part of the foundations of the state, there is no better place than this Festspielhaus to say: No."

Katharina Wagner welcomed former Chancellor Angela Merkel (center) and Bavarian Minister-President Markus Söder (right) and his wife, as well as Michel Friedman Image: Karl-Josef Hildenbrand/dpa/picture alliance

In his speech, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz explained why, for him personally, Wagner's legacy and music represent the contradictions of German intellectual history:

"Richard Wagner's person and work are exemplary of both the greatness and the darker depths of Germany's artistic and historical legacy. They represent the uniquely German combination of the most admirable and the most questionable aspects of our past. When we engage with Wagner, we have the opportunity to see and hear so much of ourselves across the centuries in a single body of work."

And nowhere, Merz said, is this opportunity felt more profoundly than in Bayreuth.

With such direct statements during the anniversary event, the Bayreuth Festival has opened a new chapter in its culture of remembrance. In doing so, the festival seeks to make a broader social statement and take a firm stand against antisemitism.

This article was translated from German and edited by Teresa O'Connell.

World.title: La Comunidad de Madrid compra un ático de lujo en Chamberí para que lo use Ayuso como “oficina” temporal
World.content:
Ayuso: "Yo no me estoy comprando nada, insisto, y no se me está comprando nada"

La Comunidad de Madrid ha comprado un ático de 485 metros cuadrados en Chamberí, una de las zonas más caras de la capital, para que lo use la presidenta Isabel Díaz Ayuso “durante la rehabilitación de la Real Casa de Correos, cuyos trabajos comenzarán en agosto”, según le ha respondido este martes una portavoz a EL PAÍS. La noticia se conoce tres meses y medio después de la adquisición del piso y solo después de que este diario planteara la pregunta tras descubrir la compraventa, que aparece en el Registro de la Propiedad.

La portavoz solo ha precisado que Ayuso trabajará en el inmueble “con un mínimo equipo” y no ha respondido otras cuestiones planteadas ―si Ayuso también planea vivir en él, el precio de la compra, las razones por las que se había guardado este secreto o por qué no se ha optado por alquilar un inmueble―. Tampoco queda claro a qué obras se refiere. La Real Casa de Correos, sede de la presidencia madrileña, concluyó el año pasado las obras de restauración de su fachada.

Tras la publicación de la noticia, una fuente de la máxima confianza de la presidenta ha explicado a este diario que la decisión sobre el uso del ático como oficina “no está tomada al cien por cien”. Ha dicho que van a reformar el inmueble y decidirán sobre el traslado en octubre o noviembre. También ha añadido, tras ser preguntado por ello, que no piensan destinarlo a residencia presidencial.

La compra fue realizada el 14 de abril por la empresa autonómica que comercializa suelo público y gestiona las oficinas propias, Planifica Madrid. Esta agencia, presidida por el portavoz del Gobierno y consejero de Presidencia, Miguel Ángel García Martín, no había incluido esta inversión en el presupuesto para este año. El valor de mercado de un ático de estas características en esa zona privilegiada ronda los seis millones de euros.

El ático del paseo del General Martínez Campos de Madrid, que en abril fue comprado por el Gobierno regional. Claudio Álvarez

El ático se encuentra en la planta novena de un portal del paseo del General Martínez Campos, un edificio residencial en una de las principales arterias del acomodado distrito de Chamberí. El bloque colinda con el Museo Sorolla, a tan solo 300 metros del paseo de la Castellana. La vendedora ha sido la economista y escritora Astrid Gil-Casares, según dos fuentes conocedoras de la operación. Una pareja residía en el inmueble como inquilinos.

La vivienda mide 485 metros cuadrados, de los cuales 199 corresponden a la terraza. Varios pisos del edificio pertenecen a familias de aristócratas y, según un empleado del bloque, ninguno está destinado a oficinas.

El gasto sorprende porque no estaba previsto en el presupuesto para 2026 de Planifica Madrid, que sí detalla minuciosamente otras operaciones de venta de inmuebles o de inversión en obra nueva. El Consejo de Gobierno tampoco ha concedido una extensión de crédito para la compra de esta vivienda (algo necesario para incurrir en este tipo de gasto) y, lo que es más importante, Planifica Madrid no ha informado de la adquisición en su página de transparencia, actualizada por última vez el pasado lunes 20 de julio, y donde se enumeran las actuaciones abiertas más relevantes.

Planifica Madrid es dueña de diez edificios enteros destinados a oficinas y un local, que luego arrienda, en casi todos los casos a distintos departamentos de la Comunidad de Madrid. En su mayoría son inmuebles históricos en el centro de Madrid con distintos grados de protección, como la Consejería de Sanidad (Calle Aduana, 29) o la de Cultura y Turismo (Alcalá, 31).

El registrador de la propiedad de la zona ha denegado a EL PAÍS la solicitud para conocer la identidad del vendedor, argumentando que el solicitante debe tener “un interés directo, legítimo y patrimonial”. No obstante, dos fuentes que conocen esta compraventa han indicado que se trata de Gil-Casares. Esta escritora estuvo casada hasta 2016 con Rafael del Pino Calvo-Sotelo, el presidente de Ferrovial y segundo hombre más rico de España,

El precio pagado por el ático es una incógnita, pero varias fuentes sugieren que puede haber rondado los seis millones de euros. Para tener una idea del monto, habría que multiplicar los 486 metros cuadrados por el precio del metro cuadrado en el código postal del barrio de Almagro, donde se ubica la vivienda, que según el portal del Notariado es de 9.414 euros. Esto supone 4,5 millones de euros. A esto habría que añadir un plus por tratarse de un ático que depende principalmente del tamaño de la terraza. Esta en concreto, de 200 metros cuadrados, es tan grande que el precio puede ser muy superior. En los portales inmobiliarios se ofertan áticos con grandes terrazas por precios que oscilan entre los cinco y los siete millones de euros.

La terraza de casi 200 metros cuadrados es tan grande que uno de los expertos inmobiliarios en Almagro, el gerente de la oficina de Don Chamberí en Paseo General Martínez Campos, responde que nunca ha visto algo así: “Yo no conozco un ático así. No creo que exista”.

Empresa con pasado oscuro

Planifica Madrid es la heredera de Arpegio, la empresa pública que se vio inmersa en un gran escándalo conocido como el caso Púnica, y que está judicializado. Esta sociedad protagoniza una de las piezas del macrocaso por haber participado en presuntas irregularidades cometidas en la adjudicación de suelo público y contratos de infraestructuras. En aquellos años era consejero de la empresa Francisco Granados, hombre de confianza de Esperanza Aguirre. La pieza que pertenece a estos presuntos amaños fue enviada en mayo a juicio. Allí se sentará Granados, que ya ha sido condenado por otros delitos.

La presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, y el consejero de Presidencia, Justicia y Administración Local, Miguel Ángel García Martín, durante un pleno en la Asamblea de Madrid el 2 de julio. Gabriel Luengas (Europa Press)

La empresa está adscrita a la Consejería de Presidencia de García Martín, tiene una plantilla de 90 empleados y su presupuesto para 2026 es de 127 millones de euros. Su consejero delegado es desde julio de 2023 Pedro Corbalán Ruiz, que antes había tenido puestos en la administración autonómica dentro de los sucesivos gobiernos del Partido Popular.
