World.title: Russian lawmaker makes another bid to enter South Ossetian politics
World.content:
North Ossetia parliament member Dzambolat Tedeyev, who represents the A Just Russia – Patriots – For Truth party and is a former head coach of Russia’s national freestyle wrestling team, is officially returning to South Ossetian politics. What role he intends to play, however, remains unclear. His previous attempts to establish himself in the region’s political scene have all ended in failure.

A native of South Ossetia, Tedeyev once even sought to become the region’s president.

At the recent third congress of the Patriots of Alania party, which was already under Tedeyev’s influence, he was elected its chairman. The high-profile move in Tskhinvali coincided with the party’s nomination of Murat Valiyev — a serving officer in the State Protection Service and former KGB officer — as its presidential candidate.

Tedeyev said the party’s main goal would be to ensure that the views of South Ossetian citizens are heard by the republic’s leadership.

“Our position has never changed, but now we have our own platform from which we can defend the interests of our citizens and our country. Today, we see people leaving because they cannot find work. Despite an investment programme aimed at creating new businesses, unemployment remains a serious problem.

There are many issues to address. But today we have hope because, thanks to you, we now have a party where we can make our voices heard. We must unite and build the future of our republic together,” he told delegates at the party congress.

Commenting on the nomination of little-known State Protection Service officer Murat Valiyev as the party’s presidential candidate, Tedeyev appeared to acknowledge that Valiyev was being put forward as a “technical candidate.” He urged acting president and election frontrunner Marat Kambolov to “rely on” Valiyev and his allies.

Tedeyev also recalled his own failed presidential bid in 2011, when the Central Election Commission refused to register him as a candidate.

“There was a time when I wanted to run, but I wasn’t allowed to. Today, I see that Marat has greater potential, stronger connections, and is capable of achieving more. Why shouldn’t he rely on me? That’s why I decided that even if we nominate Murat Valiyev today, Marat should rely on him, on us, on all of us.

And let’s all put our ambitions aside a little. We all know what we’re capable of.”

Tedeyev’s remarks have prompted mixed reactions in South Ossetia. Local analysts say it remains unclear whether he genuinely intends to challenge for power or is instead demonstrating loyalty by putting forward his ally as a “technical candidate” in the hope of negotiating with Kambolov after the election.

The events of 2011, when Dzambolat Tedeyev unsuccessfully challenged the outgoing president, Eduard Kokoity, for power, remain fresh in South Ossetia’s collective memory.

After the Central Election Commission refused to register his presidential candidacy, Tedeyev threw his support behind former education minister Alla Dzhioyeva. Although the former official had been accused of corruption and placed under house arrest, her alliance with Tedeyev helped unite the protest vote and secure victory in the election.

The pair, however, were never allowed to take power. The Supreme Court annulled the election results, triggering days of street protests. The opposition, led by Dzhioyeva and Tedeyev, unsuccessfully sought to defend what they said was their electoral victory.

The standoff ended in a compromise that ultimately fell short of Tedeyev’s ambitions. Kokoity announced his resignation, even though his second and final term was already nearing its end, while the opposition agreed to end the protests. A repeat presidential election was scheduled for March 2012, but Dzhioyeva did not take part.

Since then, Tedeyev has periodically sought to influence political developments in South Ossetia, but without much success. Ahead of the 2024 parliamentary elections, for example, he formed an alliance with the parliamentary People’s Party, whose members were once supporters of former president Eduard Kokoity.

According to local analysts, in exchange for Tedeyev’s financial backing, the party agreed to include his allies on its electoral list. However, the alliance ultimately failed to secure a majority of seats in parliament.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Dzambolat Tedeyev takes over South Ossetia party

World.title: ‘Moscow will only push Armenia out of Russian-led blocs’: Reaction to Russia’s foreign intelligence claim
World.content:
SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

“Brussels understands that Armenia will face a severe economic crisis if Yerevan leaves the Eurasian Economic Union,” Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service said on the previous day.

The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) is a Russia-led economic bloc. Its members are Russia, Armenia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Kyrgyzstan.

“Brussels should not expect the EAEU countries to keep Yerevan’s political crew afloat or bankroll its marathon swim toward the European Union,” the SVR said.

In Armenia, observers noted that the statement followed a phone call between Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Russian President Vladimir Putin on July 27. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said one of the main topics was a referendum in Armenia on European Union membership or continued participation in the EAEU.

“We stressed the need for Armenia to hold a referendum as soon as possible so Armenians can decide which direction they want to take,” Peskov said.

The Kremlin’s readout of the call did not mention Pashinyan’s response. However, the Armenian prime minister’s office said he told Putin:

“Holding such a referendum would only become possible after Armenia submits an official application to join the European Union and the issue takes on practical significance.”

The Armenian authorities have given Russia the same response on several previous occasions.

Local analysts viewed the Kremlin’s remarks and the SVR statement as another attempt to pressure Armenia.

In their view, the crisis in bilateral relations continues, and “there is still no solution in sight”. They also questioned why Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, rather than the EAEU itself, had spoken on the bloc’s behalf.

The Armenian prime minister’s office said that, during the call, “Pashinyan stressed that restrictions on exports of Armenian-made goods to the Russian market violate the legal framework governing Armenia-Russia relations and Eurasian Economic Union regulations. He asked Russia to take steps to resolve the issue.” Pashinyan appears to have called Putin primarily over Russia’s ban on imports of numerous Armenian food products and other goods. Russia introduced the restrictions at the end of May.

Statement by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service

The SVR titled its statement, “The EU Lures Armenia but Cannot Help It.” The statement argues that Armenia would face a severe economic crisis if it left the EAEU.

“Armenia will lose the income it currently receives from Eurasian integration. The remaining EAEU members will not bankroll the Armenian authorities as they row toward the European Union. EU institutions acknowledge that the bloc’s worsening economic problems, driven by anti-Russian sanctions and what they describe as Brussels’ obsession with supporting the war in Ukraine, will leave the EU unable to offset Armenia’s multi-billion-dollar losses. Several European countries have already told EU leaders they are unwilling to open their markets to Armenian goods at the expense of domestic producers.”

Russia’s foreign intelligence service also claims the EU will continue to assure Yerevan of its unwavering support.

“The EU plans to explain the lack of tangible assistance by arguing that accession depends entirely on Yerevan and on its own ‘progress’ toward European integration.”

According to the SVR, the EU has already presented Pashinyan’s government with the following demands:

reduce the presence of Russian businesses in strategic sectors;

sever humanitarian ties with Russia;

suppress domestic opponents who resist those policies.

The statement adds that the EU will encourage Armenia by “holding out the prospect of visa liberalisation for Armenian citizens and promising that, at some distant point in the future, Armenia will become a ‘prosperous crossroads of peace.’

How Armenians View European Integration: Poll Results

Against the backdrop of Russia’s call for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether to remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership, local broadcaster Factor TV conducted an online poll. Participants answered the following question: “If a referendum on choosing between the EAEU and the EU were held this Sunday, which would you vote for?”

According to the broadcaster, more than 3,300 people have already taken part in the poll. The results are as follows:

74% said they would vote for EU membership;

said they would vote for EU membership; 21% said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU;

said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU; 5% said they were undecided.

Reactions

Political analyst Samvel Melkisetian said:

“Statements like these from Moscow are nothing new. They fit a long-established Russian pattern. The aim is to show both domestic and international audiences that Russia remains actively involved in regional developments. They also seek to expose what they portray as the EU’s and the West’s ‘hidden mechanisms’ of harmful influence across the post-Soviet region.”

He also noted that Moscow’s rhetoric often portrays Armenia not as a sovereign state making its own decisions, but as an object of external influence.

Political analyst Hovsep Khurshudyan said:

“What does Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service have to do with the EAEU that allows it to speak on behalf of the bloc’s member states? Has the SVR become the press office for the EAEU or its members?”

Khurshudyan also questioned Russia’s intelligence service:

“How can Brussels be accused of driving Armenia’s economy into crisis when it is Brussels that is compensating for the losses caused by the sanctions Russia has imposed?”

He was referring to EU support programmes launched after Russia restricted imports of Armenian goods.

Khurshudyan argues that, in the end, Russia’s actions will only accelerate:

Armenia’s withdrawal from Russian-led integration structures, including the EAEU and the Collective Security Treaty Organization;

the withdrawal of Russian border guards from Armenia’s borders with Iran and Turkey;

the termination of the concession agreement under which a Russian company operates Armenia’s railways.

Khurshudyan believes Armenia still has room to take further steps, while Russia has already exhausted most of its leverage.

SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

World.title: Imam of Georgia’s Akhaltsikhe mosque and family members brutally beaten
World.content:
Georgia‘s Interior Ministry has launched an investigation into an attack on the family of a Meskhetian Muslim in the city of Akhaltsikhe. According to the victims, more than 10 people assaulted the imam of the local mosque, Shevket Dvalidze, and members of his family during the incident on 18 July.

The attack was first reported by the news outlet Batumelebi. According to the publication, the assault began after the imam’s son and an underage relative visiting from Turkey were heard speaking Turkish to each other.

Meskhetian Muslims, also known as Meskhetian Turks or Ahiska Turks, are a Turkic ethnic group originating from the historical region of Meskheti in southwestern Georgia.

Shevket Dvalidze, imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque

According to the imam’s family, the group initially confronted them verbally, hurling insults over their use of the Turkish language, before the argument escalated into a physical assault.

The victims said the attackers followed them to their home and brutally beat them in the courtyard. Shevket Dvalidze, the imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque, sustained the most serious injuries and was later taken to hospital.

Batumelebi reported that Dvalidze was also urged to withdraw his police complaint.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry said it had opened an investigation under Article 126 of the Criminal Code, which covers physical violence.

The Georgian-based Social Justice Center responded to the incident by calling on the authorities to conduct a prompt and effective investigation and to properly assess whether the attack was motivated by discrimination.

According to the organisation, the victims said that between 10 and 12 people took part in the assault, and that most of them had been identified. However, only two suspects were arrested and were later released on bail by a court.

The Social Justice Center said the circumstances suggested the case could constitute not only an act of violence but also a hate crime, as the attack may have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation said investigators should examine whether the assault was motivated by the victims’ ethnic, religious or linguistic identity and ensure those circumstances are properly reflected in the legal classification of the case.

According to the Social Justice Center, correctly classifying the attack as a hate crime is important not only because of its legal consequences, but also because it acknowledges the true nature of the offence and helps prevent similar incidents.

The organisation called on the Interior Ministry and the Prosecutor’s Office to identify all those involved in the attack, rather than limiting the investigation to the two detained suspects. It also urged investigators to examine allegations that pressure had been put on the imam to withdraw his police complaint.

The Social Justice Center also called on the government and the Office of the State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality to publicly condemn the violence against the Meskhetian Muslim family, which it said appeared to have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation further urged the authorities to strengthen policies promoting equality, rebuilding trust and supporting cultural diversity in Akhaltsikhe’s Meskhetian Muslim communities, while reviewing barriers related to the repatriation and citizenship of Meskhetian Muslims.

Imam beaten in Georgia after speaking Turkish

World.title: Nauru cuts diplomatic ties with occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The Pacific island nation of Nauru has cut diplomatic ties with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, Georgia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.

According to the ministry, Nauru’s cabinet decided on 21 July 2026 to terminate diplomatic relations “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of South Ossetia, also known as the State of Alania,” and “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of Abkhazia.”

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation based on shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions to be independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to back the Moscow-backed move.

Nauru is a small island nation in the Pacific Ocean, in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 square kilometres, the country is smaller than several districts of Tbilisi, while its population is estimated at around 12,000 to 13,000 people.

Nauru ends ties with Abkhazia and South Ossetia

World.title: Five fined and four jailed in Tbilisi activists’ case
World.content:
A court in Georgia has concluded hearings in the cases of 10 activists detained outside Tbilisi City Hall on 26 July. Four were sentenced to administrative detention, while five were fined. Proceedings against one remaining activist have been postponed until 31 July.

What happened

The incident began when activist Tornike Toshkhua staged a solo protest outside Tbilisi City Hall holding a banner reading: “Bidzina d*ck? Yes – No.” The slogan referred to Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Police detained Toshkhua at the scene.

Tornike Toshkhua

In response, a group of activists gathered outside Tbilisi City Hall carrying banners with the same slogan to express solidarity with Toshkhua. Within minutes, police began detaining them as well. In total, nine more people were arrested alongside Toshkhua.

They have been charged with using abusive language in a public place and disobeying lawful police orders.

Fines and detentions

The activists began appearing in court from the afternoon of 28 July, before the 48-hour detention period had expired.

The first ruling was delivered in the case of Vaso Beridze. The judge fined him 5,000 lari ($1,850), rejecting the Interior Ministry’s request to place him under administrative detention.

In the case of Ia Melitauri, the Interior Ministry sought the maximum administrative detention, but the judge sentenced her to five days in custody instead. Police accused Melitauri of using abusive language in a public place and disobeying lawful police orders. The judge found no evidence that she had disobeyed police and convicted her only of petty hooliganism.

Melitauri had previously been found guilty twice of administrative offences involving disobeying police and insulting a police officer. A third offence under the same provision carries criminal liability.

According to people present at the hearing, Melitauri told the court she had been mistreated by police following her arrest and showed the judge injuries she said she had sustained during her detention.

The hearing in the case of the third detainee, Tornike Tikaradze, was postponed until 31 July. Tikaradze did not attend the hearing in protest.

Another judge heard the cases of seven other activists and, after several hours of witness testimony and reviewing video evidence, delivered the following verdicts:

Tornike Toshkhua was fined 3,000 lari ($1,110);

Mariam Mekantsishvili was fined 6,000 lari ($2,220);

Nato Bolkvadze was sentenced to five days of administrative detention;

Shako Bagdoshvili was sentenced to 10 days of administrative detention;

Lasha Dgebuadze was sentenced to 10 days of administrative detention;

Marine Nanava was fined 5,000 lari ($1,850);

Sandro Sekhniashvili was fined 5,000 lari ($1,850).

Scuffle outside the courthouse

Several reports of scuffles between members of the public and court bailiffs emerged throughout the day as the hearings were under way.

Videos circulating on social media showed bailiffs forcibly removing people from the courthouse.

During the final hearing, activist Ruska Mchedlidze and lawyer Marika Arevadze said court bailiffs used force against them.

Ruska Mchedlidze

“Zonder bailiff Davit Matiashvili and other zonder bailiffs physically assaulted me in the courtyard of this unjust court. Yes, I spat at them, and yes, I spat at them again after the assault, once I was outside the gates.

These bruises will heal, but everyone will remember his disgrace forever. His, and that of the other zonder bailiffs carrying out unlawful orders. There were around 20 police officers standing there, watching as these aggressive men assaulted me, and not one of them intervened,” Mchedlidze wrote on social media.

Activist Lado Jakhua also shared footage showing several court bailiffs dragging Ruska Mchedlidze out of the courthouse courtyard.

Tbilisi activists sentenced over protest

World.title: Opposition grows in Abkhazia over monument to citizens killed in Ukraine war
World.content:
A group of Abkhaz politicians and public figures has spoken out against plans to erect a monument in Sukhum to citizens of Abkhazia who were killed while fighting in the war in Ukraine.

They appealed to the republic’s president, Badra Gunba, and the city authorities to cancel or postpone the decision, which was approved by the Sukhum City Assembly at the initiative of the city administration.

The appeal was signed by former parliament speaker Valery Kvarchia, People’s Artist Batal Jopua, historian Guram Gumba, former education minister Adgur Kakoba, Akhyatsa civic organisation head Akhra Bzhania, and former leader of the Aruaa veterans’ movement Ilya Guniya.

The signatories argue that any memorial erected in the Abkhaz capital should commemorate historical events only after they have stood the test of time.

“Fighting is still under way, people are dying, yet the local authorities in Abkhazia have taken the unprecedented decision to erect a monument to a war that has not yet ended.

“No one knows how, when or on what terms these two closely related peoples will first reach understanding and then reconciliation. But that will inevitably happen. Only then, years later, will we be able to return to the question of creating a memorial to this historical event,” the appeal says.

The authors also point out that Sukhum still has no monuments to Abkhazia’s first president, Vladislav Ardzinba, or to volunteers from the North Caucasus republics who fought alongside Abkhazia during the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war.

“If we intend to begin preserving our historical memory, we should start with them. Otherwise, not only the people of Abkhazia but also our friends in the North Caucasus and the parents of the fallen volunteers will not understand us,” the appeal says.

The signatories also argue that the issue has an important foreign policy dimension. Despite its strategic partnership with Russia, they say, Abkhazia is not at war with Ukraine.

“Our state has never carried out any mobilisation or organisational measures in connection with what Russia calls its ‘special military operation’. The relevant authorities have no information about either the total number of our citizens in the conflict zone or the terms under which they entered military service,” the appeal says.

They argue that officially recognising the participation of Abkhaz citizens in the fighting would provide diplomatic grounds for Ukraine and its regional allies, including Turkey, to regard Abkhazia as a party to the conflict. As a result, they say, “our citizens’ participation in the war would cease to be a matter of personal choice and instead become our collective choice.”

Although the appeal has been signed by only six people, its authors say they believe their views are widely shared across Abkhaz society.

“We are in contact with people from all walks of life and can say with confidence that thousands of residents of Sukhum and citizens of Abkhazia share our views and the arguments set out above.”

The signatories call on the president and the city authorities to act with prudence and wisdom.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Monument to Abkhazians who fought in Ukraine

World.title: Turkey takes practical steps to restore rail link with Armenia
World.content:
Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

Turkey has begun restoring the entire railway infrastructure along the Akyaka–Gyumri route, the section connecting it with Armenia. Preliminary estimates suggest the work will take two to three months to complete. Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas told this to a group of Armenian journalists visiting Turkey.

According to Toptas, the construction work now under way in Turkey signals preparations for reopening the Armenian-Turkish border. He said reopening the border would give Turkey another route to the Caucasus. It would also allow Armenia to establish transport links with Middle Eastern countries through Turkey.

Kadir Bozan, chairman of the Kars Chamber of Commerce and Industry, also told the Armenian journalists that freight traffic on the Akhalkalaki–Kars railway has increased by 400% in recent months. He did not specify whether Armenia uses the route for exports or imports.

However, on 24 May, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said that “the Akhalkalaki–Kars railway is now open for exports from Armenia and imports into Armenia.” He described the development as extremely important for the country’s economy.

Armenian journalists’ impressions from their visit to Turkey

According to official information, a group of Armenian journalists travelled to Turkey as part of a journalist exchange programme. The purpose of the visit was to observe progress on the work to reopen the railway on the Turkish side.

The journalists also wanted to see how Turkey’s railway infrastructure operates more broadly. In particular, they travelled by train from Kars to Akyaka. The 57-kilometre journey took just 50 minutes.

After returning, they wrote that Akyaka station lies only 18–20 kilometres from the Armenian city of Gyumri. That means the journey would take just 30–40 minutes. However, the closed border currently makes it impossible to travel from Akyaka to Gyumri.

Tender announced for Akyaka–Gyumri highway

Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas said Turkey plans to restore not only the railway but also the highway.

“The tender for the construction of the road from Akyaka to Gyumri has already been announced. We now expect work on that project to begin as well,” he said.

According to Toptas, these developments indicate that both governments are moving towards establishing good-neighbourly and friendly relations.

The mayor said reopening the Armenian-Turkish border and expanding bilateral economic cooperation would benefit both countries. He believes the two sides have opportunities to cooperate in both agriculture and industry.

The Armenian journalists also spoke with residents of Turkish settlements near the Armenian border. Most said they hope the border will reopen as soon as possible. They also believe it will create new economic opportunities for local communities on both sides of the border.

“We do not expect any obstacles to reopening the border”

Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas expressed optimism about the prospects for normalising relations between Armenia and Turkey. In his view, once Armenia and Azerbaijan normalise their relations, reopening the Armenian-Turkish border should not present any difficulties.

He said that, on the instructions of the Turkish president and under the coordination of the transport ministry, officials have begun preparatory work at the border crossing points ahead of the border’s reopening. Railway infrastructure also requires restoration. However, he said the closed border remains the main obstacle to resuming rail services.

At the beginning of 2026, Armenian media reported that the Armenian-Turkish border would open on 1 February to third-country nationals and holders of diplomatic passports. Armenia’s and Turkey’s special envoys for normalisation, Ruben Rubinyan and Serdar Kilic, reached that agreement in July 2022. The Margara border crossing on the Armenian side has stood ready to receive travellers since December 2023. Despite those agreements, however, Turkey has kept the border closed.

Even so, the two countries periodically announce positive steps. For example, from 1 January 2026, Armenia and Turkey simplified visa procedures for holders of diplomatic, special and service passports. They can now obtain a free electronic visa (e-visa) for short-term trips of up to 20 days.

Background

Since 2008, Armenia’s railway network has operated under a concession held by the South Caucasus Railway company, a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The concession agreement runs for 30 years, with an option to extend it by another 10 years if both sides agree.

Armenian experts say freight traffic on the country’s railways has halved since 2008. Some routes have ceased operating, while the mandatory investment commitments have never materialised.

Despite this, Yerevan asked Moscow to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

Rebuilding these lines would reconnect Armenia with the borders of Azerbaijan and Turkey. This is strategically important for Yerevan, which seeks to fully unblock regional transport links.

Russia has neither acted on Armenia’s request nor indicated a willingness to do so. At the same time, Moscow has said it does not intend to give up its railway concession.

Meanwhile, the Armenian government is considering revoking Russia’s concession and taking control of the railway network itself. It has also left open the possibility of transferring the concession to a third party.

At the beginning of July, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan announced that Armenia had begun preparatory work to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

“We will carry out this work ourselves. As for the remaining sections, we will continue working-level discussions, including with our Russian partners,” he said.

Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘Dictator wants to be liked by everyone. Those who don’t like him must be neutralised’
World.content:
Transparency International Georgia researcher Zviad Koridze believes that Georgia’s current system of governance is built on fostering civil confrontation and deepening divisions within society. In his view, authoritarian regimes rely on social polarisation and the portrayal of people with different opinions as enemies in order to maintain power.

Koridze said that Georgian society still retains the capacity to resist, and that, ultimately, it is civic engagement that will serve as the main force pushing back against these processes.

On 26 July, MMA (mixed martial arts) fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, together with several supporters, announced the creation of a civic movement that will “respond immediately” to issues involving ancestors, religion, history and other subjects that the group considers offensive. According to Kartvelishvili, the movement will be “highly active, well-organised and constructive”, and any “patriotic Georgian” will be able to join. Members of the group also said they were prepared to take responsibility for their actions, including serving prison sentences if necessary.

Zviad Koridze: “the system of governance that has taken hold in Georgia — Bidzina Ivanishvili’s dictatorship — regards civil confrontation as its natural state, just like any other dictatorship. Without it, those in power cannot consolidate their rule. They cannot persuade citizens that their continued grip on power and authoritarian governance serve the public interest. To do that, they need civil confrontation.

“All dictatorships are structured and develop in exactly this way. They need to identify groups and segments of society whose views differ from those of the autocrat. Then another social group must emerge to confront and suppress them. That is the language of civil confrontation.”

“When parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili says that we do not need to join the European Union because we should have the right to make our own decisions, that is clearly not his independent position but Bidzina Ivanishvili’s. Papuashvili’s role is to voice that position and to support the creation of precisely these kinds of vigilante groups. He is expected to welcome their emergence. He sees this as a form of sovereign governance, and that is exactly why he does not want Georgia to join the European Union.

“How can a writer be liked by everyone? Is there a single writer who is universally admired? How can anyone even make such a claim? Or say that a public figure must be liked by everyone? Only a dictator wants that. He wants everyone to like him. And anyone who does not must be neutralised, driven out, persecuted and beaten. That is why he creates groups like these.

“These restrictions are designed to instil a climate of irrational fear, discouraging people from thinking independently, protesting and speaking out. The current situation is exactly the one Bidzina Ivanishvili wants most, and he is using every mechanism at his disposal to maintain it. The only force capable of dismantling these mechanisms is society itself — a society with a firm stance. I do not believe society is silent. I am convinced that our society will resist.”

Civil confrontation in Georgia

World.title: Norwegian teen guilty of UK murder plot tied to Iran-linked group
World.content:
A Norwegian teenager has been convicted of conspiracy to commit murder in Britain after being recruited by a Swedish organised crime group that prosecutors said was being used by the Iranian government.

Johannes Natland, now 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, northern England, in March last year with two firearms and ammunition in his possession.

Prosecutors said Natland had been recruited by the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group used by the Iranian state and sanctioned by both Britain and the United States.

Natland had admitted possessing a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver and ammunition, but denied conspiracy to murder, saying he did not intend to carry out the plan.

After a retrial at London's Old Bailey court, Natland was found guilty of conspiracy to murder. A jury at his initial trial in June could not reach a verdict on that charge.

Prosecutors say the intended target of the plot has never been identified.

Natland is the latest young adult to stand trial in Britain and elsewhere over serious criminal acts allegedly carried out after being recruited online for money, often as an unwitting proxy for a foreign state.

Prosecutor Alistair Richardson told jurors that Natland was recruited by the Foxtrot Network, after someone using the name "Agent 47" organised hiring an assassin with 25,000 euros ($40,000) "in the pot" to pay for it.

Natland "neither knew, nor cared who he was to kill … to him, this was all about the money", Mr Richardson said.

Footage posted on social media by the UK's Crown Prosecution Service after the conviction showed Natland using his hands to pretend to shoot at officers during his arrest.

The vision also shows him walking through woodland to retrieve ammunition and firearms in Huddersfield.

During a police raid, which prosecutors said was carried out two days before the planned hit, officials found live ammunition, firearms and cash.

Frank Ferguson, Head of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said the case demonstrated how organised crime networks were operating across borders and using young people.

"This conviction sends a clear message: if you come to this country to commit serious violence on behalf of organised criminals, you will be caught and we will make sure you are brought to justice," he said.

The CPS said in a statement that a 17-year-old had been convicted and sentenced to 14 years in Norway in relation to recruiting Natland to the conspiracy, while a 16-year-old in Norway was awaiting trial for alleged involvement in the conspiracy.

World.title: Trump vows to retaliate 'hard' against Iran in expletive-laden warning
World.content:
Donald Trump has unleashed another fiery threat against Iran after a missile barrage launched towards American forces in Jordan.

In a phone interview with Fox News, which was not broadcast, the US president reportedly said the US would "beat the f****** s***" out of Iran in response to the surprise strikes on Tuesday night, local time.

He added that the US military would be "hitting them hard, they're going to get a beating".

Mr Trump paused US attacks against Iran over the weekend, after 13 straight days of strikes.

In turn, Iran had stopped launching retaliatory strikes against American personnel and bases across the Middle East, including in the Gulf states and in Jordan.

A number of US media outlets had reported the decision to halt strikes was made, in part, because of concerns that interceptor missiles used to defend American bases and allies from Iranian attacks were running low — something US officials publicly rejected.

The aftermath of an airstrike on a Popular Mobilization Forces base in Mosul, Iraq. (AP: Farid Abdulwahed)

But on Tuesday, local time, the US joined with Saudi Arabian forces to hit Iranian-backed militia groups in Iraq, which US Central Command (CENTCOM) said had been directed by Tehran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to attack Saudi and US forces in the region.

"The unwarranted attacks against US forces were not successful," CENTCOM said in a statement.

" The IRGC and its terrorist proxies must cease these attacks to avoid further US military response. "

The Iraqi Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) had said at least 20 of its members were killed and 32 injured in the US and Saudi strikes.

If Mr Trump followed through on his latest threat, it would shatter the current calm in the region and once again risk returning the region to all-out war.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump met face to face on Tuesday for the first time since the war began. (X: Benjamin Netanyahu)

The US president had said he was prepared to attack Iran again if negotiations on a lasting peace deal remained stalled, while Iran had accused the US of consistently undermining progress toward any agreement by making repeated threats.

On Tuesday, in Washington DC, Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held his first face-to-face meeting with Mr Trump since the start of the war in late February.

Despite being one of the instigators of the war, Israel had held fire and refrained from joining the US in attacking Iran after the interim deal to end the war, signed in June, collapsed.

That had been triggered by the ongoing dispute over control of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow and busy shipping channel which Iran has blocked for much of the war.

Hours before the US and Saudi strikes, a new proposal by Oman on management of the waterway had been rejected by Iranian negotiators.

World.title: Russia charges Telegram founder with aiding terrorism
World.content:
Russia says it has charged Telegram founder Pavel Durov with facilitating terrorist activity, alleging that his hugely popular messaging app is being used by Ukrainian spies to organise attacks inside Russia.

In response, Telegram's official account on X posted an image of the Russian-born billionaire making an obscene gesture with his middle finger.

The charges, announced by the Federal Security Service (FSB), marked the culmination of a long investigation against Dubai-based Durov and Telegram.

Moscow has effectively throttled the service as part of a wider campaign to cut off access to foreign tech platforms and tighten control over the internet.

What is Telegram and why was its founder arrested? French authorities arrest Pavel Durov under unusual circumstances in Paris. He is being questioned over alleged criminal activity on Telegram, which has been enabled through a lack of moderation.

Russians can only access Telegram now by using a VPN to encrypt traffic and conceal their location. Yet state bodies including the Kremlin and the defence ministry continue to post to it on a daily basis.

The app has been described as a "virtual battlefield" in the war between Russia and Ukraine, where it is used by officials, soldiers and influential bloggers on both sides.

In statements, the FSB and the state Investigative Committee said a chatbot available on Telegram called "Daivinchik/Leo" had been used by Ukrainian special services to recruit young Russians to carry out sabotage and terrorist operations.

Daivinchik/Leo is a popular dating chatbot in Russia, where Tinder is no longer available. The statement said Ukrainian spies posting as young women were using it to contact and entrap Russians before coercing them into committing crimes.

The FSB said 46 Russians aged 12 to 22 had been arrested in the past year after being recruited in this way to carry out attacks on law enforcement officers or set fire to transport, energy, communications or financial infrastructure.

Vladimir Putin unsuccessfully attempted to block Telegram between 2018 and 2020. (Reuters: Anastasia Barashkova)

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

The FSB statement said Mr Durov was being placed on an international wanted list, but it did not specify what mechanism Russia would use to do this.

The global police organisation Interpol did not immediately respond to a request for comment. If Moscow does request a Red Notice, however, the process is unlikely to be quick, said a source with knowledge of the situation.

Dubai, where Mr Durov lives, has friendly relations with Moscow and growing ties in energy, business and finance. But handing him over to Russia could risk damaging the Emirate's image as an attractive hub for enterprise and technology.

Mr Durov posted that he was in Georgia last week, but his current whereabouts are unclear.

Born in Russia, he now holds Emirati and French passports. He founded Russia's Facebook equivalent, VKontakte, before selling his remaining stake in 2014 amid pressure from Russian authorities.

In 2024 he was arrested in France over allegations that Telegram failed to adequately counter criminal activity on the platform and did not sufficiently cooperate with law enforcement requests. He was later allowed to leave the country while investigations continue.

Mr Durov denies wrongdoing and says Telegram has exceeded its obligations to moderate content and cooperate with authorities to fight crime.

A Russian government newspaper reported in February that Durov was under investigation in a terrorism-related case. In April, he posted on Telegram that a summons for "Suspect P.V. Durov" had been delivered to an apartment in Russia where he lived 20 years ago.

"They must be suspecting me of defending Articles 29 and 23 of the Russian Constitution — which guarantee freedom of speech and the right to private correspondence. Proud to be guilty!" he wrote at the time.

Reuters

World.title: Nasty crash denies Aussies chance to hit back at defector Richardson
World.content:
One of the most hotly anticipated showdowns of the 2026 Commonwealth Games has been unceremoniously called off with the news England's Matt Richardson will not ride in the track cycling.

The sprint champion who represented Australia before defecting to the country of his birth following the Paris Olympics in 2024 has been ruled out by injury, Team England announced.

Richardson was racing in Japan and had been set to arrive in Scotland just before the track cycling program in Glasgow gets underway on Thursday.

Live: Commonwealth Games day six We are past the halfway mark in Glasgow, which means the end of the swimming program as athletics kicks into high gear. Follow live.

He sustained an undisclosed injury after taking a nasty fall while riding in the Keirin World Series in Tachigawa.

"We wish him a speedy recovery and look forward to seeing him back on the track soon," the English team said.

Richardson was set to compete in the men's individual and team sprints in Glasgow, setting up a high-profile showdown with his former Australian teammates.

"It's definitely weird seeing him in GB kit," Australian sprinter Leigh Hoffman said before the withdrawal was announced.

"At the time it just came out of nowhere, we'd just finished the [Olympic] Games, brought a few medals back for Australia and then he went on holiday and never came back.

"I'm not really going to be sad about it or anything, I'm just going to focus on riding my bike and I think he does the same as well."

The Aussies generally played down the match-up earlier at the Games.

Matt Richardson (left) and Leigh Hoffman have competed before, but on friendlier terms. (Supplied: AusCycling/Mackenzie Sweetnam)

"I'm excited to beat everyone in the world, he's just another domino to fall, hopefully," said Hoffman, who won 2022 Commonwealth Games gold and 2024 Olympic bronze in the team sprint with Richardson.

"The Australia-England rivalry goes back very far with the Ashes and all our other sports. It's always Australia vs England, [but] for the Commonwealth Games, we've got some really stacked riders.

"Azizul Awang from Malaysia, who's come in in great form; Trinidad and Tobago, Nicholas Paul — there's a lot of great riders.

"But the fans are definitely looking forward to an Australia-England match-up."

Hoffman admitted to being hurt by Richardson's defection after years riding together.

"We'd never experienced something like that," Hoffman said.

"You grow up racing with someone and you think you're both Aussies and then he's not. That's life."

On the way out the door, Richardson fired shots at the AusCycling set-up — comparing riding in Australia vs England to attending a normal high school vs Hogwarts — a quote Hoffman chuckled about "biting [Richards] in the arse".

World.title: Oscar-winning Irish musician Glen Hansard dies in motorcycle crash
World.content:
Irish musician Glen Hansard, who won a Best Original Song Oscar and was lead singer for rock group The Frames, has died in a motorcycle crash at the age of 56.

Irish police said a man in his 50s had died after a single-vehicle motorcycle collision in the west of Dublin.

Emergency services were alerted shortly before 04:30 am local time and the man was pronounced dead a short time after being treated at the scene.

Newstalk Radio and the Irish Independent reported that Hansard died in the crash.

In a statement ot the ABC, ATC Management "with broken hearts" confirmed Hansard's death.

"We are still dealing with the shock of it all, so we kindly ask that the privacy of Glen’s family, colleagues and friends is respected at this difficult time," a spokesperson said.

Glen Hansard was the frontman of The Frames. (Reuters: Stephan Savoia/Pool)

Hansard combined acting and a musical career.

He played a member of a Dublin soul band in 1991 movie The Commitments and won an Oscar in 2008 for the song Falling Slowly from the film Once, in which he starred alongside Markéta Irglová.

He was the long-serving frontman for rock band The Frames, half of rock duo The Swell Season and released solo albums including Didn't He Ramble, which was nominated for a Grammy for Best Folk Album in 2016.

For years, Hansard led the Christmas Eve charity busk outside Dublin's Gaiety Theatre, where members of the public gathered to see famous Irish musicians perform in aid of the Dublin Simon Community.

At the funeral of The Pogues frontman Shane MacGowan in 2023, Hansard performed The Pogues' song Fairytale Of New York with Irish singer Lisa O’Neill, which prompted dancing in the aisles of the church.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said he was "deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Glen Hansard".

"A talented musician and actor who made a significant contribution to Ireland's cultural landscape over many years," Mr Martin posted on X.

Reuters/AP

World.title: New data shows Indigenous children face lengthy periods on remand
World.content:
Under the vast outback sky of Mount Isa, community leader Corina James is a familiar face at the local courthouse, a place she visits weekly out of a deep-seated commitment to supporting her young relatives and other local children.

"I go there every week; I'm still going to the courthouse because I worry," she said.

Corina also heads to the local police station when she gets a call that someone she knows has been arrested. Those visits are tough on her heart.

"I just broke down and cried for the little fella. It makes you feel really sad for them," she said.

With 30 grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren, Corina's home serves as an open-door sanctuary for many young people in the community seeking guidance.

Corina James believes the youth justice system is broken. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"I support … anyone else that wants to come along and ask for a bit of support … I point them in the right direction," she said.

While families like Corina's work to keep kids out of trouble, First Nations children continue to be over-represented in the criminal justice system.

The latest Closing the Gap data shows little progress to reach the nationally agreed target of at least a 30 per cent reduction in the number of Indigenous children behind bars by 2031.

The Productivity Commission's annual data compilation report found that First Nations children nationally have been held without a sentence on average for 57 days while they await trial, sentencing or a bail decision.

Over the past five years, the rate has increased from 69 per cent to 76 per cent.

Queensland has the highest proportion of children detained without a sentence, ranging from 80 to 90 per cent, with an average of 96 days, the highest in the country.

Corina opens her Mt Isa home as a safe place for youth. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Corina keeps detailed records about the children she supports who are navigating the youth justice system.

She knows one child who recently spent 48 days unsentenced in the Cleveland Youth Detention Centre in Townsville, followed by a 24-hour curfew upon release.

"[He] was in custody for a very long time because he had to wait for a lawyer," Corina said.

"They kept chopping and changing his lawyer, and it's really sad because they had to deal with lawyers from Brisbane."

She said he was "really sad and frustrated" while in custody.

At home, families are doing what they can to stop kids ending up behind bars.

Christine says she is often out on the streets looking for her grandchildren in the middle of the night. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Christine Doyle, Corina's sister, said it is often the exhausted grandparents and parents who take to the streets to track down the kids.

"When we go to bed at night, we all go to sleep here, [but] our kids are sneaking out the door," said Christine.

" Then when we wake up at like three o'clock in the morning, the kids are all gone … I drive around and look for my grandsons. "

Target to reduce youth in detention not on track

The Closing the Gap National Agreement is a formal commitment by all Australian governments to work in partnership with Indigenous communities to achieve equal life outcomes.

But the latest Productivity Commission assessment released today found there has been no significant improvement since the target to reduce young people in detention was established, and it is not on track to be met.

Indigenous young people continue to make up more than half of all people held in juvenile detention.

Sue-Anne Hunter says it is easier to demonise children than to deal with the root problems. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People Sue-Anne Hunter said the picture was damning.

"These numbers should worry every Australian; this is active harm, and it's compounding every year," she said.

"Most First Nations young people sitting in detention today have not been sentenced; they have not been found guilty of anything."

She said the detention figures reflected how governments respond to children in contact with the justice system, rather than a simple measure of youth offending.

" We see a demonisation in this country of youth, it's easier to lock them up. "

A rise in unsentenced detention

The data highlighted how limited access to secure housing could be a factor contributing to Indigenous children being exposed to longer periods of incarceration.

Katherine Hayes, the CEO of Youth Advisory Centre in Brisbane, said unstable homes were just one of the reasons why young people are detained without a sentence.

Katherine Hayes is working to reduce the number of children in custody through early intervention and diversionary programs. (Supplied)

"They don't have an appropriate bail address, so they don't have a permanent home or a safe home, and so they're held on remand," she said.

"[But also] it takes a really long time for their matters to get to the trial stage and that can be multifaceted … but also the way that defence lawyers conduct the matter or the police prosecutors can be slow to provide briefs of evidence."

Of all the states and territories in Australia, the highest number of children incarcerated are in Queensland.

More children are being held in unsentenced detention, with Queensland holding kids for more than 90 days. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Ms Hayes said detaining children in custody was not the solution fit for all youth crime.

"Give them a safe home, engage them in education, address all the mental health concerns and make sure that they have a safe home that is free from domestic and family violence," she said.

A spokesperson for Queensland's Department of Youth Justice and Victim Support told the ABC the state was prioritising "the rights of victims".

"The Queensland government is addressing youth crime and restoring safety where Queenslanders live by introducing tough new laws to prioritise the rights of victims and deliver consequences for actions for youth offenders," the spokesperson said.

"The Queensland government is also investing in early intervention and rehabilitation to reduce offending and reoffending and break the cycle of crime."

Experts say that prison is not rehabilitating for children. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Anne Hollonds, spokesperson for Justice Reform Initiative and former National Children's Commissioner, said incarcerating children without a sentence was "completely unacceptable".

"These are children who have not been found, at this stage, to have been guilty of any crime, [and] some of them are as young as 10," Ms Hollonds said.

"To deprive them of their liberty in these places of incarceration … is really punishing them for circumstances that are beyond their own control."

The data also revealed more than one in 10 First Nations young people who completed a community-based sentence in 2022-23 were back in detention within a year.

Community supervision is intended to keep young people out of detention by allowing them to serve court orders in the community.

Ms Hollonds said governments were failing to stop vulnerable children from becoming entrenched in the justice system once they have come in contact with it.

"The recidivism rates in Australia are extraordinarily high, and what that's demonstrating is that incarcerating children, whether on remand or sentenced, is doing no one any good," she said.

"It's not keeping the community safer, but it's certainly harming these children who just go on to commit more serious crimes."

The emotional toll of remand

Skye Cooney, a youth service coordinator at Darwin's CAAPS Aboriginal Corporation, works closely with vulnerable adolescents aged 10 to 17.

Many of her clients are navigating the aftermath of juvenile detention.

Skye says she has seen the negative impacts that holding children in unsentenced detention can have. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"When they get released to us, they participate in our Youth Service AOD program, so our goal is obviously to support them and try and give them a bit more of a positive life while they're still either serving [a] sentence or they have coming court dates," she said.

Skye frequently supports youth who have been held in unsentenced detention. She said these types of cases exacerbate substance dependency as a coping mechanism for confinement.

"If a client has been on remand in prison for two months or three months for committing a crime, [and] if they are not found guilty of that crime, then they're trying to cope with what's just happened," she said.

A 'blueprint' for success

The Productivity Commission updated nine out of the 19 Closing the Gap targets with new data.

Out of the nine updated targets, child protection continues to worsen, as well as suicide rates and adult incarceration.

The target for preschool enrolment has been met for the first time.

Employment, land rights and sea rights are on track to be met, while youth detention and babies born with a healthy birth weight have seen no significant change from the baseline.

Indigenous young people make up more than half of all people held in juvenile detention. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

The minister for Indigenous Australians said in a statement it was an "encouraging" result that the gap in preschool enrolments had officially closed.

"This is a significant milestone and shows that collective efforts can drive meaningful and lasting change," Senator Malarndirri McCarthy said.

But she noted it was "very concerning" that other critical targets for early childhood development, children in out-of-home care, suicide and adult incarceration continued to worsen.

Senator McCarthy urged states and territories that have primary responsibility for prisons, youth detention and child protection systems to do more.

"State and territory governments must also back in their commitments under the National Agreement with investments and policies that improve outcomes for First Nations people," she said.

The commissioner, Sue-Anne Hunter, said handing over power to community-controlled organisations was the way forward.

Ms Hunter wants to see the government use the successful targets as "blueprints" for addressing youth crime and child protection targets, with more funding into early intervention and support for family services.

World.title: 'Time-limited rotation': Conroy puts an end date on US subs in WA
World.content:
Defence Industries Minister Pat Conroy has put a time limit on US submarines rotating through the HMAS Stirling naval base in Western Australia.

Mr Conroy spelled out, for the first time, that 2032 will be the end date for the rotation of US Virginia-class submarines through Stirling — known as Submarine Rotation Force West (SRF-West) — and due to begin next year.

"This is a time-limited rotation," Mr Conroy told 7.30.

"It's a five-year commitment beginning in 2027… That's the arrangement that we've put in place, with the plan being that as we acquire our own nuclear-powered submarines, they would move into HMAS Stirling and the rotational presence would come to an end."

Mr Conroy is in Washington, DC, for talks about the AUKUS submarine program with senior Pentagon officials, including US Navy Secretary Hung Cao and US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll.

He will also visit a submarine factory in South Carolina, announcing a contract worth $2 million for the use of Australian steel products in US submarines.

A military analyst and former Royal Australian Navy warfare officer, Jennifer Parker, responded to Mr Conroy's statement that US nuclear-powered submarines would cease rotating through Stirling,

"I am surprised to hear an end date for SRF-West articulated so clearly and think it's likely US submarines will continue to rotate from Stirling post 2032," Ms Parker said.

US Navy Virginia-class fast-attack submarine USS Vermont at HMAS Stirling in Western Australia last year. (Royal Australian Navy: ABIS Jayden Fahy)

Mr Conroy was also at pains to reject the characterisation from critics of the AUKUS program, including former foreign minister Gareth Evans and former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull, that Stirling will be a de facto US base, despite the large-scale logistical infrastructure being put in place to support next year's arrival of American subs, crews and their families.

"The rotation each year is time-limited," Mr Conroy said.

"That's why they're not based there; they're only in HMAS Stirling for a limited amount of time each year."

Asked how much time each year that would be, Mr Conroy said he could not disclose the answer.

"That goes to the operational employment that the United States uses for those submarines, but they won't be there all year long," he said.

'Statements of the bleeding obvious'

As the date for the arrival of US nuclear-powered submarines in Australian waters gets closer, so do sensitivities around the US deployment.

Donald Trump's plans have raised concerns about when Australia will get AUKUS subs. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a visit to Stirling by US Rear Admiral Lincoln Reifsteck, where he spelled out the advantages to the US Navy of access to the base for refitting and resupply in the event of a conflict with China.

"If you're in some kind of conflict and your ships are getting damaged, you're going to want to return to the fight quickly," he told the WSJ.

"Having this geography to enhance what you have in Guam, to enhance what you have in Pearl Harbour, it's going to make the US Navy get back to it faster."

Mr Conroy acknowledged the strategic advantages of Stirling to the US.

"It [also] is obviously an entry point into the Indian Ocean; they're statements of the bleeding obvious," he told 7.30.

"It has a strategic utility, but that's an important factor for Australia as well as the United States."

Mr Conroy rejected questions about what access the US Navy would get to HMAS Stirling, beyond the rotation ending in 2032, as hypothetical.

"Nothing we're doing pre-commits Australia to any future conflict. It'll be up to the government of the day to decide what we do with our military and secondly, what we allow other militaries to do on our sovereign territories," he said.

The Australian Submarine Agency told 7.30 that it expected US and UK navies would use Stirling post 2032.

"US and UK nuclear-powered submarines have been visiting HMAS Stirling for decades, and we expect this to continue well beyond SRF-West."

Former home affairs secretary Mike Pezzullo wrote in The Australian at the weekend to urge open debate on US military plans in Australia, referring to a recent decision by the US Congress to enable American Virginia-class submarines and other vessels to carry tactical nuclear weapons from 2032.

"By deploying these types of weapons, the US is seeking to give itself the option of being able to conduct limited nuclear strikes on military and strategic targets," Mr Pezzullo wrote.

Mr Conroy argued that the question of whether US nuclear-powered subs could also be carrying nuclear weapons after 2032 would be moot because the submarine rotation would already have ended.

"Submarine Rotation Force West is due to come to an end in the early 2030s. So the time-frames don't exactly overlap," he said.

7.30 contacted the Pentagon for comment.

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays at 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Texts reveal alleged drug ring used aliases Duke Dingbat and Bush Jesus
World.content:
Two alleged major players in an interstate drug syndicate will remain behind bars after their bail applications were refused by a Northern Territory judge this week.

Andrew Washington faced Darwin Local Court today charged with the possession and supply of commercial quantities of methamphetamine, ketamine, cocaine and cannabis.

The court heard Mr Washington and co-accused Jossire Nditije, both 26, were integral parts of an alleged drug ring with interstate ties, who at the height of their trade handled more than $1.5 million in cash.

Mr Nditije faced court on the same charges as Mr Washington yesterday and the court today heard Mr Washington's charges might not "scratch the surface" of the alleged offending over a period of years.

The court heard the clothes dryers allegedly contained methamphetamine, ketamine, cocaine and cannabis. (Getty Images: Jonathan Raa/NurPhoto)

Prosecutor Sean Nottle read aloud from a text message sent in December 2024, in which Mr Washington allegedly said "I've been doing this for three years with mass supply and no arrests".

Mr Nottle said police had also accessed group chat messages detailing the alleged transportation of five clothes dryers into the NT with large quantities of drugs secreted inside.

"[They found] photos, messages and overt expressions that the group had found the truck, deconstructed the dryers and then sent photos through of what had in fact been recovered," he said.

" [It is] one of the more significant drug enterprises the Northern Territory has seen in recent times. "

The court heard Mr Washington had been on bail for prior alleged offending, but was re-arrested on the more serious charges once his alleged role at the "apex" of the drug ring was discovered.

"The significance of the allegations are such that bail should and must be refused, and bail is refused," Judge David Woodroffe said.

'Duke Dingbat', 'Hot Plate' and 'Bush Jesus'

The court heard Mr Washington, Mr Nditije and others allegedly communicated in group chats using codenames such as Duke Dingbat, Hot Plate and Bush Jesus but "the attribution of those particular handles and devices is still ongoing".

Mr Nottle told the court police were still working their way through a backlog of group chat messages sent and received in 2024 and 2025, with 90 pages of messages sent in the month the five clothes dryers were transported.

The court heard the machines allegedly contained 3 kilograms of methamphetamine, 2 kilograms of ketamine, 394 grams of cocaine and more than 9 kilograms of cannabis.

Judge Elizabeth Morris said the risk Mr Nditije would abscond or commit further offences was too great to grant bail. (ABC News: Ian Redfern)

Chief Judge Elizabeth Morris yesterday rejected Mr Nditije's lawyer's suggestion an around-the-clock curfew, a $10,000 bond from his mother and police access to his devices would mitigate any risk in granting him bail.

Judge Morris said the allegations were "extremely serious".

"The risk then of course is that he would not appear, that further offending might be committed, or that he might interfere with any further police investigation," she said.

Mr Washington and Mr Nditije are both expected to return to court next month.

World.title: Three dead in house fire in Sydney’s south-west
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWFire Three dead in house fire in Sydney’s south-west Sarah McPhee July 30, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three people have died in a house fire in Sydney’s south-west. Emergency services were called to a fire at the home on Cornelia Street in Wiley Park about 9.45pm on Wednesday. Fire and Rescue NSW (FRNSW) crews extinguished the blaze and found the bodies of three people inside. The victims are yet to be formally identified. The property suffered extensive damage, police said. Officers from Campsie Police Area Command have established a crime scene and are investigating the circumstances surrounding the fire. A report will be prepared for the coroner.



While the cause is still being investigated, earlier this month FRNSW issued a safety reminder about “the most dangerous time of the year for house fires”. As of July 15, FRNSW had already attended 480 residential fires this winter and 2025 this year. FRNSW Commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell encouraged residents to use the service’s free home fire safety visit program which includes smoke alarm checks. “You can also take some simple steps to keep you and your family safe. For example, regularly check your smoke alarm, always keep looking when cooking, keep a fire blanket and extinguisher in your kitchen, keep flammable materials a metre from the heater, and don’t overload power board or power points,” Fewtrell said. “Always check electric and heated blankets before turning them on, and look for frays, scorch marks, exposed wires or controller damage. If anything looks off, bin it.”



More to come Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Alzheimer’s blood test to give Australians invaluable gift of time
World.content:
NationalHealthcare Alzheimer’s blood test to give Australians invaluable gift of time Rachel Rasker and Kate Aubusson July 30, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australians will soon have access to the first diagnostic blood test for Alzheimer’s disease that researchers say will transform early detection, treatment and potentially prevention. The Therapeutic Goods Administration has approved a blood plasma test known as pTau217, paving the way for a blood test for Alzheimer’s disease to become part of routine GP health checks. John Gethin-Jones with his wife, Felicity Nicholson. John was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease in 2021. World.title: Three dead in house fire in Sydney’s south-west
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWFire Three dead in house fire in Sydney’s south-west Sarah McPhee July 30, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three people have died in a house fire in Sydney’s south-west. Emergency services were called to a fire at the home on Cornelia Street in Wiley Park about 9.45pm on Wednesday. Fire and Rescue NSW (FRNSW) crews extinguished the blaze and found the bodies of three people inside. The victims are yet to be formally identified. The property suffered extensive damage, police said. Officers from Campsie Police Area Command have established a crime scene and are investigating the circumstances surrounding the fire. A report will be prepared for the coroner.



While the cause is still being investigated, earlier this month FRNSW issued a safety reminder about “the most dangerous time of the year for house fires”. As of July 15, FRNSW had already attended 480 residential fires this winter and 2025 this year. FRNSW Commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell encouraged residents to use the service’s free home fire safety visit program which includes smoke alarm checks. “You can also take some simple steps to keep you and your family safe. For example, regularly check your smoke alarm, always keep looking when cooking, keep a fire blanket and extinguisher in your kitchen, keep flammable materials a metre from the heater, and don’t overload power board or power points,” Fewtrell said. “Always check electric and heated blankets before turning them on, and look for frays, scorch marks, exposed wires or controller damage. If anything looks off, bin it.”
